83	## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)
84	
85	- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` — `feat/04a-join`, `spec/04b-generation`.
86	- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `ci:`, plus `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
87	- **Stacks:** bottom pull request targets `main`; each above targets its parent — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. **At most four deep** — which is why stack 04 is two stacks.
88	- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
89	- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.**
90	
91	### Keep child branches linear — it decides how painful the merge is
92	
93	When a parent branch gains commits after its child was cut, **rebase the child onto the parent** (the child is unpushed or yours alone) rather than merging the parent in. Stack 03 learned this the expensive way; see below.
94	
95	### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)
96	
97	**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:
98	
99	```bash
100	gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
101	  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
102	gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
103	```
104	
105	After a parent merges:
106	
107	1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
108	2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
109	   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
110	   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
111	3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
112	4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
113	5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 6. Your environment (checked 2026-09-17)
118	
119	| Tool | Version here | Note |
120	|------|--------------|------|
121	| `gh` | 2.101.0, signed in as `kgang` | Repo `kgang/katalyst`, private |
122	| `uv` | 0.12.15 | |
123	| Python | 3.12.4 | |
124	| Node | 23.3.0 locally | Docker and CI pin **24**. Use `npm ci`, not `npm install`, in a fresh worktree |
125	| Docker | 27.5.1 | |
126	| Playwright | `@playwright/test` in `frontend/` | `npx playwright install chromium` once; `npx playwright test` starts both halves itself |
127	
128	**`.env` in the main checkout is Kent's.** It is git-ignored and holds his real keys. **Never copy it into a worktree, never read it into a brief, never commit it.** `.env.example` is the one agents use.
129	
130	**Hooks:** `.claude/settings.json` runs the `entire` checkpoint tool on session events; its output on `git push` is normal. The git hooks directory has a `commit-msg` hook but **no `pre-commit` hook wired**, so the linters do not run on commit — run `uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .` and `npm run lint` yourself before committing.
131	
132	**Model API key: stack 04b needs one to record cassettes and demos — and Kent must name a spending ceiling first.** Before writing *any* code that calls Claude, load the `claude-api` skill; decision record 0006 holds the verified specifics, and memory is unreliable. Continuous integration never gets a key.
133	
134	**Running the app to look at it:** backend `cd backend && env -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -u FRED_API_KEY uv run uvicorn katalyst.api.main:app --port 80NN`; frontend `KATALYST_API_URL=http://localhost:80NN npm run dev -- --port 51NN --strictPort`. Give each agent its own pair of ports. For screenshots, a throwaway Playwright script **outside the repo** (the session scratchpad) at 1600 × 1000.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## 7. The worktree pattern
139	
140	Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.
141	
142	- **One agent per worktree**, except chapter writers, who may share one **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command** — the coordinator commits for them.
143	- **Disjoint owned files**, listed in the brief. "Touch nothing outside it. If something outside it must change, write why in your report."
144	- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
145	- A resumed agent (send it a message) keeps its context — use that for fix rounds and for sweeps of files it wrote. You can point a resumed agent at a *different* worktree when the fix has to land on another branch.
146	- Remove worktrees after the merge.
147	
148	---
149	
150	## 8. Lessons — read these twice
151	
152	1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
153	2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
154	3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
155	4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
156	5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
157	6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
158	7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
159	8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
160	9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
161	10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
162	11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
163	12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
164	13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
165	15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
166	16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
167	17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
168	18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
169	19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
170	20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
171	21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
172	22. **A green bar here is not a green bar there — and more runs of the same bar is not the answer.** On 2026-09-21 a replay test passed 20 cold runs of 20 on this machine and failed the build's FIRST run: the layout is worked out on its own thread, the build machine's thread was slower, and a claim took a rectangle's place at the origin. Throttling the processor did not reproduce it (that slows the page, not the layout thread); starting the layout thread 900 ms late did, at once. The same day a generated numbers file matched byte for byte across macOS/Arm and Linux/x86-64 — and its own margin test still went red on Linux, because with 280 numbers some value sits on a rounding boundary on some machine at ANY digit count. **Rules:** a test that reads a MOMENT (what stood when X arrived) gets a no-browser twin that injects the bad timing on purpose; a check that compares NUMBERS uses a stated tolerance, never text; and the amount of browser testing follows the three tiers in `PLAN.md`'s working rules — one cold run and the build by default, a repeat bar only for a rare failure that has actually been seen. The "20 cold runs" bar was never a recorded standard; it cost about fifty-two minutes that day (twice in full, a third time to five runs of twenty) and caught nothing one run plus the build would not have.
173	23. **The whole suite, through the queue, before EVERY push; and never edit a worktree while a bar is running in it.** Both broken once on 2026-09-21: a push after two test files let three stale health tests reach the build (#41's first run); an edit under a running bar hot-reloaded a fix into its dev server and voided three runs. Check `plans/.heavy.log` for an open START before touching a worktree.
174	14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.
175	
176	---
177	
178	## 9. The road from here
179	
180	| Stack | What it proves | Plan |
181	|-------|----------------|------|
182	| ~~01 skeleton~~ · ~~02 schema~~ | **Merged.** | history |
183	| ~~03a engine ∥ 03b canvas~~ | **Merged 2026-09-17.** Changing one step re-computes only what is downstream; the map is dense, readable and keyboard-driven | `stack-03a-engine.md`, `stack-03b-canvas.md` (history) |
184	| **04a join + growth ∥ 04b generation** | **Next.** The canvas shows the engine's numbers; the model draws a real map for any hypothesis, streamed step by step; with no key the four examples replay | `stack-04-generation.md` |
185	| 05 thesis | The map compiles to a trade with a derived stop-loss and live market prices | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
186	| 06 probes | Extra modeling effort where the user points it (stretch) | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
187	| 07 presentable (proposed) | README walkthrough, a pastcast self-test, a last accessibility sweep | `roadmap-03-to-06.md` |
188	
189	**This table is history as of 2026-09-21. Start with `PLAN.md`** — stacks 05, 06 and 07 mean different things now, and several of their lines wait on Kent (`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`).

# HANDOFF — take over Katalyst and carry it to a working prototype

You are a fresh agent. You have no memory of how this project got here. This file gives you everything you need to continue. Read it fully, then read `STATUS.md` (newest entry on top), then **`PLAN.md`**.

> **2026-09-21 — the road changed; this file's §2 and §9 describe the project before it did.** Two independent reviews were digested that day. They found three real defects in the engine's arithmetic on the demo map, and that the trade the brief ends in has no code. The road is now: finish stack 04 → **05 sound numbers, then settled shapes** → **06 the trade** → **07 a map you can argue with**. Read **`PLAN.md`** (what, in what order, the definition of done), **`design-after-midpoint-review.md`** (why), and **`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`** (Kent's decisions, R1 onward — binding; he answered every question the same day, and more have been added since). §4–§8 below — how Kent works, git, the environment, worktrees, the lessons — are unchanged and binding. Three working rules are new: **every whole suite, browser run and repeat bar goes through `plans/scripts/heavy.sh`, one at a time — it works across sessions**; **how much browser testing a change needs is decision record 0008's dated amendment (three tiers), not "20 cold runs"**; and **only Hormuz is recorded until the one shape freeze at the end of stack 05, when all four are recorded once (R9).**

---

## 1. The mission

Build **Katalyst**: a take-home prototype for Catalyst (catalyst.app), a seed-stage company that turns a trading idea stated in plain English into live execution.

**What the tool does, in one sentence:** you type an event you think will happen; Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades — and lets you change any step to see how the trades change.

The brief is `ASSIGNMENT.md`. The owner is **Kent Gang**, a solo developer. He cares most about four things, in his words: well structured with Docker and tests; proper code design; rigorously documented decisions; and a beautiful, elegant, delightful interface.

**"Done" means:** a reviewer clones the repo, runs one command, and walks the full flow on all four example events from the brief — type a hypothesis, watch the cause-and-effect map draw itself, change a step, compare the two versions, and end on a thesis card with a derived stop-loss. Tests pass with no API key. Every number on screen can show why. Full checklist: `roadmap-03-to-06.md`, "Definition of done" (the boxes stack 03 ticked are ticked).

---

## 2. What is built, as of 2026-09-17 (end of stack 03)

Stacks 01 (skeleton), 02 (schema), **03a (engine) and 03b (canvas)** are merged to `main`. Every pull request up to #27 is squash-merged (a few numbers were never used), and `main` is green on five checks.

**The one sentence to hold on to:** *the engine computes everything and the canvas draws everything, and they have not met.* The canvas reads the stored example and shows every computed number as an absence with a reason ("no engine yet"). Joining them is the first code of stack 04.

**Documents.** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md`; `ARCHITECTURE.md` (every section says *built* or *planned*); fourteen decision records in `docs/adr/`, **0001–0014, all accepted** — next is **0015**. The spec is a book: `spec/graph/` (4 chapters), `spec/multiverse/` (4: `interventions`, `branches-and-worlds`, `propagation`, `diff`), `spec/workbench/` (6: `color-motion-type`, `tiles-ports-wires`, `layout-and-zoom`, `keyboard-and-access`, `diff-view`, `inspector`, plus the landing page's **worked example cast** and **twelve-line visual review checklist**), and `spec/vocabulary.md` with its **Interface words** table and **Words for a number that is not there**. `spec/generation/` and `spec/thesis/` are landing pages only.

**The server** — `backend/src/katalyst/`:

- `domain/` — the pure core, twelve files, 100% covered, `mypy --strict` clean. Models (`belief`, `proposition`, `link`, `graph`, `intervention`, `branch`, `ids`), `validity.py` (`validate` returns every fault at once; **nineteen codes**: fourteen map faults, four refused edits, one refused comparison), **`patch.py`** (`Assignment`, `apply`, `flatten`, `affected_set`, `introduced_by`), **`propagation.py`** (`World`, `Retraction`, `SeriesState`, `propagate`, `versions_of` — two thousand versions of the map × eight worlds; a supposition is a hard fact until undermined; two seed streams derived per claim), **`diff.py`** (`diff`, `DeltaRow`, `sensitivity` — `shifted` read off the paired difference; rank = size of move × weakest arrow on the best-backed route).
- `engine/` — `ids.py` (the only place an identifier is made) and `worlds.py` (the only place that knows a store or a date). Nothing has ever called a model.

## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)

- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` — `feat/04a-join`, `spec/04b-generation`.
- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `ci:`, plus `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
- **Stacks:** bottom pull request targets `main`; each above targets its parent — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. **At most four deep** — which is why stack 04 is two stacks.
- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.**

### Keep child branches linear — it decides how painful the merge is

When a parent branch gains commits after its child was cut, **rebase the child onto the parent** (the child is unpushed or yours alone) rather than merging the parent in. Stack 03 learned this the expensive way; see below.

### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)

**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:

```bash
gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
```

After a parent merges:

1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.

## 8. Lessons — read these twice

1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
22. **A green bar here is not a green bar there — and more runs of the same bar is not the answer.** On 2026-09-21 a replay test passed 20 cold runs of 20 on this machine and failed the build's FIRST run: the layout is worked out on its own thread, the build machine's thread was slower, and a claim took a rectangle's place at the origin. Throttling the processor did not reproduce it (that slows the page, not the layout thread); starting the layout thread 900 ms late did, at once. The same day a generated numbers file matched byte for byte across macOS/Arm and Linux/x86-64 — and its own margin test still went red on Linux, because with 280 numbers some value sits on a rounding boundary on some machine at ANY digit count. **Rules:** a test that reads a MOMENT (what stood when X arrived) gets a no-browser twin that injects the bad timing on purpose; a check that compares NUMBERS uses a stated tolerance, never text; and the amount of browser testing follows the three tiers in `PLAN.md`'s working rules — one cold run and the build by default, a repeat bar only for a rare failure that has actually been seen. The "20 cold runs" bar was never a recorded standard; it cost about fifty-two minutes that day (twice in full, a third time to five runs of twenty) and caught nothing one run plus the build would not have.
23. **The whole suite, through the queue, before EVERY push; and never edit a worktree while a bar is running in it.** Both broken once on 2026-09-21: a push after two test files let three stale health tests reach the build (#41's first run); an edit under a running bar hot-reloaded a fix into its dev server and voided three runs. Check `plans/.heavy.log` for an open START before touching a worktree.
14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

## A. Needed before stack 05 can start

### A1. What a number on a tile means — and the engine that works it out

**Today:** a claim's number is a snapshot read on its deadline. Three defects follow, all on the Hormuz map today: *This happened* on Brent does not move what caused it; supposing the insurance premium or OPEC+ restraint moves Brent and moves **neither trade at all**; and a claim nobody believes can wipe out your own *Suppose*.

**Proposed:** the number becomes *the chance it happens by its deadline*. Whether each claim happens is solved exactly; when it happens is sampled forward. The arrows keep their lag, shape and half-life. Measured on small adversarial maps: right to four decimal places for *Suppose*. **Not yet right for *This happened*** — the first design was off by up to .12 there, so the stack opens with a one-session spike (three candidates, a kill criterion) before any product code.

*On screen:* every number on the Hormuz map changes once, in one reviewable diff. Supposing OPEC+ restraint finally moves the Brent trade.
*In code:* `propagation.py` and much of `diff.py` rewritten behind a flag, then one flip. Branches, the validator, locality and the wire shapes stay. **8–12 sessions for the stack.**

- **Recommended: yes, opening with the spike.** It is the cheapest way found to honour both of your answers — exact, and the time model kept. `review2`'s own version of "exact" measured at 0.7–8 seconds a range on a 20-claim map; this one at half a millisecond.
- Alternative: repair today's engine in place. Costed: it breaks the range or the locality proof, and leaves the third defect. Not recommended.
- Alternative: do nothing and ship the thesis on today's numbers. The card would then rest on trades that are deaf to half their causes.

### A2. `sustain`: events and states, or events only? — *you must pick; "leave it" is not available*

Once something that happened can never un-happen, a `sustain` arrow and a `trigger` arrow become **identical** (measured: six decimal places). Record 0005 called that pair the best idea in the brainstorm, and you asked to keep it. It survives only in one of these forms:

- **(i) Events and states — recommended.** *The strait reopens* is an event: once it happened, it happened. *The strait stays open to commercial transit through 1 November* is a state: it can stop holding. A `sustain` arrow may only leave a state. **Automatic retraction is deleted** — so *"Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck"* finally leaves both events standing, and the strike lowers the state everything downstream depends on. *On screen:* the strike branch reads *opened (supposed) · stays open through 1 Nov: .08 · Brent below $68: .30* instead of *opened: withdrawn*; the retraction badge and two day-states go. *In code:* mostly deletion on the canvas; a state needs an on-time and an off-time in the engine; the model must say which kind each claim is, so it rides the one shape freeze. **Reverses record 0014, decision A — yours.** About 3 sessions more than (ii).
- **(ii) Events only; a sustained push is two arrows** — one from the event that starts it, an inhibitor from the event that ends it. Same arithmetic, one validity rule, one prompt sentence, no new field. `mode` and the word *sustain* leave the vocabulary. Cheapest sound option.
- Either way the third defect dies, because both delete retraction-by-calendar.

### A3. The path product → the shift, the joint, and the weakest arrow

INV-8 and FR-11 (P0) require *"the multiplied-out likelihood of the path."* Both reviews and three analysts: multiplying along a route is not the chance of anything when claims share a cause (if Y always equals X and both are .5, the product says .25; the truth is .5).

- **Recommended: replace it.** The Verify door says instead: *"Reopening moves the Brent claim by 32 points, from .24 to .56. Every step on the best-backed route goes right in 19% of worlds. The arrow carrying most of that shift is 'reopening → shipping recovers'; delete it and 71% of the effect goes."* (Illustrative numbers — the real ones come from the engine.) Three real quantities, one or two extra solves each. INV-8 becomes *"chains are worked out, not multiplied."* The item that would have moved the product into `domain/` is already dropped.
- Alternative: keep it, labelled as what it is. It stays a number that is not a probability, on the screen that answers the brief's first use case.

### A4. The spread changes the scripted strike — look, then say yes or overturn

With the provenance spread on (your rule, record 0014), the strike branch shows **two ranked rows instead of three**. Brent (B) and *talks resume* (N1) read `unchanged`. | 05-2 | `test/05-oracles` | **Two oracles.** `test_the_elimination_is_exact` (`1e-9`, over the core's own tables). `test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time` (the measured tolerance; forbidden the core's tables; *Suppose* and *This happened*; an impulse and a diamond). Failing cases marked expected-to-fail, strictly, by name. Reverse `test_an_observation_moves_a_cause_even_when_no_arrow_pushes` into a test of invariance. The locality oracle restated as "cut off from the evidence ⇒ bit for bit" |
| 05-3 | `feat/05-exact-core`, then **the flip** as its own pull request | The new core beside the old, behind a flag, default unchanged; both oracles run against both. **Then the flip, alone:** default changes; Hormuz re-derived *and its six honest fixture fixes made here* (this lane owns `fixtures/hormuz.py`); the numbers file regenerated — its diff is the review; `diff.py` moved over; the sampler, the noise correction, version weights and `moved_only_by_reweighting` deleted; the browser's two readers and the "8 worlds under each" sentence corrected |
| 05-4 | `feat/05-verdict` · `feat/05-events` — two pull requests, either order | The Verify door's product replaced by **shift · joint · weakest arrow** (R3; INV-8 and FR-11 rewritten). **Events and states** (R2), with retraction and its badge deleted; `Observe` gains a date |
| 05-5 | `feat/05-shape-freeze` — **last, so it is paid for once** | Every change to what we ask the model for, together: one number per arrow that means one thing, the claim's own number restated as its no-cause chance, `persistence: event | state` (R2), `quote` and `role` on a source, `what_would_change_my_mind`, `kind` required (the held branch), `move` as a range, the *what would stop this* and *what would falsify this* sentences, a real venue contract where one exists, no search on the first call and five at once, base rates only where a reference class can exist. **The coordinator records the cassettes and then ALL FOUR examples on the branch — Hormuz, midterms, export-controls, photonics, in parallel, each with its own $15 stop and its own line-buffered log (R9: ~45 min, ~$20) — and the new files are committed in the same pull request**, so `main` is never green over a stale recording. Three fingerprint-free items may go earlier, with 05-2: a refusal says *our rules* or *the answer*; dropped sources and base rates reach the wire; one clause on PRD anti-pattern 2 |

### Stack 06 — the trade

*Proves: a reader with a position is told the chance of being stopped first, which events take them out, what is priced in — and leaves with a thesis that says what it does not know.*

| # | Pull request | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| 06-0 | docs | Records **0018** (like with like: an edge comes from the world with no supposition in force), **0019** (a stop is a price the reader owns; amends INV-14, FR-22, FR-23, FR-24; reverses PRD anti-pattern 11), **0020** (quotes recorded first; FRED is an observation; amends 0010). One short `spec/thesis/` chapter per idea — the shape and its reasons, not class bodies |
| 06-1 | `feat/06-quote` | `Quote`, the recorded loader and its committed file, opt-in live Polymarket; `priced()`, `Edge`, `NotComparable`, the break-even, the mixture term by term. *May run while 05-3 is in flight — it needs only* Suppose*, which is exact* |
| 06-2 | `feat/06-position` — *after the flip and the freeze* | `Draws`, **fed by the same forward sample the engine uses for observations**; daily paths; `Position`; first touch; *what takes you out* by lift; the two-way sweep and the watchlist; sizing from the reader's own risk budget. The record says which distribution the event times came from |
| 06-3 | `feat/06-card` | The card; the export with its refusals as data; the shock row; ranked tradeable endings; a price ending as a first-class trade (position, first touch, break-even, *edge not calculable*) so **the walk runs on one map, the recorded one**; the not-advice line |
| 06-4 | `feat/06-dock` | The pinned YOUR TRADE strip; the change list run on a second question; the outcome strip on the tradeable tile (tiles first collapse their two empty belief columns); guess-before-reveal on an ending; *Run details* (R16); **the formatter moves from `domain/` to the browser, then likelihoods print as `36%` and moves as `8.1 pts`** (R17) |

### Stack 07 — a map you can argue with, shown to be good

*Proves: the reader can push back on any step; and we can say, with a sheet of paper, how good the maps are.*

Verify becomes a real search (a backward frontier from the destination, on machinery that exists) · *expand this claim* · *challenge this arrow* (the honest form of the role-played expert) · *add an event* proven live · *spend here* given a place on screen (already computed) · seven counting columns on the scorecard · **a hand rubric**: ten maps, six questions, graded by a person, never by a model · README opens with a 90-second capture then a five-minute walkthrough · a test that `ARCHITECTURE.md`'s built/planned markers are true · fetching a cited page to check its quote · **a finished generation served back by its id from the file a kept run already is** (R12 — FR-31 shrunk: one format, one loader, no database) · one page, *what I would do next*.

---

## NOT DOING — see `design-after-midpoint-review.md` §7

The path product · `refine`, feedback loops, the simulation probe · the pastcast · a one-call skeleton · an ensemble · expected shortfall, ruin, automatic sizing · a fifth kind of claim · *Release* · exact inference over event times as the default · freezing the spec or merging the root documents · a slider, small multiples, screenshot baselines.

---

## Definition of done — the whole prototype

**THE WALK — a stranger, a fresh clone, no key, no typing, on ONE map: the recorded Hormuz.** This is the six-step end-to-end test, and the test *is* this list.

- [ ] **0. It starts.** `docker compose up`, open the browser. Under five minutes.
- [ ] **1. A map they did not build.** It draws itself through the same stream and canvas a live run uses; every refusal on screen in the validator's words; the receipt says what it cost. *(after stack 04)*
- [ ] **2. Is this chain reasonable?** The shift the opening makes to Brent, from what base, with the weakest arrow named — or an honest *no supported route*. Every number one click from its reason, its sources, and how often such things have happened. *(05, 07)*
- [ ] **3. …but Iran is struck.** Added **with the mouse**, on a branch. Only what is downstream moves — *and everything downstream does*; both events stand; nothing re-positions; the ranked change list leads the panel. *(04 polish, 05)*
- [ ] **4. What takes me out.** A short with a stop and a target: the chance of each first, and which events are over-represented where the stop is hit. *(06)*
- [ ] **5. What else can I trade.** Ranked, with what is priced in and what the model thinks kept apart. *(06)*
- [ ] **6. A thesis to carry away.** What carries it, what takes you out, what to watch, what it does not know — exported, stamped with map, branch and seed. *(06)*
- [ ] The walk needs no narration and shows no endpoint name, prompt fingerprint or build number; it is a required check at three window sizes and **cannot skip**.
- [ ] **All four of the brief's examples open from the launchpad** *(FR-3, P0 — recorded together at stack 05's freeze, R9)*.

**IT IS HONEST** — [x] two significant figures with a range *(03)* · [x] *Suppose* and *This happened* are two buttons, vocabulary word for word *(03)* · [x] three beliefs, never merged *(03)* · [x] an overridden supposition says so *(03; replaced if record 0017 is accepted)* · [ ] **two oracles agree with every displayed number on small maps, to a tolerance written in the record** · [ ] no document carries an engine-computed number the generated file does not own · [ ] no screen labels a quantity as something it is not.

**IT IS WELL BUILT** — [x] the build is green with no key *(03)* · [x] `domain/` imports nothing from other layers *(03)* · [x] types generated; stale fails the build *(03)* · [ ] `domain/` coverage gated, not just reported · [ ] every invariant has a named test — **INV-10 by a named refusal, and this list says so** · [ ] `ARCHITECTURE.md`'s markers checked by a test · [ ] **every decision — including every requirement cut — has an accepted record**.

**IT IS BEAUTIFUL** — [ ] Kent has looked and nothing triggers the template veto · [x] no dialogs, spinners, hairball, colour-only meaning *(03)* · [x] keyboard end to end; reduced motion *(03)* · [ ] the visual checklist, cited by name, a *yes* on every line at three window sizes.

---

## Working rules (what changed on 2026-09-21)

- **One queue for heavy work** — `plans/scripts/heavy.sh`; its log is `plans/.heavy.log`. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue, at most twice. Playwright, repeat bars and anything paid: the coordinator only.
- **One agent per file-owning area; never two agents writing prose about one subject; never two pull requests open on one file.** `fixtures/hormuz.py` belongs to the engine lane; the Inspector, panel and tile to one browser agent at a time. Read-only analysts and reviewers in parallel are fine.
- **A read-only Opus review before every pull request — and one adversarial pass over every plan.** The first has found a must-fix on every branch of this stack; the second found ten in the first draft of this one.
- **A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion.**
- **How much browser testing a change needs — three tiers, not "20 cold runs".** (Kent asked on 2026-09-21 where the 20 came from: **nowhere in the committed repo** — no record, no chapter, no Makefile target; it was a coordinator's habit written only in these notes, grown out of five "flaky" tests that were real defects. Measured the same day: the 23-minute bar ran twice in full and a third time to five runs of twenty — 51.9 minutes by the queue's log (an earlier note here said ~70: that was 3 × 23, not the measurement) — and caught nothing one run plus CI would not have — the panel-wording mismatch failed 17 of 17; the layout race passed 20 of 20 locally and failed CI's first run.) **Tier 1 — every browser pull request:** ONE cold run of all end-to-end tests locally (~70 s) and the build, which is a second, slower, different machine on purpose. **Tier 2 — a change to timing-sensitive code** (canvas, layout, stream, growth, focus): tier 1, plus a NO-BROWSER test that injects the adverse timing (a late layout answer, a dropped size notification) — that is what pinned both real races of 2026-09-21, in milliseconds. **Tier 3 — a repeat bar only when a specific rare failure has been SEEN:** that one test, not the suite, sized to the rate (about 3k clean runs to be 95% sure a 1-in-k fault is gone). **Kent accepted both proposals and both are on `main` (#46, `26149d7`): record 0008 carries the tiers as a dated amendment — it is the rule, this bullet is its summary — and one cold run takes about 27 s instead of 69** (the suite runs side by side; the replay's pace is ONE setting, `KATALYST_REPLAY_PACE`, 0.4 s in the end-to-end run; `e2e/lateLayout.spec.ts` keeps the late-layout race as a permanent check with no hook in product code; `e2e/theSuite.ts` fails any test that meets the browser's *ResizeObserver loop* message without saying it expects one). Measured on the way: at 0.15 s a replayed event, two events folded into one render — which exposed an assertion (one render per claim) the product never promised; the test now asserts what IS promised.
- **Pay once.** Anything that moves the prompt fingerprint — or the request body the cassettes match on — is batched, recorded on the branch, and committed with the code. **Hormuz only until stack 05's freeze; then all four, once (R9).** `make eval` runs `ONLY=hormuz` until then.
- **Development runs on `claude-sonnet-5` at `medium` effort** *(Kent, R34, 2026-09-21)*: `make eval` and the live route ask for `medium`; **only the recorder sends nothing.** `make eval EFFORT=as-recorded` scores the recordings' effort. The recorder, the cassettes and `run-demo` are untouched until the freeze (R5).
- **Stacks two deep** *(Kent, R13 — in force; the dated amendment to record 0009 rides in the next docs pull request)*: a docs bottom and one code pull request on it; otherwise straight onto `main`, one at a time per lane.
- **Keep the evidence.** An analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
- **Spend:** about $27–29 of $500 on 2026-09-21; nothing spent in this session.

1	/**
2	 * Which boxes the map draws, and where.
3	 *
4	 * The layout runs on a background thread and **answers later**, so at every
5	 * moment a map is growing there are boxes nobody has found a place for yet. This
6	 * file is the one answer to what happens to them, written apart from the canvas
7	 * so that it can be read, and checked, without a browser.
8	 *
9	 * On this machine the window is shorter than a frame and nobody ever sees it. On
10	 * a slower one it is long enough to read, and what is drawn in it is the whole of
11	 * what this file is about.
12	 */
13	
14	import type { Position } from "./elkGraph";
15	import type { MapNode } from "./toFlow";
16	
17	/** Where the map starts. The only place this file ever puts a box itself. */
18	export const THE_ORIGIN: Position = { x: 0, y: 0 };
19	
20	/** One box, and the place it is drawn at. */
21	export type PlacedBox = MapNode & { position: Position };
22	
23	/** What the map has on the glass. */
24	export interface OnTheGlass {
25	  /** Every box that is drawn, each with the place it is drawn at. */
26	  readonly boxes: readonly PlacedBox[];
27	  /**
28	   * The reserved rectangles among them, with their places.
29	   *
30	   * Handed back so that the next answer can be worked out from this one: a
31	   * rectangle comes down when the claim it was holding a place for is drawn, and
32	   * that cannot be decided without knowing which rectangles were standing.
33	   */
34	  readonly rectangles: readonly PlacedBox[];
35	}
36	
37	/** Is this box a reserved rectangle rather than a claim? */
38	function isRectangle(box: MapNode): boolean {
39	  return box.type === "skeleton";
40	}
41	
42	/**
43	 * Work out what the map draws.
44	 *
45	 * Three rules, which are one rule seen from three sides: **the map draws a box
46	 * where the layout put it, and a reserved rectangle keeps saying where the next
47	 * claim goes until that claim is drawn.**
48	 *
49	 * **A box is drawn where the layout put it, and nowhere else.** A box the layout
50	 * has not placed has no place, and drawing it at the map's origin gives it one
51	 * the layout never agreed to — so it appears at the origin and then hops to
52	 * wherever the layout actually wanted it, on the one screen whose whole promise
53	 * is that nothing already drawn ever moves (INV-workbench.64).
54	 *
55	 * **A reserved rectangle stands until the claim it was holding a place for is on
56	 * the glass** — not until the event carrying that claim arrived. Those are
57	 * different moments, and everything between them is a map with a claim on its
58	 * way and no rectangle anywhere: a growing map that has stopped saying where it
59	 * is going. It is not a corner case. A generated map's frontier is usually one
60	 * claim wide, so it turns over completely every few proposals, and each turnover
61	 * is one of these moments. The rectangle goes the instant the map is whole
62	 * again, and a rectangle whose claim closed with nothing coming after it — a
63	 * third refusal, a broken run, the likelihoods landing — goes at once, because
64	 * then nothing on the map is waiting for a place.
65	 *
66	 * **And before the layout has answered anything at all, the map holds the first
67	 * rectangle at the origin itself.** The origin is nobody's place then: there is
68	 * nothing to be drawn on top of, and a generation's first paint may not be an
69	 * empty stage (INV-workbench.61 — a rectangle carrying the reader's own sentence
70	 * is on screen before the first proposal comes back). The box that takes it is a
71	 * rectangle and never a claim.
72	 *
73	 * @param boxes Every box the map holds, in reading order.
74	 * @param places Where the layout has said each box goes. Empty until it answers.
75	 * @param standing The rectangles this returned last time it was asked, so the
76	 *   ones still holding a place can go on holding it.
77	 */
78	export function whatIsOnTheGlass(
79	  boxes: readonly MapNode[],
80	  places: ReadonlyMap<string, Position>,
81	  standing: readonly PlacedBox[],
82	): OnTheGlass {
83	  const drawn: PlacedBox[] = [];
84	  let somethingHasNowhereToGo = false;
85	  for (const box of boxes) {
86	    const at = places.get(box.id);
87	    if (at === undefined) {
88	      somethingHasNowhereToGo = true;
89	      continue;
90	    }
91	    drawn.push({ ...box, position: at });
92	  }
93	  if (!somethingHasNowhereToGo) {
94	    return { boxes: drawn, rectangles: drawn.filter(isRectangle) };
95	  }
96	
97	  // Something on the map is waiting for a place, so every rectangle that was
98	  // standing goes on standing: each of them is holding the place of a claim that
99	  // is on its way and not yet drawn. They were placed in the arrangement that is
100	  // still on the glass, so none of them can land on anything.
101	  const alreadyDrawn = new Set(drawn.map((box) => box.id));
102	  const held = standing.filter((box) => !alreadyDrawn.has(box.id));
103	
104	  // Nothing has ever been placed, and nothing is being held. This is a
105	  // generation's first paint: the map puts its own first rectangle at the origin
106	  // rather than show an empty stage. A map with no rectangles at all — every
107	  // finished map — waits, because it has nothing to say yet and no reason to
108	  // guess where it would go.
109	  const first =
110	    drawn.length === 0 && held.length === 0
111	      ? boxes
112	          .filter(isRectangle)
113	          .slice(0, 1)
114	          .map((box) => ({ ...box, position: THE_ORIGIN }))
115	      : [];
116	
117	  const all = [...drawn, ...held, ...first];
118	  return { boxes: all, rectangles: all.filter(isRectangle) };
119	}

1	/**
2	 * Turning a world into the tiles and wires the canvas draws.
3	 *
4	 * One function, no arithmetic, and nothing invented: every tile below stands
5	 * for a claim the server sent, every wire for an arrow the server sent, and the
6	 * only judgement made here is which tiles there is room to draw.
7	 */
8	
9	import type { Node } from "@xyflow/react";
10	import type { ClaimView, WorldView } from "../world";
11	import { NOT_ON_THIS_MAP } from "../world/naming";
12	import type { LayoutEdge, LayoutTile } from "./elkGraph";
13	import { TILE_MIN_HEIGHT, TILE_WIDTH, tileHeight } from "./geometry";
14	import { assignLayers, capLayers } from "./layers";
15	import { portsForAWire, portsOf } from "./ports";
16	import type { CausalEdge } from "./wires/CausalWire";
17	
18	/** A tile standing for one claim. */
19	export type ClaimNode = Node<
20	  { claim: ClaimView; isHypothesis: boolean; versions?: number; height: number },
21	  "claim"
22	>;
23	
24	/** A tile standing for the claims a column had no room for. */
25	export type OverflowNode = Node<{ count: number }, "overflow">;
26	
27	/** A rectangle held open where a claim is about to arrive. Never a claim. */
28	export type SkeletonNode = Node<{ words: string }, "skeleton">;
29	
30	/** Everything the canvas draws as a box. */
31	export type MapNode = ClaimNode | OverflowNode | SkeletonNode;
32	
33	/**
34	 * One rectangle the map is holding open, reduced to what drawing one needs.
35	 *
36	 * Stated here rather than imported from the reducer that produces them, so that
37	 * the picture depends on no part of the machinery that reads a stream: this is
38	 * the whole of what the canvas needs to know about a thing that is not a claim.
39	 */
40	export interface ReservedBox {
41	  /** The rectangle's name. A box's name, never a claim's. */
42	  readonly id: string;
43	  /** The one line it carries. */
44	  readonly words: string;
45	  /** The open claim it hangs off, so the layout puts it one column further right. */
46	  readonly after: string | null;
47	}
48	
49	/**
50	 * A wire, carrying everything it needs to say its five things at once.
51	 *
52	 * How it is routed is filled in by the canvas rather than here: a wire that has
53	 * to skip a column needs to know where the other tiles ended up, and only the
54	 * canvas knows that.
55	 */
56	export type MapEdge = CausalEdge;
57	
58	/** What the canvas needs in order to draw a world. */
59	export interface MapDrawing {
60	  /** The tiles, without positions — those come from the layout. */
61	  readonly nodes: readonly MapNode[];
62	  /** The wires, as they will be drawn. */
63	  readonly edges: readonly MapEdge[];
64	  /**
65	   * Every tile with the height it will be drawn at, which is the height the
66	   * layout reserves for it. One number, worked out once, used by both.
67	   */
68	  readonly tiles: readonly LayoutTile[];
69	  /**
70	   * The arrows the layout gets a look at.
71	   *
72	   * Not the same list as the wires. Feedback arrows are left out, because a
73	   * left-to-right order cannot be worked out from a map with a loop in it, and
74	   * an arrow that stands in for collapsed tiles is put in, so the collapsed tile
75	   * lands in the column it belongs to.
76	   */
77	  readonly layoutEdges: readonly LayoutEdge[];
78	}
79	
80	/**
81	 * What the tile standing in for a column's collapsed claims is called.
82	 *
83	 * The canvas reads the column back out of it, so that activating one of those
84	 * tiles can open the outline filtered to that column — the claims behind it
85	 * already have items there, and the tile only has to point at them.
86	 */
87	export const OVERFLOW_PREFIX = "more-in-column-";
88	
89	/** The identifier of the tile standing in for a column's collapsed claims. */
90	function overflowId(layer: number): string {
91	  return `${OVERFLOW_PREFIX}${layer}`;
92	}
93	
94	/**
95	 * What every reserved rectangle's name starts with.
96	 *
97	 * It is how the canvas tells a box from a claim without asking the reducer:
98	 * nothing may be selected, focused or asked about under one of these names,
99	 * because there is nothing there yet.
100	 */
101	export const RESERVED_PREFIX = "skeleton:";
102	
103	/**
104	 * Work out the tiles, the wires, and what the layout gets to see.
105	 *
106	 * @param world The world as the source handed it over.
107	 * @param heights How tall each tile is to be drawn, when something outside knows
108	 *   better than this claim alone does. A diff draws two worlds in one coordinate
109	 *   space, and a claim can need more room in one of them than in the other — it
110	 *   grows badges when an edit touched it — so the box is reserved for the taller
111	 *   of the two and neither painting moves anything. Left out, each tile is as
112	 *   tall as its own content.
113	 * @param reserved The rectangles being held open at the growing edge of a map
114	 *   that is still being built. Empty on every finished map. Each one is drawn at
115	 *   a tile's floor height and is pulled into the column after the claim it hangs
116	 *   off by an arrow the layout sees and nobody draws — the same trick the tile
117	 *   standing in for a full column already uses.
118	 */
119	export function toFlow(
120	  world: WorldView,
121	  heights?: ReadonlyMap<string, number>,
122	  reserved: readonly ReservedBox[] = [],
123	): MapDrawing {
124	  const ids = world.claims.map((claim) => claim.id);
125	  const { shown, overflows } = capLayers(assignLayers(ids, world.links));
126	  const drawn = new Set(shown.map((one) => one.id));
127	  const byId = new Map(world.claims.map((claim) => [claim.id, claim]));
128	
129	  const nodes: MapNode[] = [];
130	  for (const placed of shown) {
131	    const claim = byId.get(placed.id);
132	    if (claim === undefined) {
133	      continue;
134	    }
135	    nodes.push({
136	      id: claim.id,
137	      type: "claim",
138	      position: { x: 0, y: 0 },
139	      draggable: false,
140	      data: {
141	        claim,
142	        isHypothesis: claim.id === world.hypothesisId,
143	        versions: world.versions,
144	        height: heights?.get(claim.id) ?? tileHeight(claim),
145	      },
146	    });
147	  }
148	  for (const overflow of overflows) {
149	    nodes.push({
150	      id: overflowId(overflow.layer),
151	      type: "overflow",
152	      position: { x: 0, y: 0 },
153	      draggable: false,
154	      data: { count: overflow.count },
155	    });
156	  }
157	
158	  // Only arrows between two tiles that are actually drawn become wires. An
159	  // arrow into a collapsed claim has nowhere to land, and the collapsed tile
160	  // says in words that those claims are still on the map.
161	  const claimWords = new Map(world.claims.map((claim) => [claim.id, claim.claim]));
162	  const edges: MapEdge[] = world.links
163	    .filter((link) => drawn.has(link.source) && drawn.has(link.target))
164	    .map((link) => {
165	      const { source, target } = portsForAWire(link.mode);
166	      return {
167	        id: link.id,
168	        source: link.source,
169	        target: link.target,
170	        sourceHandle: source,
171	        targetHandle: target,
172	        // One kind of wire, drawn by us. How it gets from one end to the other
173	        // is worked out by the canvas, which is the only thing that knows where
174	        // the other tiles ended up.
175	        type: "causal" as const,
176	        // What a reader who never sees the picture hears instead. Everything
177	        // the stroke says, said in words.
178	        ariaLabel:
179	          `arrow from ${claimWords.get(link.source) ?? NOT_ON_THIS_MAP} ` +
180	          `to ${claimWords.get(link.target) ?? NOT_ON_THIS_MAP}`,
181	        data: {
182	          shape: link.shape,
183	          strength: link.strength,
184	          mode: link.mode,
185	          lag: link.lag,
186	          reflexive: link.reflexive,
187	          provenance: link.provenance,
188	          conditional: link.conditional,
189	        },
190	      };
191	    });
192	
193	  // What the layout sees. Feedback arrows are set aside: an arrow that points
194	  // backwards cannot help decide what comes first, and leaving it in would make
195	  // the map a loop with no beginning.
196	  const layoutEdges: LayoutEdge[] = world.links
197	    .filter((link) => !link.reflexive && drawn.has(link.source) && drawn.has(link.target))
198	    .map((link) => ({ id: link.id, source: link.source, target: link.target }));
199	
200	  // The collapsed tile is pulled into the right column by the same arrows that
201	  // would have reached the claims it stands for. These are never drawn.
202	  for (const overflow of overflows) {
203	    const hidden = new Set(overflow.hidden);
204	    const causes = new Set(
205	      world.links
206	        .filter((link) => !link.reflexive && hidden.has(link.target) && drawn.has(link.source))
207	        .map((link) => link.source),
208	    );
209	    for (const cause of causes) {
210	      layoutEdges.push({
211	        id: `standing-in:${cause}->${overflowId(overflow.layer)}`,
212	        source: cause,
213	        target: overflowId(overflow.layer),
214	      });
215	    }
216	  }
217	
218	  // The rectangles held open at the growing edge. They are boxes, not claims:
219	  // they never join `world.claims`, never reach the network, and carry nothing a
220	  // reader could mistake for a reading. Each is pulled into the column after the
221	  // claim it hangs off by an arrow the layout sees and nobody draws.
222	  for (const box of reserved) {
223	    nodes.push({
224	      id: box.id,
225	      type: "skeleton",
226	      position: { x: 0, y: 0 },
227	      draggable: false,
228	      // A rectangle is not a thing you can be on or ask about: it stands for a
229	      // claim that does not exist yet, and there is nothing to read out.
230	      selectable: false,
231	      focusable: false,
232	      data: { words: box.words },
233	    });
234	    if (box.after !== null && drawn.has(box.after)) {
235	      layoutEdges.push({
236	        id: `holding-open:${box.after}->${box.id}`,
237	        source: box.after,
238	        target: box.id,
239	      });
240	    }
241	  }
242	
243	  // **Every tile is told how big it is and where its ports are, and the layout,
244	  // the tile and the drawing library are all told the same numbers.**
245	  //
246	  // A tile's box is not something to be discovered: it is 280 pixels wide
247	  // (`TILE_WIDTH`) and exactly as tall as the height this file worked out from
248	  // the claim, and the components draw themselves at precisely that size. The
249	  // layout engine has always been told. The drawing library was not — it was
250	  // left to measure each tile with a `ResizeObserver`, and **it draws nothing
251	  // it has not measured**: a node with no size is rendered `visibility:
252	  // hidden`, and a wire with no measured port at either end is not rendered at
253	  // all.
254	  //
255	  // That is a promise the browser does not keep. When too many size
256	  // observations fall due in one frame the browser abandons the rest of them —
257	  // *"a ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications"* — and an
258	  // abandoned one is never delivered. A tile whose box then never changes size
259	  // again is never observed again, so it stays invisible for the life of the
260	  // page, and its arrows stay off the glass for the life of the page: the map
261	  // holds its claims, in their places, and says nothing about how they are
262	  // joined. Both halves are reachable today, on a busy machine, on the stored
263	  // example.
264	  //
265	  // Saying it is not a guess and not a duplicate: it is the one set of numbers,
266	  // handed to every thing that needs them, from the one place that worked them
267	  // out. A port's box comes from `ports.ts`, which is also what the tile writes
268	  // onto the element it draws — so what is declared here is what the browser
269	  // would have measured, and the library correcting itself afterwards from its
270	  // own measurement changes nothing. Nothing downstream reads any of it back.
271	  //
272	  // **A reserved rectangle says how big it is too**, and it is the box that
273	  // needs saying most: it stands where a claim is about to arrive, so it is on
274	  // screen at the exact moment the page is busiest and the browser is likeliest
275	  // to drop an observation — and a rectangle nobody can see is a growing edge
276	  // that has stopped saying where the map is going. It declares no port: nothing
277	  // is at the end of an arrow until the claim itself arrives.
278	  const tiles: LayoutTile[] = [];
279	  const sized = nodes.map((node) => {
280	    const height = node.type === "claim" ? node.data.height : TILE_MIN_HEIGHT;
281	    tiles.push({ id: node.id, height });
282	    const box = { ...node, initialWidth: TILE_WIDTH, initialHeight: height };
283	    // Only a claim's tile has ports, because only a claim is ever at the end of
284	    // an arrow. The tile standing in for a column's collapsed claims has none,
285	    // and neither has a rectangle held open where a claim is about to arrive:
286	    // both are told none rather than told the wrong ones.
287	    return node.type === "claim" ? { ...box, handles: portsOf(height) } : box;
288	  }) as MapNode[];
289	
290	  return { nodes: sized, edges, layoutEdges, tiles };
291	}
