1	# Layout and zoom — a map that never becomes a hairball
2	
3	## Purpose
4	
5	A causal map drawn by a physics simulation is a hairball: every run looks different, nothing lines up, and crossings hide the one arrow you were looking for. This chapter makes the map **arrive already arranged** — left to right, cause before effect, one claim per box, in an order that does not change under your feet. You open the Hormuz map and it is legible in the first second, without touching anything. You zoom out and the tiles turn into summaries rather than into unreadable specks. You add a claim, or open a branch, and the tile you were reading stays where your eye left it.
6	
7	Three chapters sit next to this one and are not repeated here: `tiles-ports-wires.md` says what is inside a tile and how a wire is drawn, `color-motion-type.md` carries the colour law and the motion budget, and `diff-view.md` says how two worlds are painted once they share a coordinate space. This chapter owns only **where things go and how big they are**.
8	
9	## Data model
10	
11	### The layout options — the whole list, and nothing else
12	
13	The automatic layout is ELK, an open-source graph-layout engine compiled to JavaScript. Five options, and no others:
14	
15	```ts
16	const ELK_OPTIONS = {
17	  "elk.algorithm": "layered",
18	  "elk.direction": "RIGHT",
19	  "elk.layered.nodePlacement.strategy": "NETWORK_SIMPLEX",
20	  "elk.layered.crossingMinimization.semiInteractive": "true",
21	  "elk.layered.spacing.nodeNodeBetweenLayers": "120",
22	} as const;
23	```
24	
25	These five are set once, for the whole graph. One further ELK property, `elk.position`, is set **per tile** rather than here — it is how an already-placed tile says where it wants to stay (B3) — so "no others" stays true of this list.
26	
27	In plain words:
28	
29	ELK's word is *layer*; the code and the test names use it. On screen and in this chapter the word is **column**, because that is what a reader sees.
30	
31	| Option | What it buys |
32	|---|---|
33	| `layered` | Claims are assigned to columns; every arrow points from a lower column to a higher one. This is what makes cause-before-effect a fact of the picture rather than a hope |
34	| `direction: RIGHT` | The columns run left to right. Time and causality read the way English reads |
35	| `nodePlacement.strategy: NETWORK_SIMPLEX` | Decides each tile's position **within** its column so that wires come out as straight as possible. Straight wires are short wires; short wires cross less |
36	| `crossingMinimization.semiInteractive: true` | When ordering a column, the crossing minimiser treats a tile's existing position as where that tile *wants* to sit. This is the switch that makes pinning work at all |
37	| `spacing.nodeNodeBetweenLayers: 120` | 120 pixels of gutter between one column and the next — enough room for a midpoint chip and an origin mark on the wire without the chip touching a tile |
38	
39	One thing the list does not say out loud: **which column a claim lands in** is decided by ELK's *layering* strategy, which is a separate setting from `nodePlacement.strategy` above. We do not set it, so it is ELK's default — also network simplex — which picks the column assignment with the smallest total arrow length. The worked examples below are that assignment, and they are the unique minimum, so the picture is reproducible rather than merely likely.
40	
41	### The worker seam
42	
43	Decision record 0007 measures ELK at 50–150 milliseconds on sixty tiles. On the main thread that is a frozen page, a dropped keystroke, and a scroll that stutters. So it runs in a **Web Worker** — a second browser thread with no access to the page — and the main thread only posts and listens. (That upper figure is already over NFR-7's budget; see B9 and Open questions.)
44	
45	```ts
46	/** What the page sends the layout worker. */
47	interface LayoutRequest {
48	  /** Every tile to place. Width is always 280. Height varies per tile: content-fit,
49	   *  clamped to 152–320 pixels, on the 8-pixel grid, **computed from the content** and
50	   *  never measured off the screen — so layout stays a pure function of the map
51	   *  (`tiles-ports-wires.md` owns the height rule, and the ceiling's reason). */
52	  tiles: { id: string; width: 280; height: number; pinnedAt?: { x: number; y: number } }[];
53	  /** Every wire. `reflexive` wires are marked here and set aside before layering. */
54	  wires: { id: string; from: string; to: string; reflexive: boolean }[];
55	}
56	
57	/** One coordinate per tile, plus which column it landed in and where in that column.
58	 *  This is the type other chapters read: `diff-view.md` takes a `positions: PositionMap`
59	 *  and paints two worlds into it. */
60	type PositionMap = Record<string, { x: number; y: number; layer: number; orderInLayer: number }>;
61	
62	/** What comes back. */
63	interface LayoutResult {
64	  tiles: PositionMap;
65	  /** For each column that overflowed seven tiles, the claims behind its "+n more" tile. */
66	  collapsed: Record<number, string[]>;
67	  /** How long ELK took. NFR-7's 100-millisecond budget is measured, not hoped for. */
68	  elapsedMs: number;
69	}
70	```
71	
72	The page never imports ELK. The worker file is the only place `elkjs` appears in `frontend/src/`, and a test says so.
73	
74	### What a tile tells the layout
75	
76	```ts
77	interface TileLayoutProps {
78	  /** Set by the zoom watcher, never by the tile itself. */
79	  detail: "summary" | "full";
80	  /** Always false, on every tile, forever in this stack. */
81	  draggable: false;
82	  /** Drives `setCenter` and the focus ring. One tile at a time. */
83	  focused: boolean;
84	}
85	```
86	
87	### Tokens this chapter reads
88	
89	From `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css`: `--space-1` (8 px, the grid everything sits on), `--space-2` (16 px), `--hairline` (the 1-pixel border at 10% of the text colour), `--surface` and `--surface-raised`, `--focus` (the keyboard ring), and the type scale `--text-sm` / `--text-md` / `--text-lg` (13 / 15 / 22 px).
90	
91	**Two numbers in this chapter are not tokens yet:** the 280-pixel tile width and the 120-pixel gutter between columns. See Open questions.
92	
93	## Behaviour
94	
95	Worked on the Hormuz map (the cast is in [`README.md`](README.md)). This chapter uses all seven base claims — H, C, B, R, M1, M2, N1 — the reflexive arrow `B → R`, and the claim **S** that the strike branch adds.
96	
97	### B1 — The base map lands in four columns
98	
99	Reflexive arrows are set aside before columns are assigned (B4). What is left is seven claims and seven arrows, and the minimum-total-length assignment is:
100	
101	| Column | Tiles |
102	|---|---|
103	| 0 | H |
104	| 1 | C · N1 · R |
105	| 2 | B |
106	| 3 | M1 · M2 |
107	
108	R sits in column 1, tight against B, because its only live arrow is `R → B`. Nothing pulls it further left, and network simplex does not leave a wire longer than it has to be.
109	
110	The widest column holds three tiles. The cap is seven, so nothing collapses (B5).
111	
112	### B2 — Opening the map frames it once
113	
114	On the first layout of a map, and only then, `fitView` frames the whole thing. Every layout after that calls `setCenter` on the focused tile instead, so the tile you were reading stays under your eye.
115	
116	Losing your place after a re-layout is anti-pattern 8 in `docs/research/03-ui-ux-directions.md`.
117	
118	### B3 — A later tile does not reshuffle an earlier column
119	
120	Every tile that already has a place is handed back to ELK carrying `elk.position`. With `crossingMinimization.semiInteractive` on, the crossing minimiser treats that as where the tile wants to sit and orders the column around it.
121	
122	So when a claim arrives downstream of what is already drawn — a second market ending hanging off B, say — M1 and M2 keep their exact coordinates and the newcomer finds a gap. Nothing above it moves. This is what keeps streaming growth calm (`streaming-growth.md`, stack 04) and what keeps a branch from scrambling the map you were reading.
123	
124	**Pinning holds positions inside a column. It does not hold column assignment** — see B7 and Open questions.
125	
126	### B4 — The reflexive arrow is set aside, then drawn as a loop
127	
128	`B → R` is the one feedback arrow on the map: a run of sub-$68 settlements pressures OPEC+ revenue and brings a restraint announcement forward, fourteen days later. Together with `R → B` it is the map's only loop.
129	
130	A layered layout cannot assign columns to a graph with a loop in it. So the layout pass removes every arrow marked `reflexive` before it starts, assigns columns to what is left, and puts the reflexive arrow back for drawing. The loop is real, it is on screen, and it takes no part in deciding who sits where.
131	
132	It therefore points *backwards*: B is in column 2, R is in column 1. That is correct and it is the honest shape of feedback.
133	
134	Setting feedback arrows aside is not this chapter's invention. It is one rule, written once in `spec/multiverse/interventions.md` (Kent, 2026-09-17):
135	
136	> *The map the engine works through is the map with feedback arrows set aside. Anything that asks **what can move** reads that map — the affected set, diff states, propagation's ordering, layering. Anything that asks **what can I walk to** reads the whole map — the hover lens, `h`/`l`, the outline.*
137	
138	Layering asks what can move, so it reads the map with `B → R` removed. That is also why R comes out `untouched` on the strike branch. `test_a_feedback_arrow_never_carries_a_change` fails loudly the day stack 06 unrolls feedback arrows in time, and points at the one sentence to change. **How that wire looks — the loop, the lag chip reading "14 days" — is `tiles-ports-wires.md`.** This chapter only guarantees that the wire exists, that it never decides a column, and that removing it can never fail: INV-6 (no loops except through reflexive arrows, each with a delay greater than zero) is already enforced in the engine, so a map that reaches the canvas is one the loop check has passed.
139	
140	### B5 — Seven tiles per column, then "+n more"
141	
142	No column paints more than seven tiles. The eighth and beyond collapse into one **"+n more"** tile, where n is exactly how many are behind it — `+4 more` for eleven claims in a column.
143	
144	Hormuz never reaches the cap; a generated map does. The rule exists because a column of eighteen tiles is a wall, and a wall is the hairball problem wearing a different hat.
145	
146	**Which seven survive, and what "+n more" does** (Kent, 2026-09-17): the seven that survive are the **first seven in the layout's own within-column order** — the order ELK already produced, so nothing new has to be ranked and the answer is the same every run. Activating the "+n more" tile **opens the outline view filtered to that column** (`keyboard-and-access.md`), which is a list that already exists, already reads each claim as a sentence, and already works on the keyboard. Nothing expands in place, so the cap is never briefly broken.
147	
148	**A collapsed claim's wires do not disappear.** A wire that vanishes is a state a user cannot trace, which is the second veto. The wires of the hidden claims attach to the "+n more" tile. *How they bundle is still open — see Open questions.*
149	
150	### B6 — Level of detail: the tile changes representation, it does not shrink
151	
152	**There is one rule, and the two thresholds are consequences of it** (Kent, 2026-09-17). The rule: **no text ever lands below 11 pixels on the glass.** There is no counter-scaling anywhere — a tile at 0.7 zoom really is drawn at 0.7, text and all — so the thresholds are arithmetic, not taste:
153	
154	| Consequence | Sum | Why |
155	|---|---|---|
156	| **Summary below ≈ 0.85 zoom** | 11 ÷ 13 = 0.846… | A full tile's smallest type is `--text-sm`, 13 px. Below 0.846 that text lands under 11 px on the glass, so the tile must change representation first |
157	| **Zoom floor 0.5** | 11 ÷ 22 = 0.5 | A summary tile's type is `--text-lg`, 22 px. At 0.5 it lands at exactly 11 px. You cannot zoom out past that, because the next pixel out is unreadable |
158	
159	**This supersedes the 0.6 threshold in the plan and in decision record 0007, dated 2026-09-17.** 0.6 was a chosen number; 0.846 is a derived one, and deriving it is what makes the 11-pixel promise true rather than approximately true.
160	
161	Below the summary threshold a tile paints its **summary**: the claim and the three belief chips inside the same kind silhouette, nothing else. The outline never goes — it is the tile's shape, and dropping it would lose the claim's kind at exactly the zoom where you are scanning for one. Above it the tile paints in full — claim, chips, evidence clippings, resolve-by date (`tiles-ports-wires.md`).
162	
163	**The honest cost.** Measured on the Hormuz map: on a 1440-pixel-wide window the first frame is summary tiles, because `fitView` cannot fit the map any larger. At 1600 wide it is full tiles, at about 11.4 pixels — legible, and only just. A narrow window therefore opens on summaries and you zoom in to read. That is the price of the promise, and it is cheaper than the alternative, which is text nobody can read at a zoom the interface offered them.
164	
165	UX-4 (level of detail by zoom) names three rungs. This stack builds two of them:
166	
167	| UX-4 rung | What it shows | Where |
168	|---|---|---|
169	| **Near** | The full tile, with evidence | This stack — at or above 0.85 zoom |
170	| **Mid** | Wiring and belief chips | This stack — between the 0.5 floor and 0.85, the summary tile |
171	| **Far** | Worlds and their terminal deltas | **Not this stack.** It needs several worlds side by side (FR-17, three or more branches as small multiples), which arrives later |
172	
173	### B7 — The union of two worlds is laid out once
174	
175	A diff shows the base map and the branch at the same time. Both are laid out **once, together, as one graph** — every claim in either world, every wire in either world — and then painted twice in those same coordinates. One layout, two paintings. **How they are painted is `diff-view.md`.**
176	
177	The Hormuz strike branch adds **S**, a confirmed military strike on Iranian territory, with three arrows: `S → B`, `S → C`, and `S → H`. That last one points at the hypothesis itself. The union is five columns:
178	
179	| Column | Tiles |
180	|---|---|
181	| 0 | S |
182	| 1 | H |
183	| 2 | C · N1 · R |
184	| 3 | B |
185	| 4 | M1 · M2 |
186	
187	**Read that against B1 and notice what happened: every base claim moved one column right.** It had to. S causes H, so S must sit before H, and everything H causes shifts with it. Pinning cannot prevent this, because pinning orders tiles *inside* a column and does not decide which column a tile is in.
188	
189	**Following focus is enough, and columns are not pinned** (Kent, 2026-09-17). Two reasons. The shift is a **rigid translation** — every base tile moves the same 400 pixels, so relative to any other base tile nothing has moved at all, and `setCenter` on the focused tile makes even that invisible. And pinning the columns would be worse than the shift it prevents: S would have to stay where the base map had nothing, which puts a cause to the right of its effect and breaks the one promise the layout exists to make.
190	
191	One rule makes it land well: **creating a claim moves focus to it.** So the moment the strike branch is made, focus is on S and `setCenter` frames S — you are looking at the thing you just added, not hunting for it.
192	
193	A claim present in both worlds has exactly one coordinate. That is the property that makes a ghost overlay readable at all: if the two worlds were laid out separately, every tile would appear to have moved and nothing would stand out.
194	
195	### B8 — Tiles do not move, and the interface says so
196	
197	No tile is draggable. Not "mostly", not "except the ones you pinned" — none, anywhere, in this stack.
198	
199	Half-supported dragging looks broken (anti-pattern 13 in the research). Pinning, grouping and annotating arrive later as **explicit buttons**, not as free drag.
200	
201	Nobody should have to discover this by failing, so the shortcuts sheet says it out loud. That line is written in `keyboard-and-access.md`, which owns the sheet.
202	
203	### B9 — Sixty tiles in under 100 milliseconds
204	
205	NFR-7 (performance: sixty tiles render and re-layout in under 100 milliseconds on a laptop) is measured, not assumed. The worker returns `elapsedMs` on every layout, and INV-workbench.30 fails if a sixty-tile map crosses the budget.
206	
207	**What the budget covers is not settled.** `elapsedMs` is ELK's own time and nothing else; NFR-7's words are "render and re-layout", which is ELK plus React Flow's paint. And decision record 0007 already puts ELK alone at up to 150 milliseconds on sixty tiles — over the budget before a single pixel is drawn. So the test may land as a **known-red pin** that records the real figure rather than as a passing check. Which of the two the budget means, and what to do when it is missed, is under Open questions.
208	
209	## INVARIANTS
210	
211	Each is *for all X, statement P holds*, and each names what checks it. "Visual review checklist line *n*" is line *n* of the visual review checklist in [`README.md`](README.md) — a checklist line is a checkable thing; it is checked by a person.
212	
213	| ID | Statement | Checked by |
214	|---|---|---|
215	| **INV-workbench.20** | For every layout call, the options passed to ELK are exactly the five in `ELK_OPTIONS` and no others; `elk.position` is set per tile and nowhere else | `test_layout_options_are_the_five_named` in `frontend/src/graph/__tests__/layout.test.ts` |
216	| **INV-workbench.21** | For every module under `frontend/src/`, `elkjs` is imported by the worker file and by nothing else — layout never runs on the thread that draws | `test_elk_is_imported_only_by_the_worker` in `layout.test.ts` |
217	| **INV-workbench.22** | For every map and every claim added strictly downstream of the tiles already placed, every already-placed tile's coordinates are identical before and after | `test_pinned_tiles_keep_their_positions` in `layout.test.ts` |
218	| **INV-workbench.23** | For every map and every re-layout of it, no already-placed tile changes its order within its column | `test_within_layer_order_is_stable` in `layout.test.ts` |
219	| **INV-workbench.24** | For every base map and branch, layout runs once over their union, and every claim present in both worlds has exactly one coordinate | `test_union_layout_is_stable` in `layout.test.ts` |
220	| **INV-workbench.25** | For every map opened, `fitView` is called exactly once; every later layout calls `setCenter` on the focused tile and the focused tile stays in the viewport; and every newly created claim takes focus | `test_fit_view_runs_once_then_set_center` in `layout.test.ts`; `frontend/e2e/hormuz.spec.ts` |
221	| **INV-workbench.26** | For every map, no column paints more than seven tiles; where one would, the first seven in the layout's within-column order are painted and the rest sit behind a single "+n more" tile whose n equals the number hidden | `test_layer_cap_collapses_the_rest` in `layout.test.ts`; visual review checklist line 6 (is the map layered left to right, or a hairball?) |
222	| **INV-workbench.27** | For every zoom from the 0.5 floor to the ceiling, the smallest rendered type size × the zoom is at least 11 — below ≈0.85 because the tile has switched to its summary, above it because 13 × 0.85 already clears 11 | `test_no_text_lands_under_eleven_pixels_at_any_zoom` in `layout.test.ts`, a sweep over the whole zoom range; visual review checklist line 7 (is any text below 11 pixels?) |
223	| **INV-workbench.28** | For every tile in every state, `draggable` is false | `test_no_tile_is_draggable` in `layout.test.ts` |
224	| **INV-workbench.29** | For every map, column assignment is computed on the graph with reflexive arrows removed, and every reflexive arrow is still drawn | `test_reflexive_links_are_set_aside_for_layering` in `layout.test.ts` |
225	| **INV-workbench.30** | For every map of sixty tiles, the worker's `elapsedMs` is under 100 milliseconds (NFR-7) — see B9 on what the budget covers | `test_sixty_tiles_lay_out_under_100ms` in `layout.test.ts` |
226	
227	## ANTI-PATTERNS
228	
229	1. **Do not run ELK on the main thread**, because a 150-millisecond freeze eats keystrokes and stutters the scroll, and the user reads that as a slow product rather than as a busy layout. Post to the worker and render the previous coordinates until the new ones arrive.
230	2. **Do not call `fitView` after every layout**, because the map jumps to a new framing each time and the user loses the tile they were reading. Frame once on open; `setCenter` on the focused tile thereafter.
231	3. **Do not let text land under 11 pixels on the glass**, because an unreadable label is worse than no label. Switch the tile to its summary at 0.85 and stop the zoom at 0.5 — and do not counter-scale the text to dodge the rule, because a tile whose contents ignore the zoom stops being a picture of the map.
232	4. **Do not make tiles "a bit" draggable**, because a tile that moves and then snaps back reads as a bug. Offer no drag at all and say so in the shortcuts sheet.
233	5. **Do not hide a wire when its tile collapses into "+n more"**, because a wire that vanishes is a state nobody can trace — the second veto. Attach it to the "+n more" tile.
234	6. **Do not feed reflexive arrows into the layering pass**, because a layered algorithm has no answer for a loop and will either fail or invent an order. Remove them, assign columns, put them back for drawing.
235	7. **Do not re-layout on hover or selection**, because nothing about the graph changed and the map should be still while you read it. Hover dims; selection opens the Inspector; neither moves a tile.
236	8. **Do not lay out two worlds separately and overlay them**, because every tile will appear to have moved and the diff will say nothing. Lay out the union once and paint it twice.
237	
238	## Open questions
239	
240	*Dated 2026-09-17. Each is something the plan does not settle; none is decided here.*
241	
242	1. **How do a collapsed claim's wires bundle?** One thick wire to the "+n more" tile with a count on it, or n thin wires all landing on the same socket? The first is legible; the second is literal. The chapter requires only that no wire disappears. *(Which seven survive, and what activating "+n more" does, were* **Decided 2026-09-17** *— both are in B5.)*
243	2. **Should 280 and 120 become tokens?** Every other pixel number in the product lives in `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css`. The tile width and the column gutter currently would not. Adding them touches a file this stack's wire agent owns (the new colour block), so it is a coordination question, not a design one.
244	3. **Does UX-4's "far" rung need its own zoom threshold?** This stack has a floor, one threshold and two renderings. When several worlds appear side by side, "far" will need a third number — and probably a different interaction altogether, since at that scale you are choosing a world rather than reading a map.
245	4. **What does NFR-7's 100 milliseconds actually cover, and what happens when it is missed?** "Render and re-layout" reads as ELK plus paint; `elapsedMs` measures ELK alone. Decision record 0007 already puts ELK alone at up to 150 milliseconds on sixty tiles, so on the pessimistic reading the budget is missed before anything is drawn. Either the invariant measures `elapsedMs` and the budget is a layout budget, or it measures both and the number needs revisiting. Until Kent says, INV-workbench.30 measures `elapsedMs` and the test records the real figure so the gap is visible rather than hidden.
246	
247	**Decided 2026-09-17 and now in the body:** which seven tiles survive the cap and what "+n more" opens (B5) · the two zoom numbers and the removal of counter-scaling (B6) · whether following focus is enough when the union layout shifts every column, and the rule that creating a claim moves focus to it (B7) · the minimum zoom, which is 0.5 and falls out of the 11-pixel rule (B6).

# Layout and zoom — a map that never becomes a hairball

## Purpose

A causal map drawn by a physics simulation is a hairball: every run looks different, nothing lines up, and crossings hide the one arrow you were looking for. This chapter makes the map **arrive already arranged** — left to right, cause before effect, one claim per box, in an order that does not change under your feet. You open the Hormuz map and it is legible in the first second, without touching anything. You zoom out and the tiles turn into summaries rather than into unreadable specks. You add a claim, or open a branch, and the tile you were reading stays where your eye left it.

Three chapters sit next to this one and are not repeated here: `tiles-ports-wires.md` says what is inside a tile and how a wire is drawn, `color-motion-type.md` carries the colour law and the motion budget, and `diff-view.md` says how two worlds are painted once they share a coordinate space. This chapter owns only **where things go and how big they are**.

## Data model

### The layout options — the whole list, and nothing else

The automatic layout is ELK, an open-source graph-layout engine compiled to JavaScript. Five options, and no others:

```ts
const ELK_OPTIONS = {
  "elk.algorithm": "layered",
  "elk.direction": "RIGHT",
  "elk.layered.nodePlacement.strategy": "NETWORK_SIMPLEX",
  "elk.layered.crossingMinimization.semiInteractive": "true",
  "elk.layered.spacing.nodeNodeBetweenLayers": "120",
} as const;
```

These five are set once, for the whole graph. One further ELK property, `elk.position`, is set **per tile** rather than here — it is how an already-placed tile says where it wants to stay (B3) — so "no others" stays true of this list.

In plain words:

ELK's word is *layer*; the code and the test names use it. On screen and in this chapter the word is **column**, because that is what a reader sees.

| Option | What it buys |
|---|---|
| `layered` | Claims are assigned to columns; every arrow points from a lower column to a higher one. This is what makes cause-before-effect a fact of the picture rather than a hope |
| `direction: RIGHT` | The columns run left to right. Time and causality read the way English reads |
| `nodePlacement.strategy: NETWORK_SIMPLEX` | Decides each tile's position **within** its column so that wires come out as straight as possible. Straight wires are short wires; short wires cross less |
| `crossingMinimization.semiInteractive: true` | When ordering a column, the crossing minimiser treats a tile's existing position as where that tile *wants* to sit. This is the switch that makes pinning work at all |
| `spacing.nodeNodeBetweenLayers: 120` | 120 pixels of gutter between one column and the next — enough room for a midpoint chip and an origin mark on the wire without the chip touching a tile |

One thing the list does not say out loud: **which column a claim lands in** is decided by ELK's *layering* strategy, which is a separate setting from `nodePlacement.strategy` above. We do not set it, so it is ELK's default — also network simplex — which picks the column assignment with the smallest total arrow length. The worked examples below are that assignment, and they are the unique minimum, so the picture is reproducible rather than merely likely.

### The worker seam

Decision record 0007 measures ELK at 50–150 milliseconds on sixty tiles. On the main thread that is a frozen page, a dropped keystroke, and a scroll that stutters. So it runs in a **Web Worker** — a second browser thread with no access to the page — and the main thread only posts and listens. (That upper figure is already over NFR-7's budget; see B9 and Open questions.)

```ts
/** What the page sends the layout worker. */
interface LayoutRequest {
  /** Every tile to place. Width is always 280. Height varies per tile: content-fit,
   *  clamped to 152–320 pixels, on the 8-pixel grid, **computed from the content** and
   *  never measured off the screen — so layout stays a pure function of the map
   *  (`tiles-ports-wires.md` owns the height rule, and the ceiling's reason). */
  tiles: { id: string; width: 280; height: number; pinnedAt?: { x: number; y: number } }[];
  /** Every wire. `reflexive` wires are marked here and set aside before layering. */
  wires: { id: string; from: string; to: string; reflexive: boolean }[];
}

/** One coordinate per tile, plus which column it landed in and where in that column.
 *  This is the type other chapters read: `diff-view.md` takes a `positions: PositionMap`
 *  and paints two worlds into it. */
type PositionMap = Record<string, { x: number; y: number; layer: number; orderInLayer: number }>;

/** What comes back. */
interface LayoutResult {
  tiles: PositionMap;
  /** For each column that overflowed seven tiles, the claims behind its "+n more" tile. */
  collapsed: Record<number, string[]>;
  /** How long ELK took. NFR-7's 100-millisecond budget is measured, not hoped for. */
  elapsedMs: number;
}
```

The page never imports ELK. The worker file is the only place `elkjs` appears in `frontend/src/`, and a test says so.

### What a tile tells the layout

```ts
interface TileLayoutProps {
  /** Set by the zoom watcher, never by the tile itself. */
  detail: "summary" | "full";
  /** Always false, on every tile, forever in this stack. */
  draggable: false;
  /** Drives `setCenter` and the focus ring. One tile at a time. */
  focused: boolean;
}
```

### Tokens this chapter reads

From `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css`: `--space-1` (8 px, the grid everything sits on), `--space-2` (16 px), `--hairline` (the 1-pixel border at 10% of the text colour), `--surface` and `--surface-raised`, `--focus` (the keyboard ring), and the type scale `--text-sm` / `--text-md` / `--text-lg` (13 / 15 / 22 px).

**Two numbers in this chapter are not tokens yet:** the 280-pixel tile width and the 120-pixel gutter between columns. See Open questions.

## Behaviour

Worked on the Hormuz map (the cast is in [`README.md`](README.md)). This chapter uses all seven base claims — H, C, B, R, M1, M2, N1 — the reflexive arrow `B → R`, and the claim **S** that the strike branch adds.

Reflexive arrows are set aside before columns are assigned (B4). What is left is seven claims and seven arrows, and the minimum-total-length assignment is:

| Column | Tiles |
|---|---|
| 0 | H |
| 1 | C · N1 · R |
| 2 | B |
| 3 | M1 · M2 |

R sits in column 1, tight against B, because its only live arrow is `R → B`. Nothing pulls it further left, and network simplex does not leave a wire longer than it has to be.

The widest column holds three tiles. The cap is seven, so nothing collapses (B5).

### B2 — Opening the map frames it once

On the first layout of a map, and only then, `fitView` frames the whole thing. Every layout after that calls `setCenter` on the focused tile instead, so the tile you were reading stays under your eye.

Losing your place after a re-layout is anti-pattern 8 in `docs/research/03-ui-ux-directions.md`.

> *The map the engine works through is the map with feedback arrows set aside. Anything that asks **what can move** reads that map — the affected set, diff states, propagation's ordering, layering. Above it the tile paints in full — claim, chips, evidence clippings, resolve-by date (`tiles-ports-wires.md`).

**The honest cost.** Measured on the Hormuz map: on a 1440-pixel-wide window the first frame is summary tiles, because `fitView` cannot fit the map any larger. At 1600 wide it is full tiles, at about 11.4 pixels — legible, and only just. A narrow window therefore opens on summaries and you zoom in to read. That is the price of the promise, and it is cheaper than the alternative, which is text nobody can read at a zoom the interface offered them.

UX-4 (level of detail by zoom) names three rungs. This stack builds two of them:

| UX-4 rung | What it shows | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Near** | The full tile, with evidence | This stack — at or above 0.85 zoom |
| **Mid** | Wiring and belief chips | This stack — between the 0.5 floor and 0.85, the summary tile |
| **Far** | Worlds and their terminal deltas | **Not this stack.** It needs several worlds side by side (FR-17, three or more branches as small multiples), which arrives later |

### B7 — The union of two worlds is laid out once

A diff shows the base map and the branch at the same time. Both are laid out **once, together, as one graph** — every claim in either world, every wire in either world — and then painted twice in those same coordinates. One layout, two paintings. **How they are painted is `diff-view.md`.**

The Hormuz strike branch adds **S**, a confirmed military strike on Iranian territory, with three arrows: `S → B`, `S → C`, and `S → H`. That last one points at the hypothesis itself. The union is five columns:

| Column | Tiles |
|---|---|
| 0 | S |
| 1 | H |
| 2 | C · N1 · R |
| 3 | B |
| 4 | M1 · M2 |

**Read that against B1 and notice what happened: every base claim moved one column right.** It had to. S causes H, so S must sit before H, and everything H causes shifts with it. Pinning cannot prevent this, because pinning orders tiles *inside* a column and does not decide which column a tile is in.

**Following focus is enough, and columns are not pinned** (Kent, 2026-09-17). Two reasons. The shift is a **rigid translation** — every base tile moves the same 400 pixels, so relative to any other base tile nothing has moved at all, and `setCenter` on the focused tile makes even that invisible. And pinning the columns would be worse than the shift it prevents: S would have to stay where the base map had nothing, which puts a cause to the right of its effect and breaks the one promise the layout exists to make.

One rule makes it land well: **creating a claim moves focus to it.** So the moment the strike branch is made, focus is on S and `setCenter` frames S — you are looking at the thing you just added, not hunting for it.

A claim present in both worlds has exactly one coordinate. That is the property that makes a ghost overlay readable at all: if the two worlds were laid out separately, every tile would appear to have moved and nothing would stand out.

### B8 — Tiles do not move, and the interface says so

No tile is draggable. Not "mostly", not "except the ones you pinned" — none, anywhere, in this stack.

Half-supported dragging looks broken (anti-pattern 13 in the research). Pinning, grouping and annotating arrive later as **explicit buttons**, not as free drag.

Nobody should have to discover this by failing, so the shortcuts sheet says it out loud. That line is written in `keyboard-and-access.md`, which owns the sheet.

### B9 — Sixty tiles in under 100 milliseconds

NFR-7 (performance: sixty tiles render and re-layout in under 100 milliseconds on a laptop) is measured, not assumed. The worker returns `elapsedMs` on every layout, and INV-workbench.30 fails if a sixty-tile map crosses the budget.

**What the budget covers is not settled.** `elapsedMs` is ELK's own time and nothing else; NFR-7's words are "render and re-layout", which is ELK plus React Flow's paint. And decision record 0007 already puts ELK alone at up to 150 milliseconds on sixty tiles — over the budget before a single pixel is drawn. So the test may land as a **known-red pin** that records the real figure rather than as a passing check. Which of the two the budget means, and what to do when it is missed, is under Open questions.

## INVARIANTS

Each is *for all X, statement P holds*, and each names what checks it. "Visual review checklist line *n*" is line *n* of the visual review checklist in [`README.md`](README.md) — a checklist line is a checkable thing; it is checked by a person.

| ID | Statement | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| **INV-workbench.20** | For every layout call, the options passed to ELK are exactly the five in `ELK_OPTIONS` and no others; `elk.position` is set per tile and nowhere else | `test_layout_options_are_the_five_named` in `frontend/src/graph/__tests__/layout.test.ts` |
| **INV-workbench.21** | For every module under `frontend/src/`, `elkjs` is imported by the worker file and by nothing else — layout never runs on the thread that draws | `test_elk_is_imported_only_by_the_worker` in `layout.test.ts` |
| **INV-workbench.22** | For every map and every claim added strictly downstream of the tiles already placed, every already-placed tile's coordinates are identical before and after | `test_pinned_tiles_keep_their_positions` in `layout.test.ts` |
| **INV-workbench.23** | For every map and every re-layout of it, no already-placed tile changes its order within its column | `test_within_layer_order_is_stable` in `layout.test.ts` |
| **INV-workbench.24** | For every base map and branch, layout runs once over their union, and every claim present in both worlds has exactly one coordinate | `test_union_layout_is_stable` in `layout.test.ts` |
| **INV-workbench.25** | For every map opened, `fitView` is called exactly once; every later layout calls `setCenter` on the focused tile and the focused tile stays in the viewport; and every newly created claim takes focus | `test_fit_view_runs_once_then_set_center` in `layout.test.ts`; `frontend/e2e/hormuz.spec.ts` |
| **INV-workbench.26** | For every map, no column paints more than seven tiles; where one would, the first seven in the layout's within-column order are painted and the rest sit behind a single "+n more" tile whose n equals the number hidden | `test_layer_cap_collapses_the_rest` in `layout.test.ts`; visual review checklist line 6 (is the map layered left to right, or a hairball?) |
| **INV-workbench.27** | For every zoom from the 0.5 floor to the ceiling, the smallest rendered type size × the zoom is at least 11 — below ≈0.85 because the tile has switched to its summary, above it because 13 × 0.85 already clears 11 | `test_no_text_lands_under_eleven_pixels_at_any_zoom` in `layout.test.ts`, a sweep over the whole zoom range; visual review checklist line 7 (is any text below 11 pixels?) |
| **INV-workbench.28** | For every tile in every state, `draggable` is false | `test_no_tile_is_draggable` in `layout.test.ts` |
| **INV-workbench.29** | For every map, column assignment is computed on the graph with reflexive arrows removed, and every reflexive arrow is still drawn | `test_reflexive_links_are_set_aside_for_layering` in `layout.test.ts` |
| **INV-workbench.30** | For every map of sixty tiles, the worker's `elapsedMs` is under 100 milliseconds (NFR-7) — see B9 on what the budget covers | `test_sixty_tiles_lay_out_under_100ms` in `layout.test.ts` |

## ANTI-PATTERNS

1. **Do not run ELK on the main thread**, because a 150-millisecond freeze eats keystrokes and stutters the scroll, and the user reads that as a slow product rather than as a busy layout. Post to the worker and render the previous coordinates until the new ones arrive.
2. **Do not call `fitView` after every layout**, because the map jumps to a new framing each time and the user loses the tile they were reading. Frame once on open; `setCenter` on the focused tile thereafter.
3. **Do not let text land under 11 pixels on the glass**, because an unreadable label is worse than no label. Switch the tile to its summary at 0.85 and stop the zoom at 0.5 — and do not counter-scale the text to dodge the rule, because a tile whose contents ignore the zoom stops being a picture of the map.
4. **Do not make tiles "a bit" draggable**, because a tile that moves and then snaps back reads as a bug. Offer no drag at all and say so in the shortcuts sheet.
5. **Do not hide a wire when its tile collapses into "+n more"**, because a wire that vanishes is a state nobody can trace — the second veto. Attach it to the "+n more" tile.
6. **Do not feed reflexive arrows into the layering pass**, because a layered algorithm has no answer for a loop and will either fail or invent an order. Remove them, assign columns, put them back for drawing.
7. **Do not re-layout on hover or selection**, because nothing about the graph changed and the map should be still while you read it. Hover dims; selection opens the Inspector; neither moves a tile.
8. **Do not lay out two worlds separately and overlay them**, because every tile will appear to have moved and the diff will say nothing. Lay out the union once and paint it twice.

## Open questions

*Dated 2026-09-17. Each is something the plan does not settle; none is decided here.*

1. **How do a collapsed claim's wires bundle?** One thick wire to the "+n more" tile with a count on it, or n thin wires all landing on the same socket? The first is legible; the second is literal. The chapter requires only that no wire disappears. *(Which seven survive, and what activating "+n more" does, were* **Decided 2026-09-17** *— both are in B5.)*
2. **Should 280 and 120 become tokens?** Every other pixel number in the product lives in `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css`. The tile width and the column gutter currently would not. Adding them touches a file this stack's wire agent owns (the new colour block), so it is a coordination question, not a design one.
3. **Does UX-4's "far" rung need its own zoom threshold?** This stack has a floor, one threshold and two renderings. When several worlds appear side by side, "far" will need a third number — and probably a different interaction altogether, since at that scale you are choosing a world rather than reading a map.
4. **What does NFR-7's 100 milliseconds actually cover, and what happens when it is missed?** "Render and re-layout" reads as ELK plus paint; `elapsedMs` measures ELK alone. Decision record 0007 already puts ELK alone at up to 150 milliseconds on sixty tiles, so on the pessimistic reading the budget is missed before anything is drawn. Either the invariant measures `elapsedMs` and the budget is a layout budget, or it measures both and the number needs revisiting. Until Kent says, INV-workbench.30 measures `elapsedMs` and the test records the real figure so the gap is visible rather than hidden.

**Decided 2026-09-17 and now in the body:** which seven tiles survive the cap and what "+n more" opens (B5) · the two zoom numbers and the removal of counter-scaling (B6) · whether following focus is enough when the union layout shifts every column, and the rule that creating a claim moves focus to it (B7) · the minimum zoom, which is 0.5 and falls out of the 11-pixel rule (B6).

1	# Streaming growth — the map drawing itself
2	
3	## Purpose
4	
5	Until now a map arrived finished. You opened the stored example and seven tiles were already
6	there. This chapter is about the other way in: you type a sentence, and the map **builds itself in
7	front of you** — a reserved rectangle first, then a claim, then the arrow that justifies it, then
8	the next one, out to the things you could trade — with every proposal the rules refused visible on
9	the way past, and a receipt at the end saying what it cost.
10	
11	The growing is not a decoration wrapped around a wait. **The growing is the loading state** (UX-8,
12	FR-5). There is no spinner in this product, and there is no moment where a blank screen turns into
13	a finished picture — because that moment is the "spinner then dump" the anti-patterns list vetoes
14	(PRD §10 anti-pattern 9), and because a map that simply appears hides the half of the work worth
15	watching: our own rules turning the model down.
16	
17	Three things a reader can do after this chapter that they could not before. **Type any sentence and
18	watch what it would cause.** **Name a destination and get a graded path to it, or an honest "no path
19	reaches this" naming the nearest claim that was reached** (FR-7, UX-13). And, **with no model key at
20	all, watch a recorded example run** (record 0012) — the same stream, the same canvas, the same
21	refusals, labelled as a replay everywhere a reader looks.
22	
23	This chapter owns the eight stream events as the browser types them, the `growth` reducer that folds
24	them into a world, the skeleton tile, the refusal strip, the receipt strip, the Verify door's two
25	cards, the input bar, and the replay badge. It owns no arithmetic: every number on every one of
26	those surfaces is a field on an event.
27	
28	---
29	
30	## Data model
31	
32	### The transport, in one paragraph
33	
34	The browser sends `POST /api/generate` and **reads the reply as a stream** rather than opening an
35	`EventSource`. Two reasons, both hard. The request carries a body — the sentence, an optional
36	destination, the reader's own likelihood, a seed — and an `EventSource` can only send a GET with no
37	body. And an `EventSource` reconnects by itself, which would silently re-run a generation and spend
38	the money twice. The wire format is still server-sent events — an `event:` line naming the event and
39	a `data:` line carrying one JSON object — so the whole thing stays readable in a terminal with
40	`curl`. The route, the eight events and their order are `spec/generation/streaming.md`'s, written in
41	this stack's server half; this chapter says what the browser does with them.
42	
43	### The eight events, hand-typed
44	
45	```ts
46	// frontend/src/stream/events.ts
47	//
48	// Written by hand, exactly as `WorldView` was, because the server's description of
49	// itself and this canvas are built at the same time. The server's own copy is
50	// `backend/src/katalyst/engine/events.py`. A type-level test,
51	// `frontend/src/stream/__tests__/eventsMatchSchema.test-d.ts`, fails the build when
52	// the two drift. It cannot pin the eight envelopes — server-sent events have no body
53	// OpenAPI can describe — so it pins every piece they are built from, which are
54	// aliased to the generated types below rather than retyped, and the four shapes that
55	// do travel as JSON: the receipt, the request, the drafted insert and the working.
56	
57	import type { components } from "../api/schema";
58	
59	/** An identifier the engine minted for a claim. Nothing in the browser ever makes one. */
60	export type PropositionId = string;
61	
62	type Proposition = components["schemas"]["Proposition"];
63	type Link = components["schemas"]["Link"];
64	type Violation = components["schemas"]["Violation"];
65	type World = components["schemas"]["World"];
66	
67	/** The run has started. The first thing that arrives, and it arrives at once. */
68	export interface GenerationStarted {
69	  readonly event: "generation_started";
70	  /** The engine's name for this run. What the transcript is asked for by. */
71	  readonly generation_id: string;
72	  /**
73	   * The seed every random draw in this run came from — always a number here, even
74	   * when the request left it out. Whoever chose it, this event is where the browser
75	   * reads it: the one the request sent, or the one `engine/ids.py` minted when it
76	   * sent none, or, on a replay, the one in the recording's header, which wins over
77	   * both. The browser prints what this says and never works out which case it was.
78	   *
79	   * **And by the time it is a number here it may already be wrong.** A seed is
80	   * up to nineteen digits and a browser holds a whole number exactly only up to
81	   * sixteen, so `JSON.parse` has rounded it before any of our code sees it.
82	   * Nothing computes with a seed — it is printed under the map so a reader can
83	   * ask for the same one again — and a rounded seed printed there is a number
84	   * on screen that is simply wrong, in the one place that exists so an answer
85	   * can be had twice.
86	   */
87	  readonly seed: number;
88	  /**
89	   * The same seed, exactly as it was written on the wire: its digits, not a
90	   * number.
91	   *
92	   * Read off the raw text of the `data:` line by the reader, because that is
93	   * the last moment the digits exist. Absent only when a caller handed the
94	   * events over by hand, and then the parsed number is the whole of what is
95	   * known.
96	   */
97	  readonly seed_as_written?: string;
98	  /** The sentence the reader typed, in their own words. */
99	  readonly hypothesis: string;
100	  /** The Verify door's destination, in their words. Null when they used the Explore door. */
101	  readonly target: string | null;
102	}
103	
104	/** One proposal the rules accepted. A claim, its incoming arrows, or both. */
105	export interface ProposalAccepted {
106	  readonly event: "proposal_accepted";
107	  /** Where this sits in the transcript, counting from 0. */
108	  readonly at: number;
109	  /** The new claim, with its identifier minted by the engine. Null for an arrows-only proposal. */
110	  readonly proposition: Proposition | null;
111	  /** Its incoming arrows, identifiers minted by the engine. */
112	  readonly links: readonly Link[];
113	  /** The claims still open to expand. What the skeletons are drawn from. */
114	  readonly frontier: readonly PropositionId[];
115	}
116	
117	/** One proposal the rules refused. An event, never an error. */
118	export interface ProposalRejected {
119	  readonly event: "proposal_rejected";
120	  readonly at: number;
121	  /** What the model wrote. Never minted, never drawn as a tile, only ever quoted. */
122	  readonly claim_in_words: string;
123	  /** The validator's own codes and its own sentences. One per rule broken. */
124	  readonly violations: readonly Violation[];
125	  /**
126	   * The claims still open to expand — the same field the accepted event carries, and
127	   * for the same reason. A claim closed by its third refusal in a row leaves the
128	   * frontier on this event, so its rectangle comes down at once instead of standing
129	   * there waiting for something that is not coming.
130	   */
131	  readonly frontier: readonly PropositionId[];
132	}
133	
134	/** Every number, worked through the finished map, once. */
135	export interface BeliefsPropagated {
136	  readonly event: "beliefs_propagated";
137	  readonly world: World;
138	}
139	
140	/** The Verify door's answer. Emitted only when the reader named a destination. */
141	export interface Verdict {
142	  readonly event: "verdict";
143	  readonly kind: "reached" | "no_path";
144	  /** The steps of the path, in order. Empty on `no_path`. */
145	  readonly path: readonly PropositionId[];
146	  /** The multiplied-out likelihood of those steps (INV-8). Null on `no_path`. */
147	  readonly product: number | null;
148	  /** On `no_path`: the closest claim the map did reach. */
149	  readonly nearest: PropositionId | null;
150	  /** One plain sentence, the engine's own. */
151	  readonly why: string;
152	}
153	
154	/** What the run cost (NFR-6). */
155	export interface Receipt {
156	  readonly event: "receipt";
157	  readonly model: string;
158	  readonly calls: number;
159	  readonly input_tokens: number;
160	  readonly output_tokens: number;
161	  readonly cache_read_tokens: number;
162	  /**
163	   * How many web searches this run made. Billed apart from tokens, so `dollars`
164	   * cannot be accounted for without it — which is why it is a field of its own
165	   * rather than something a reader is expected to infer.
166	   */
167	  readonly searches: number;
168	  readonly dollars: number;
169	  readonly seconds: number;
170	  /** Live, or played from a recording. The only place in the stream this is said. */
171	  readonly mode: "live" | "replay";
172	  /**
173	   * How hard the model was asked to try, as a plain word: `default` when
174	   * nothing was asked for and the service's own applied, otherwise `low`,
175	   * `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`. A recording is made rich and a live run
176	   * is made fast (Kent, G13), so two maps of the same sentence at the same seed
177	   * can differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the sentence.
178	   */
179	  readonly effort: string;
180	  /** The day the recording was made, as the map writes a day: `2026-09-18`. Null when live. */
181	  readonly recording_date: string | null;
182	  /** A hash of the prompt this run was made against. Null never; it is always known. */
183	  readonly prompt_hash: string;
184	}
185	
186	/** Why the generation stopped. Not whether the Verify door found anything — that is `verdict`. */
187	export interface Done {
188	  readonly event: "done";
189	  readonly reason:
190	    | "reached_terminal"
191	    | "depth_cap"
192	    | "width_cap"
193	    | "claim_cap"
194	    | "spend_cap"
195	    | "refusal_cap"
196	    | "no_terminal";
197	  readonly claims: number;
198	  readonly links: number;
199	  readonly rejected: number;
200	}
201	
202	/** The run broke. One plain sentence, never a stack trace. */
203	export interface Failed {
204	  readonly event: "failed";
205	  readonly message: string;
206	}
207	
208	export type StreamEvent =
209	  | GenerationStarted
210	  | ProposalAccepted
211	  | ProposalRejected
212	  | BeliefsPropagated
213	  | Verdict
214	  | Receipt
215	  | Done
216	  | Failed;
217	```
218	
219	**The `event` field is put there by the reader, not by the server.** On the wire the name is the
220	`event:` line and the payload is the `data:` line, so the payload itself carries no name. The reader
221	joins them — `{ event: name, ...JSON.parse(data) }` — which is what makes `StreamEvent` a union a
222	`switch` can walk. It is also the one place a name the browser does not know can be caught; what
223	happens to one is B6.
224	
225	**Field names are the wire's, in full.** `input_tokens`, not `inputTokens`. A second spelling of a
226	field is a second thing that can drift, and these come straight off the stream and are printed
227	straight onto the screen. The browser's own view model, `WorldView`, keeps its own spellings because
228	it is a different thing with a different life
229	([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md), *One field, two spellings*).
230	
231	**Two fields the shapes sheet deliberately does not have twice.** `no_path` is on `Verdict` and
232	nowhere else — `Done.reason` says why the *generation* stopped and has no `no_path` among its seven.
233	And `mode`, the recording's date and the prompt hash are on `Receipt` and nowhere else —
234	`GenerationStarted` carries none of them. Two derivations of one line eventually disagree, which is
235	the same rule that moved the retraction badge onto the world ([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md) B6).
236	
237	**One field the shapes sheet deliberately does have twice, and why that is not the same mistake.**
238	`frontier` rides both growth events. It is not one fact derived two ways; it is one fact restated
239	after every change to it, so that whichever event arrives is enough on its own to redraw the set of
240	open claims. That is what lets a claim closed by its third refusal lose its rectangle immediately
241	rather than at the next accepted proposal, which might never come.
242	
243	### What the browser asks for
244	
245	```ts
246	export interface GenerateRequest {
247	  /**
248	   * The sentence the reader typed — and, with no key, the whole of how the server
249	   * knows which recording to play. See below. Required, and never empty.
250	   */
251	  readonly hypothesis: string;
252	  /** The Verify door's destination, in the reader's words. Absent is the Explore door. */
253	  readonly target?: string;
254	  /** The reader's own likelihood on the hypothesis. Absent when they chose "I don't know". */
255	  readonly user_belief?: Ranged;
256	  /** Only when reproducing a run we were given a seed for. See below. */
257	  readonly seed?: number;
258	}
259	
260	// The route takes `versions` and `worlds` too, both upper-bounded on it, and the
261	// browser sends neither: the engine's own are what every map in this product is
262	// worked out with, and a screen that could ask for fewer would be a screen that
263	// could quietly make one answer cheaper and less certain than the one beside it.
264	// If a reason to send them ever appears it will be a control a reader can see,
265	// not a default they cannot.
266	
267	/** One async generator over the stream. No component talks to the network. */
268	export async function* generate(request: GenerateRequest): AsyncGenerator<StreamEvent>;
269	```
270	
271	**The browser does not invent a seed.** `seed` is optional and the browser sends one only when it is
272	reproducing a run it was handed a seed for — a shared address, a re-run from the transcript. With
273	none, `engine/ids.py` mints one and `generation_started` says which, so the run is reproducible from
274	the moment it starts and the number on screen is still the engine's. On a replay neither matters: the
275	recording's header carries the seed the recorded run used, and that one wins. A seed is not a claim
276	about the world, but it is still a number, and the rule that no number on screen was made up by the
277	browser is easier to keep than to keep checking.
278	
279	**There is no field naming which recording to play, and there will not be.** With no key the server
280	matches the request's `hypothesis` against each recording's own `generation_started.hypothesis` —
281	exactly, after trimming surrounding spaces — and plays the one that matches; nothing matches, and it
282	says so in one plain sentence rather than guessing. So a launchpad card does the one thing any other
283	caller does: it sends its sentence. Nothing in the browser holds a table of file names, nothing
284	numbers the cards, and the live path and the replayed path send byte-identical requests — which is
285	what makes the reviewer's replay evidence about the live route rather than about a second one.
286	
287	`Ranged` — a likelihood with its two range ends, at full precision — is
288	`frontend/src/world/types.ts`'s, the same shape a belief chip takes
289	([`tiles-ports-wires.md`](tiles-ports-wires.md)).
290	
291	### The `growth` reducer
292	
293	```ts
294	// frontend/src/stream/growth.ts
295	//
296	// One pure function from (state, event) to state. It draws no pixels, makes no
297	// requests, and does no arithmetic: every number it holds is a field it was
298	// handed.
299	
300	/** One proposal the rules refused, as the strip beside the map lists it. */
301	export interface Refusal {
302	  /** Its place in the transcript, counting from 0. The engine's number. */
303	  readonly at: number;
304	  /** What the model wrote. Quoted, never drawn as a tile, never given an identifier. */
305	  readonly claimInWords: string;
306	  /** The validator's own sentences, one per rule broken, in the order it gave them. */
307	  readonly reasons: readonly string[];
308	}
309	
310	/** One reserved rectangle at the growing edge of the map. Never a claim. */
311	export interface Skeleton {
312	  /** `skeleton:<claim id>`, or `skeleton:hypothesis` for the first one. A box's name. */
313	  readonly id: string;
314	  /** The one line it carries. The reader's own sentence, or the open claim's words. */
315	  readonly words: string;
316	  /** The open claim this one hangs off. Null for the first. */
317	  readonly after: PropositionId | null;
318	}
319	
320	/** Where a generation is. Each is a different thing on screen, and none is a spinner. */
321	export type Phase = "waiting" | "growing" | "settled" | "stopped" | "failed" | "ended_early";
322	
323	export interface Growth {
324	  readonly phase: Phase;
325	  /** The engine's name for this run. Null until `generation_started`. */
326	  readonly generationId: string | null;
327	  /**
328	   * The seed every likelihood in this run was worked out from, as its digits.
329	   * Null until the run has started, and never worked out here.
330	   */
331	  readonly seed: string | null;
332	  /** The sentence the reader typed, as the run's first event repeated it back. */
333	  readonly hypothesis: string;
334	  /** The destination the reader named, or null on the Explore door. */
335	  readonly target: string | null;
336	  /**
337	   * The map as far as it has been built, in the same view model the canvas already
338	   * draws. Every number slot the engine has not spoken about reads its absence, so
339	   * a half-built map is drawn by the components that already exist, unchanged.
340	   */
341	  readonly world: WorldView;
342	  /**
343	   * One per claim still open to expand. Rebuilt from `frontier` on **either** growth
344	   * event — accepted or refused — and emptied on `beliefs_propagated`, where the
345	   * frontier is empty by definition.
346	   */
347	  readonly skeletons: readonly Skeleton[];
348	  /** Every refusal, in the order they happened. Never trimmed, never summarised away. */
349	  readonly refusals: readonly Refusal[];
350	  /** The Verify door's answer, when a destination was named. */
351	  readonly verdict: Verdict | null;
352	  /** What the run cost. Null until the receipt arrives; never estimated meanwhile. */
353	  readonly receipt: Receipt | null;
354	  /** Why the generation stopped. Null until it does. */
355	  readonly done: Done | null;
356	  /** The one sentence a `failed` event left. Null otherwise. */
357	  readonly failure: string | null;
358	  /**
359	   * Arrows whose two ends are not both on the map yet, held rather than drawn.
360	   * Expected to stay empty — the engine sends a claim and its incoming arrows in
361	   * one event — and kept because a wire with one end nowhere is a picture of a
362	   * thing that is not true.
363	   */
364	  readonly waitingWires: readonly Link[];
365	  /** Event names this build does not know, and how many of each arrived. */
366	  readonly unknown: ReadonlyMap<string, number>;
367	}
368	```
369	
370	**`beliefs_propagated` replaces the world wholesale.** Until it arrives, `world` is the browser's
371	drawing of the proposals it has watched go past — the claims, the arrows, and an absence in every
372	number slot. When the engine's own world arrives it *is* the world, and the drawing is thrown away
373	rather than merged into. A browser that kept its own version beside the engine's would be a second
374	source of truth, and two sources of truth disagree; this way there is nothing to disagree about.
375	
376	**Who turns the engine's `World` into a `WorldView`, and why it is not a second anybody.** The event
377	carries the server's `World` — the shape in `frontend/src/api/schema.ts`, with the day-by-day series,
378	the retractions and the `Mapping`s the engine writes. The reducer's state holds a `WorldView`, the
379	browser's own hand-written view model, where every number slot is a `Known<T>` carrying either a
380	reading or the reason there is none. Between them sits **exactly one function, the one
381	`ApiWorldSource` already calls** on the answer from `POST /api/worlds`
382	([`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md), *The seam — `WorldSource`*). The reducer calls that same function on
383	`world` and nothing else: no second reader, no "just for the stream" variant, no partial conversion
384	that fills a few fields and leaves the rest. Two functions turning one shape into another would drift
385	inside a week and then a generated map and a fetched map would disagree about a number neither of
386	them computed — the exact failure the whole seam exists to prevent.
387	
388	**Nothing in this reducer mints an identifier.** A claim's identifier is minted by
389	`backend/src/katalyst/engine/ids.py` and arrives on the event. The one name the browser makes is a
390	skeleton's, it names a rectangle rather than a claim, and it is thrown away the moment that claim
391	stops being open. That is the shape of PRD §10 anti-pattern 1 on this side of the wire: not a check
392	that nothing minted an identifier, but nowhere for one to be minted.
393	
394	### What a generation looks like on screen
395	
396	Nothing new is added to the page. The screen is the one
397	[`layout-and-zoom.md`](layout-and-zoom.md) and [`diff-view.md`](diff-view.md) already describe: the
398	canvas, and the **dock** beside it that holds the branch panel, the delta rail and the Inspector.
399	A generation puts three sections into that same dock, above the Inspector, in this order:
400	
401	| Section | When it is there | What it holds |
402	|---|---|---|
403	| **The verdict card** | Only when the reader used the Verify door | The graded path, or the honest *no path reaches this* (B7) |
404	| **The refusal strip** | From the first refusal, for the rest of the run | One row per refused proposal, in the validator's own words (B5) |
405	| **The receipt strip** | From the `receipt` event onward | What the run cost, and the mode it ran in (B6) |
406	
407	The delta rail and these three are never on screen together: a generation is running or a difference
408	is being read, never both. When the run is over, the refusals do not vanish — they move into the
409	Inspector's own **this generation** section with the whole transcript, which is where
410	[`inspector.md`](inspector.md) open question 2 is answered.
