432	## Behaviour
433	
434	Worked on the assignment's first example, the same run `spec/generation/proposals.md` works. A
435	reader types, into the Explore door, the sentence as a person actually types it:
436	
437	> *The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week.*
438	
439	**That sentence is not a claim yet, and the difference matters on this screen.** It says nothing
440	about how anybody would settle it or by when, so nothing can score it (INV-1, the rule that a claim
441	nobody can check is not a claim). The first thing the engine does is turn it into one — *"The Strait
442	of Hormuz is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*, with its criteria,
443	its judge and its date — and **that** is the claim **H** that lands on the map. So two strings are in
444	play from the first second and the chapter keeps them apart: the **typed sentence**, which is what
445	the skeleton carries and what the request sends, and the **claim**, which is what the tile carries
446	once it arrives. A reader watching their own words become a checkable claim is watching the most
447	auditable step in the whole pipeline, and collapsing the two would hide it.
448	
449	The map that grows is the one the rest of this part works on — the cast is in
450	[`README.md`](README.md): **H** the strait open, **C** the war-risk premium falls, **B** Brent
451	settles below $68, **R** OPEC+ announces restraint, **M1** a Polymarket contract, **M2** an
452	energy-fund claim, **N1** talks resume. B7 uses the Verify door instead, with M1 as the destination.
453	
454	**No number in this chapter is a measurement of a generation, and that is on purpose.** Real runs
455	have been made and what they cost is written down, dated, in
456	[`../../docs/measurements.md`](../../docs/measurements.md), which owns those figures. Where a run's
457	own number would go here — a token count, a cost, how long it took, a likelihood — this chapter says
458	which field it comes from and prints nothing, so a chapter about a screen never goes stale because a
459	model got cheaper.
460	
461	### B1 — The first second: a rectangle, never a spinner
462	
463	The reader presses **Build the map**. Three things happen before any model call has returned.
464	
465	1. The request goes. `generate()` posts and starts reading.
466	2. `generation_started` comes back at once — the engine emits it before its first call, so it costs
467	   nothing to wait for — carrying the generation's identifier, the seed, the sentence as typed, and
468	   the destination if there was one.
469	3. **One skeleton tile is drawn**, in the leftmost column, carrying the reader's own sentence.
470	
471	That third step is the first paint, and it is on screen in the time one round trip to our own server
472	takes. It carries no likelihood, because nothing has computed one; it carries the reader's words,
473	because the reader typed them.
474	
475	**What that first rectangle is standing in for.** One call — the one that turns the typed sentence
476	into a checkable claim. It arrives as an ordinary `proposal_accepted` at `at: 0` with an **empty**
477	`links`, because the hypothesis has nothing before it, and the rectangle becomes H's tile. On the
478	Verify door a second such call follows at `at: 1` for the destination, and it too is an ordinary
479	claim with no arrows in. There is no separate event for either, and the browser needs none: from this
480	side both are the same fact the rest of the run keeps repeating — *the map got bigger*.
481	
482	**NFR-7's wording is corrected here.** It reads *"streaming first-paint within 1s of the first
483	token"*, and this pipeline has no first token to be within a second of: the model boundary returns
484	**one whole proposal per call** (record 0006), and one proposal takes seconds to come back. A budget
485	measured from the first token would be a budget nothing could ever miss, because the thing it starts
486	timing from arrives at the same moment as the thing it times. So the budget is measured from the
487	request being accepted, and what has to be on screen within the second is a skeleton at its column —
488	which is the honest reading of what UX-8 promises anyway. **NFR-7 now reads that way**, amended
489	2026-09-20 in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` itself, so the two no longer disagree.
490	
491	**There is no spinner anywhere in this product** — not here, not on the launchpad, not on the
492	`insert` route, not while a lazily fetched midpoint chip is in flight. Waiting is always shown as the
493	shape of the thing being waited for: a reserved rectangle where a claim will go, an absence with its
494	reason where a number will go. Checklist `VR2` is the standing check and
495	`test_there_is_no_spinner_anywhere` is the automated one.
496	
497	### B2 — What a skeleton is, and what it never becomes
498	
499	A skeleton tile is **a reserved rectangle**. Not a shimmer, not a pulse, not a grey bar sliding
500	across a card.
501	
502	* **Its box is a tile's box.** 280 pixels wide (`TILE_WIDTH`), 152 tall (`TILE_MIN_HEIGHT`, the floor
503	  of the tile's own clamp), on the eight-pixel grid, with one border at `--hairline`. It is drawn on
504	  `--surface`, not on `--surface-raised`, so it reads as a space held open rather than as a card with
505	  nothing in it. **The border is dashed** — a solid hairline is what a claim's tile has, and a box
506	  the same weight as a tile beside a tile reads as a tile whose text has not loaded.
507	* **It carries two things and nothing else** *(amended 2026-09-21: this said "one line", and the code
508	  draws two)*. A mark reading **held open**, in the smallest type this product allows and no smaller,
509	  so that what the box is is readable rather than inferred — a reader meeting an empty dashed box for
510	  the first time has no way to know it is a promise rather than a fault. And one line: the first
511	  rectangle carries the reader's own sentence, every later one carries *one step on from "…"*,
512	  quoting the open claim it hangs off — so the reader can see not just that more is coming but *where
513	  from*. No chips, no dates, no clippings, no kind silhouette, no badge, and no number of any kind.
514	* **Its only movement is opacity, at most `--duration-fast`.** Nothing scales, pulses, sweeps or
515	  loops. An animated placeholder is a tool pretending to be busy; a held rectangle is a tool saying
516	  where the next thing goes.
517	* **It is not draggable**, like every other tile (INV-workbench.28).
518	
519	**Where skeletons come from — three events, and nothing else.**
520	
521	| Event | What it leaves on screen |
522	|---|---|
523	| `generation_started` | Exactly one skeleton, for the hypothesis, carrying the sentence as typed |
524	| `proposal_accepted` | One skeleton per claim named in `frontier`, each hanging off that claim. The set is **rebuilt**, so a claim that has left the frontier loses its rectangle in the same frame |
525	| `proposal_rejected` | The same, from the same field. A claim closed by its third refusal in a row is gone from `frontier` here, so its rectangle comes down on the refusal rather than waiting for an accepted proposal that may never come |
526	| `beliefs_propagated` | **Every skeleton goes.** The frontier is empty by definition once the map is finished, so there is nothing left for one to stand for |
527	| `failed` | **Every skeleton goes** *(added 2026-09-21)*. A rectangle is a promise that a claim is coming, and after a run breaks nothing is. The claims that were still open are in the working either way, so nothing is lost by taking the boxes down; what is lost by leaving them up is a reader waiting for a claim for ever |
528	| *the body ending with no terminator at all* | **Every skeleton goes** *(added 2026-09-21)*. The same rule, for the case that is not an event: see B3's *a stream that simply stops*, below |
529	
530	So the skeletons on screen are the **frontier, drawn** — rebuilt from whichever growth event arrived
531	last, and emptied when the world lands. That is a fact the stream states, never a guess the browser
532	makes, and it is the whole reason both growth events carry `frontier` rather than only the accepted
533	one.
534	
535	**Two things close a claim and neither makes an event of its own**: the model answering *Stop* on
536	that line, and its third refusal in a row. Both are recorded — a *Stop* leaves a transcript line, and
537	every refusal is already a `proposal_rejected` — and the browser is never *told* a claim closed,
538	because it can read it: the next growth event's `frontier` simply no longer names it. **So no
539	rectangle ever stands where nothing is coming**, and no event exists whose only job is to announce
540	that nothing happened.
541	
542	It is worth saying what the browser therefore *cannot* say. The stream has no "a call has gone out"
543	event, so **one skeleton stands for one claim still open, not for one model call in flight.** Three
544	calls may be out against one open claim and there is still one rectangle. If a later stack wants the
545	count of calls on screen, the stream has to say it; the browser must not count for itself. (Open
546	question 1.)
547	
548	**A skeleton is never a claim.** It has no identifier on the map — its name, `skeleton:<claim id>`,
549	names a rectangle. It never enters `WorldView.claims`, never reaches the network, never appears in
550	the outline view, cannot be selected, cannot open the Inspector, and has no belief chip to leave
551	empty. There is no number on it to be a number nobody computed, because there is no number on it at
552	all.
553	
554	**On Hormuz, three rectangles and then two.** Walking the run in B3's table: after step 3 — the
555	proposal that brings **B**, caused by **C**, with the single arrow `C → B` — the frontier names H, C
556	and B, so three rectangles stand at the growing edge, reading *one step on from "The Strait of Hormuz
557	is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*, *…from "Lloyd's war-risk
558	insurance premium for Gulf transits falls below 0.4%"* and *…from "Brent crude settles below $68 for
559	five sessions"*.
560	
561	**Step 4 takes one of them down, and it is an accepted proposal that does it.** That step adds the
562	arrow `H → B` and no claim at all; H now causes three claims, which is its full width, so H closes
563	and step 4's `frontier` names only C and B. H's rectangle goes on that event — not because anything
564	announced it, but because the frontier stopped naming it. **N1 never had one:** it arrived at step 2
565	as a `not_tradeable` ending, and an ending has nothing downstream of it, so it never joined the
566	frontier in the first place. The map is honest that the chain stops there, and it is honest about it
567	by drawing nothing rather than by drawing something that then disappears.
568	
569	### B3 — The whole run, as the canvas sees it
570	
571	The same generation `spec/generation/proposals.md` B4 writes out call by call, read from this side of
572	the wire. `at` is the transcript position; the last column is what stands at the growing edge **after**
573	that event has been folded in.
574	
575	| `at` | Event | What lands on the canvas | Rectangles standing |
576	|---|---|---|---|
577	| 0 | `proposal_accepted` | **H** — *"The Strait of Hormuz is open to unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days"*. `links` is empty; the first rectangle becomes this tile | H |
578	| 1 | `proposal_accepted` | **C** and the wire `H → C` | H · C |
579	| 2 | `proposal_accepted` | **N1** and the wire `H → N1`. An ending, so it never joins the frontier and never gets a rectangle | H · C |
580	| 3 | `proposal_accepted` | **B** and the wire `C → B` — one claim, one incoming arrow | H · C · B |
581	| 4 | `proposal_accepted` | **No claim at all**: `proposition` is null and `links` holds the one new wire `H → B`. H reaches its full width here and closes | C · B |
582	| 5 | `proposal_accepted` | **M1** and the wire `B → M1`. A tradeable ending | C · B |
583	| 6 | `proposal_rejected` | Nothing on the canvas; one row on the refusal strip (B5). The frontier is unchanged — this is B's first refusal, not its third | C · B |
584	| 7 | `proposal_accepted` | **M2** and the wire `B → M2`. A tradeable ending | C · B |
585	| — | nothing on the wire | C answers *Stop*; a transcript line and no event | B |
586	| — | nothing on the wire | B answers *Stop*; the last open claim closes | — |
587	| — | `beliefs_propagated` | Every chip fills, at once (B4). Every rectangle goes | — |
588	| — | `receipt` · `done` | The receipt strip; the stop reason, `reached_terminal`, because the last open claim answered *Stop* (B7). `claims=6`, `links=6`, `rejected=1` — count them off the rows above | — |
589	
590	Two things worth reading off that table. **The transcript's numbering has gaps** — a client sees 7
591	and then the closing events, and the two missing positions are the two stops, which make no event
592	because nothing about the map changed. And **no event ever says a claim closed**: the rectangle for H
593	comes down at step 4 because step 4's `frontier` stopped naming it, and the last two come down on
594	`beliefs_propagated`, where the frontier is empty by definition.
595	
596	The map that grows is **not the shipped fixture and does not pretend to be**: six claims where the
597	fixture has seven, and no feedback arrow `B → R`, because a proposal has no `reflexive` field and
598	nothing can propose one. Every chapter in this part works the fixture; this one works the run, and
599	the difference is a fact about generation rather than a discrepancy to smooth over.
600	
601	**Where a claim lands is decided by its causes, not by when it arrived.** The layout is the layered
602	one [`layout-and-zoom.md`](layout-and-zoom.md) owns: a claim sits in a column to the right of
603	everything that causes it. N1 arrives third and lands in column 1; B arrives fourth and lands in
604	column 2. The picture reads causality, and arrival order leaves no trace in it.
605	
606	**Nothing that is already on screen moves.** This is not new machinery and growth adds none. The
607	rule already lives in `readPositions` in `frontend/src/graph/elkGraph.ts`, in those words: *a tile
608	that had a position keeps that position, to the pixel, and only a tile that had none takes a new
609	one.* Growth is the case that rule was written for. Every claim the engine sends is strictly
610	downstream of the map so far — a `ClaimProposal` brings one claim and the one arrow into it, so that
611	arrow's source is always a claim that already exists — which is exactly the precondition
612	INV-workbench.22 names. A late arrival finds a gap; nothing above it, beside it or before it shifts.
613	
614	**The layout answers later, and a box waits for its place rather than borrowing one** *(added
615	2026-09-21)*. The layout runs on a background thread, so between a claim arriving on the stream and
616	that claim being drawn there is always a gap — a frame on this machine, most of a second on a tired
617	one. What the map does in that gap is the whole of `frontend/src/graph/onTheGlass.ts`, and it is one
618	rule: **a box is drawn where the layout put it, and a reserved rectangle stands until the claim it
619	was holding a place for is drawn.** Not until the event carrying that claim arrived — those are two
620	different moments, and everything between them would otherwise be a map with a claim on its way and
621	no rectangle anywhere, which is a growing map that has stopped saying where it is going. It is not a
622	corner case: a generated map's frontier is usually one claim wide, so it turns over completely every
623	few proposals, and each turnover is one of these moments.
624	
625	The rectangle goes the instant the map is whole again, so this can never become a way of leaving one
626	up: a rectangle whose claim closed with nothing coming after it — a third refusal, a broken run, the
627	likelihoods landing — goes at once, because then nothing on the map is waiting for a place.
628	
629	**The one box the map places itself is a rectangle, and it is the first.** Before the layout has
630	answered even once the origin is nobody's place: there is nothing to be drawn on top of, and a
631	generation's first paint may not be an empty stage (B1). So the map puts the rectangle held open for
632	the reader's own sentence there itself. It was *the first box* rather than *the first rectangle*
633	until 2026-09-21, and on a machine where the first answer lost its race to the first proposal that
634	box was the claim. Two promises broke at once. The growing edge went quiet, which is what continuous
635	integration read. And the claim was drawn at the origin, which is not where the layout puts the first
636	box of a map — the layout leaves a margin of its own around what it lays out, so the tile then moved
637	by that margin, and *nothing already drawn moves* is the loudest promise this part makes. How far it
638	moved was read off the page by the end-to-end test itself, which is what caught it: it holds the
639	first tile's place and compares it with itself at the end of the run.
640	
641	**A wire draws only after both of its ends exist.** In practice the engine makes this true by
642	construction, twice over: a `ClaimProposal` brings the claim and the arrow into it in one event, and
643	an arrows-only proposal names two claims that are already on the map. The reducer does not rely on
644	either. An arrow whose two ends are not both on the map goes into `waitingWires` and is drawn the
645	moment the second end arrives. The list is expected to stay empty for ever, and the test that proves
646	the rule **builds** a stream that fills it rather than assuming one cannot exist. A wire with one end
647	nowhere is a picture of something that is not true, and half a wire is worse than no wire.
648	
649	**The wave is the one already budgeted.** Each wire arrives with the propagation wave
650	[`color-motion-type.md`](color-motion-type.md) spends: about 200 milliseconds (`--duration-wave`),
651	its column 60 milliseconds (`--duration-stagger`) after the column before. It is already built —
652	`.canvas[data-arriving="yes"]` in `frontend/src/graph/canvas.css`, with a `wave-<n>` class per
653	column. Growth switches it on per arrival instead of once per map, and adds no fourth animation to
654	the budget of three.
655	
656	**The honest wart, and the one event that could cause it.** An arrows-only proposal — step 4 above —
657	joins two tiles that are already placed, and because the pin is absolute the wire is drawn where they
658	sit rather than re-laying out the map to suit it. On this run that costs nothing: H is in column 0
659	and B in column 2, so `H → B` points rightwards like every other wire and no column would have moved
660	anyway. But an arrows-only proposal whose source happens to sit *right* of its target would be drawn
661	pointing backwards, which is honest about where the tiles are and misleading about the argument. The
662	trade is the one [`layout-and-zoom.md`](layout-and-zoom.md) anti-pattern 7 makes: the map should be
663	still while you read it, and losing your place is the worse failure. Whether the map re-lays out once
664	when the run finishes is Open question 2, **answered below**.
665	
666	**A stream that simply stops** *(added 2026-09-21)*. Every stream a reader stayed for ends in exactly
667	one `done` or one `failed`. A body that ends with neither is a dropped connection —
668	[`spec/generation/streaming.md`](../generation/streaming.md): *"a dropped stream is a finished
669	generation with no terminator. The browser says the stream ended early and offers to run it again."*
670	A server restarted, a proxy gave up on a connection it thought was idle, a laptop slept during a
671	ten-minute run: none of those is a fault anybody on this side can name, and none is a `failed` event,
672	because none of them is the run saying anything at all.
673	
674	What the browser does is three things and no more. **The rectangles come down**, which is the other
675	half of *no rectangle ever stands where nothing is coming* — after this, nothing is, and a map left
676	growing for ever is the one screen in this product that lies without saying a word: it is drawn
677	exactly as a map about to change and it is never going to change again. **The map is kept**, every
678	claim and arrow that arrived, with nothing invented to fill the gap and nothing greyed. And **one
679	plain sentence**, in the same line under the map that says why any other run ended, with **the offer
680	to run the same sentence again beside it** — an offer that says on its face what pressing it costs:
681	*run it again — this asks the model again, and spends again* on a copy with a key, and *play it again
682	— this plays the recording again, and spends nothing* on one without. A control that quietly spends
683	money the second time it is pressed is the one control in this product that must say so before it is
684	pressed.
685	
686	It is not folded from an event, because there is no event: the reader of the stream is the only thing
687	that can notice a body ending, and it hands the reducer that fact by name (`theStreamEnded`) rather
688	than by inventing a ninth event the server never sent. The working as far as it got is still readable
689	at `GET /api/generate/{generation_id}/transcript`, which is the whole reason this state keeps the map
690	rather than clearing it.
691	
692	### B4 — Chips resolve last, and they resolve once
693	
694	**While the map grows, every model chip reads *no engine yet*.** The claims that arrive carry their
695	stated `prior`, and the tile never draws a prior — a second number beside the model's would be a
696	fourth voice ([`tiles-ports-wires.md`](tiles-ports-wires.md)). So a growing map is the same picture
697	this part already ships: real claims, real arrows, real provenance marks, and an absence with its
698	reason in every likelihood slot.
699	
700	**When `beliefs_propagated` arrives, they all fill at once.** One event, one world, every number.
701	The chip's own sentence switches from the *stated* pair to record 0014's *computed* pair with no
702	change to the component, because `WorldView.versions` arrives on the same world and that is the one
703	field the chip reads to choose (Kent, K3; `tiles-ports-wires.md`, *What the model chip says about its
704	own range*).
705	
706	**Never per tile, and never twice.** A likelihood that changed four times as its causes arrived would
707	be four numbers nobody computed: the first three would each be the answer to a question about a map
708	that no longer exists. There is exactly one propagation per generation and exactly one
709	`beliefs_propagated` event, so a chip goes from its absence to its number once and stays.
710	
711	**The reveal is not the number-roll.** The third budgeted animation rolls a likelihood from an old
712	figure to a new one, and here there is no old figure — there is an absence. So the chips appear with
713	an opacity change at `--duration-fast` and nothing rolls. The number-roll still has nothing to roll
714	until an edit moves a number, which is this stack's second pull request.
715	
716	### B5 — Every refusal is on screen, in the validator's own words
717	
718	**A rejected proposal is an event, not an error.** Nothing is retried quietly out of sight and
719	nothing is swallowed. The engine may try again — up to three fresh proposals for one open claim,
720	none of them told why the last was refused (Kent, G4; record 0003's dated amendment) — and **every
721	one of those attempts that was refused is on screen.**
722	
723	The refusal strip is one row per refusal, in the order they happened, newest last. A row carries the
724	model's own words on its first line, ellipsized at a word boundary, and beneath them the validator's
725	own sentence — **one per rule broken**, because a proposal that broke three rules and shows one is a
726	refusal the reader has half seen. The rows are short and there are few of them; a run with a strip
727	long enough to need trimming has a prompt problem, not a layout problem.
728	
729	Two rules the strip obeys, both inherited rather than invented. **The sentence is the validator's, as
730	it wrote it** — `spec/graph/validity.md` owns that copy, and its rules for it are that a message
731	names the claim by its words, never by its identifier, and says what is missing rather than that
732	something failed. The browser never composes a sentence about a refusal. And **a refused claim is
733	never drawn as a tile and never given an identifier** — `claim_in_words` is quoted and nothing else
734	is done with it, which is the same rule as B2's.
735	
736	**On Hormuz, at step 6.** Every recording must hold at least one refusal (record 0012), and the map's
737	own shape supplies it. Expanding B, the model proposes an arrow rather than a claim — `B → H`,
738	*cheaper crude reduces the incentive to close the strait*. Read on its own it is a reasonable
739	sentence; added to the map it closes `H → B → H`, because step 4 has already drawn `H → B`. The rules
740	refuse it with exactly one violation, and its message is the validator's, word for word:
741	
742	```
743	proposal 6   refused
744	   "cheaper crude reduces the incentive to close the strait"
745	   These claims form a loop with no delay in it: "The Strait of Hormuz is open to
746	   unrestricted commercial transit for 14 consecutive days" → "Brent crude settles
747	   below $68 for five sessions" → "The Strait of Hormuz is open to unrestricted
748	   commercial transit for 14 consecutive days". Mark the arrow where a market feeds
749	   back on the world as reflexive and give it a delay, or remove one arrow.
750	```
751	
752	Nothing moves on the canvas when that row appears. B is on its **first** refusal, not its third, so
753	step 6's `frontier` still names C and B and both rectangles stay exactly where they were. Step 7 is
754	the same call asked again with a byte-identical prompt — the next call is never told what was wrong
755	— and it comes back with M2.
756	
757	That row is half the product. It is the moment a reader can see that our own code, not the model,
758	decides what the map is allowed to contain — and it says the one thing that would have made the
759	arrow legal, which is the difference between a rejection and an insult.
760	
761	`proposal 6` is `at`, the engine's own position in the transcript, printed so the row can be found
762	again in the Inspector. Selecting the row opens the Inspector's **this generation** section at that
763	line.
764	
765	### B6 — The receipt strip, and where a transcript is read
766	
767	**This answers [`inspector.md`](inspector.md) open question 2.**
768	
769	When `receipt` arrives, the strip beneath the refusals fills in. It prints what the engine sent and
770	adds nothing up:
771	
772	```
773	THIS GENERATION
774	  model            <Receipt.model>
775	  calls            <Receipt.calls>
776	  tokens in        <Receipt.input_tokens>
777	  tokens out       <Receipt.output_tokens>
778	  read from cache  <Receipt.cache_read_tokens>
779	  web searches     <Receipt.searches>
780	  cost             <Receipt.dollars>, in the two places money has
781	  took             <Receipt.seconds> — "the replay took", on a replay
782	  how hard the
783	    model tried    <Receipt.effort>
784	  mode             live
785	```
786	
787	**Money has two places** *(coordinator, 2026-09-21)*. It printed up to four — `$0.6132` — which is
788	the same fake precision checklist `VR4` exists to stop, in the place a reader is most likely to
789	compare two runs: the fourth place is a rounding of a price table, and four places read as a
790	measurement. **And a guard word exactly when it is true** (K2): a run that spent nothing prints
791	`$0.00`, which is a computed zero and reads as one, and a run that spent something and less than a
792	cent prints `<$0.01`, because `$0.00` there would say a run was free when it was not. One function,
793	used by the generation's strip and the insert's alike, so the two cannot come to write a cost two
794	ways.
795	
796	**And `took` says whose clock it is.** On a live run it is how long the run took. On a replay it is
797	how long the **replay** took — a few seconds of paced playback beside a map that took eleven minutes
798	to make — so the row reads *the replay took*. A reader comparing the two figures without that word
799	would conclude this product is two hundred times faster than it is. The recorded run's own duration
800	is not on the wire; when it is, this row can carry it and say which is which.
801	
802	**Amended 2026-09-21 — there are ten readings, and the tenth is how hard the model tried.** A plain
803	word: `default` when nothing was asked for and the service's own applied, otherwise `low`, `medium`,
804	`high`, `xhigh` or `max`. One setting with two pinned defaults behind it — **a recording is made rich
805	and a live run is made fast** (Kent, G13) — so two maps of the same sentence at the same seed can
806	differ for a reason that has nothing to do with the sentence, and a reader comparing one with the
807	other is entitled to see which they are looking at. It is the word the service takes rather than a
808	number, because a number would be this browser translating one thing into another and printing the
809	translation.
810	
811	Four things about it.
812	
813	* **Every one of those is a field.** The browser does not add the two token counts together, does not
814	  work out a cost from a token count and a price, and does not time anything itself. A price table
815	  lives in exactly one module on the server (`engine/pricing.py`) with the day it was read beside it,
816	  and the dollars on this strip came from there. **Searches are a row of their own** because they are
817	  billed apart from tokens: without that row, `dollars` is a number a reader could check against the
818	  token counts and find wrong.
819	* **Checklist `VR4` is about likelihoods.** *"No number shows more than two significant figures, and
820	  none is missing its range"* is the rule that stops a fake-precise `.347` reaching the screen
821	  (NFR-1). A token count, a call count, a duration and a dollar figure are counts and measurements:
822	  they are printed whole, in `--font-mono` with fixed-width digits, and they have no range because
823	  nothing sampled them. The same reading already lets a lag chip say *14 days* and a tile be 280
824	  pixels wide.
825	* **In replay the mode reads `replay`**, the recording's date sits beside it, and `cost` reads what
826	  the rebuilt receipt carries, which is zero. That zero is a computed zero — the recording was played,
827	  nothing was called, so nothing was spent — not an empty slot, and it is printed rather than hidden.
828	* **Before the receipt arrives the strip is not there.** No running estimate, no ticking cost, no
829	  progress bar. A cost nobody has totalled is a number nobody computed.
830	
831	**The working lives in the Inspector, and it is the panel's third subject.** Until now the Inspector
832	opened on a claim or an arrow. It now also opens on the generation itself, and that section holds
833	*(amended 2026-09-21)*: the seed the run drew with and the prompt's fingerprint, whole, each with the
834	sentence saying what it is for; the whole transcript, one line per proposal in order, accepted or
835	refused, each accepted one naming the claim it became and each refused one carrying every sentence
836	the validator wrote; a line per event name this build did not know, with how many of each arrived;
837	and one sentence pointing at the strip for what the run cost. **It carries no copy of the receipt's
838	ten readings.** It is drawn from the moment there is a generation, with whatever has arrived in it
839	and an em dash in each slot that has not — a section that appeared only once everything had landed
840	would be a panel that is empty exactly while a reader is most likely to open it. The transcript is
841	read from `GET /api/generate/{generation_id}/transcript`, which the server holds
842	in memory for the life of the process — there is no storage in this stack, and a transcript outliving
843	the process is stack 05's question (FR-31).
844	
845	**An event this build does not know is ignored, and said out loud.** The reader folds it in as a name
846	and a count and changes nothing else: it does not throw, because a browser that crashes on a new
847	event makes the server unable to add one; and it does not disappear, because a dropped event makes a
848	missing feature look like a working one. The line is the only place it shows, and one line in the
849	transcript is the right size for *"this build saw two events it has no name for"*.
850	
851	Every number on the strip is therefore one click from its why in the strictest sense
852	[`inspector.md`](inspector.md) INV-workbench.51 asks for: the click opens the panel at the transcript
853	that produced the count.
854	
855	### B7 — The Verify door: a graded path, or an honest *no path reaches this*
856	
857	The Verify door is **one extra field on the same input bar**, not a second screen: the reader names
858	where they think it ends. On Hormuz: *the Polymarket contract "Brent below $70 on 2026-10-31"*. The
859	generation runs exactly as before, and one more event arrives.
860	
861	**`kind: "reached"` — the graded path.** A card at the top of the dock, naming the steps of
862	`Verdict.path` in order in the claims' own words, with the multiplied-out likelihood of those steps
863	beside it (INV-8), the number taken from `Verdict.product` and multiplied by nobody here. Under it,
864	word for word, the same wart the Inspector's path bar prints, because there is one wording and one
865	place it is written ([`inspector.md`](inspector.md) B5): the factors are each read on their own
866	resolve-by day, so the product multiplies numbers read on different days, and **it is not a joint
867	probability**. The card and the path bar share the sentence, not the component *(corrected
868	2026-09-21)*: one exported constant, `PATH_PRODUCT_WART`, which the card prints and the bar prints.
869	They are two different components — the bar is a claim's own route with its chips, the card is the
870	Verify door's answer with its steps and its control — and saying they are one would have somebody
871	look for a shared component that does not exist. What must not drift is the wording, and a constant
872	is what stops wording drifting.
873	
874	**How long the route is is printed, never counted** *(added 2026-09-21)*. `Verdict.why` is the
875	engine's own sentence and it already says it — *"…reaches it in 2 steps"*. The card used to say it
876	again underneath, worked out as one fewer than the claims on `Verdict.path`: two derivations of one
877	fact, agreeing exactly until the day the engine counts a step differently, and then the card
878	contradicts itself in two adjacent paragraphs with nothing on screen to say which is right.
879	
880	**`kind: "no_path"` — a finding, drawn as a finding.** This is not a failure state and it does not
881	look like one. The card carries `Verdict.why` — the engine's own plain sentence — and names
882	`Verdict.nearest`, the closest claim the map did reach, with one control that selects that claim on
883	the map so the reader can see where the path stopped.
884	
885	**No bridge is drawn. Ever.** No dotted arrow from the nearest claim to the destination, no ghost
886	tile for the destination, no "probably connects" wording. A path that does not exist is the most
887	valuable thing this door can tell you, and drawing a faint one would be the traceability veto with a
888	dashed stroke.
889	
890	**`no_path` is on the verdict and nowhere else.** `Done.reason` has seven values and none of them is
891	`no_path`; it says why the *generation* stopped, which is a different question with a different
892	answer. A run can reach its claim cap and still have found a path, and a run can end cleanly and
893	have found none.
894	
895	**And when the generation itself stops, the strip says why, in the engine's words for it.** One
896	reason arrives, never a list, and it names **what closed the last claim that was still open** — with
897	the spending limit and the no-ending case overriding everything above them. `spec/generation/proposals.md`
898	B4 owns that rule; this table owns the words.
899	
900	| `Done.reason` | What the strip says |
901	|---|---|
902	| `reached_terminal` | The last line closed properly: it reached something you could trade, or a stated reason there is nothing to trade, or the model had nothing more to add. |
903	| `depth_cap` | The last line still open ran as far from your sentence as one generation goes, and stopped there. |
904	| `width_cap` | The last line still open was closed because that claim already has every effect one generation draws from it. |
905	| `claim_cap` | The last line still open was closed because the map was full. |
906	| `spend_cap` | The run reached its spending limit and stopped where it was. The receipt says what it spent. |
907	| `refusal_cap` | One line was abandoned: three proposals in a row for it were refused. |
908	| `no_terminal` | One last call asked every open claim where it ends, and none of them ends in something you could trade. |
909	
910	Two things those seven sentences do on purpose. **No sentence blames the model for our own rules.**
911	Three refusals in a row is our validator turning proposals down and our cap deciding that three is
912	enough; a sentence reading *"the model stopped answering"* would be a screen accusing a third party
913	of a decision we took, which is the reverse of the receipt this product writes everywhere else. And
914	**each one names the cap and not its value**, because the stream carries no value. A limit the browser
915	printed from memory would be a number nobody on this screen computed, and a limit that had quietly
916	changed on the server would then be a number that was wrong. The values and their justifications are
917	`spec/generation/proposals.md`'s.

1374	## ANTI-PATTERNS
1375	
1376	1. **Do not put a spinner anywhere, not even for a moment, not even a small one.** *Because* a
1377	   spinner says only "wait", and the thing being waited for has a shape — a claim at a column, a
1378	   number in a slot — which says "wait" *and* what for *and* where it will land. It is also a named
1379	   veto condition (PRD §10 anti-pattern 9). **Instead:** a reserved rectangle where the claim goes,
1380	   and an absence with its reason where the number goes.
1381	
1382	2. **Do not animate a skeleton.** *Because* a shimmer is a tool performing busyness at a reader who
1383	   is waiting on a model call that takes seconds, and the fourth animation would be the one that
1384	   turns a motion budget into a suggestion. **Instead:** a still rectangle, appearing and going with
1385	   an opacity change of at most 120 milliseconds.
1386	
1387	3. **Do not let a belief chip fill in as its causes arrive.** *Because* a likelihood computed from
1388	   half a map is the answer to a question about a map that will not exist in a second, and a number
1389	   that changes four times is four numbers nobody computed. **Instead:** every chip reads *no engine
1390	   yet* until `beliefs_propagated`, and then they all resolve at once, once.
1391	
1392	4. **Do not hide, merge or summarise a refusal.** *Because* watching our own rules turn the model
1393	   down is the evidence that the model is not in charge of the map, and a run that shows only its
1394	   successes is a demo rather than a tool. **Instead:** one row per refusal, every sentence the
1395	   validator wrote, kept on screen for the run and in the transcript afterwards.
1396	
1397	5. **Do not draw a refused claim as a faint tile, a ghost or a struck-through box.** *Because* the
1398	   moment it has a box it needs an identifier, and the model would then have caused an identifier to
1399	   exist — which the schema is shaped to make impossible. **Instead:** quote its words in the strip
1400	   and give it nothing else.
1401	
1402	6. **Do not draw a bridge to a destination the map did not reach.** *Because* "no path reaches this"
1403	   is the most valuable answer the Verify door has, and a dotted arrow suggesting one might is a
1404	   fabrication in the exact place the honesty bar exists to prevent one (FR-7). **Instead:** the
1405	   engine's sentence, the nearest claim named, and nothing drawn between them.
1406	
1407	7. **Do not re-layout the map while it grows to make the picture tidier.** *Because* a map that
1408	   rearranges itself under the reader's eye costs them the tile they were reading, which is the
1409	   failure the whole layout chapter exists to prevent. **Instead:** pin absolutely, let a late arrival
1410	   find a gap, and say out loud what that costs (B3).
1411	
1412	8. **Do not estimate the cost, the progress or the remaining claims while a run is going.** *Because*
1413	   a percentage nobody computed is a number nobody computed wearing a progress bar, and the caps that
1414	   would have to be divided by are the server's and are not on the stream. **Instead:** show what has
1415	   arrived, and the receipt when the receipt arrives.
1416	
1417	9. **Do not throw on an event name the build does not know, and do not swallow it either.** *Because*
1418	   a browser that crashes on a new event makes the server unable to add one, and a browser that
1419	   drops it silently makes a missing feature look like a working one. **Instead:** ignore it, count
1420	   it, and say so in the transcript.
1421	
1422	10. **Do not let the browser build a second version of the world beside the engine's.** *Because* the
1423	    growing map and the propagated world would then be two answers to one question, and the day they
1424	    differ by half a point nobody can say which is right. **Instead:** the drawing is thrown away
1425	    when `beliefs_propagated` arrives, and the engine's world is the world.
1426	
1427	11. **Do not fill in "I don't know".** *Because* a `.5` posted on the reader's behalf is the one
1428	    number in the request that nobody elicited, and it would sit on the hypothesis as a `user` belief
1429	    for the rest of the session. **Instead:** send no user belief at all, and let the slot read its
1430	    own absence.
1431	
1432	12. **Do not give a box a place because the layout has not answered yet** *(added 2026-09-21)*.
1433	    *Because* the only place available to give is the map's origin, which either belongs to a box
1434	    already standing there or is about to belong to this one at coordinates the layout chose — so the
1435	    box lands where it does not belong and then moves, on the one screen whose whole promise is that
1436	    nothing already drawn moves. **Instead:** draw nothing that has no place, and let the rectangle
1437	    already standing go on saying where the claim is going until the claim itself is drawn.

1441	## Open questions
1442	
1443	*Raised 2026-09-17.*
1444	
1445	1. **Should the stream say when a call goes out?** The eight events say what came back, so the
1446	   browser can draw the frontier but cannot honestly say how many proposals are in flight — three
1447	   calls against one open claim show one rectangle (B2). A ninth event would fix it and would also be
1448	   the first event that carries no decision, only activity, which is a different kind of thing to put
1449	   on a stream. **Owner:** `spec/generation/streaming.md`, if anyone ever wants the count on screen.
1450	
1451	2. **Does the map re-lay out once when the run finishes?** **Answered 2026-09-21: no — and the real
1452	   question turned out to be a different one.**
1453	
1454	   The measurement, taken on the coordinator's ten-claim run at 1600 × 1000, the size the whole
1455	   interface is designed against: the stage is **1264 × 801**, the map is framed at **0.85** — the
1456	   floor below which a tile would have to become a summary — and at that framing **six of the ten
1457	   tiles are whole on the glass, four are wholly below it and none is cut**. No arrow points
1458	   backwards, on this run or on the chapter's own, so the thing a re-layout would have tidied did not
1459	   happen; what did happen is that **a third of the map was off the screen with nothing saying so**,
1460	   which is far worse and is not a layout problem at all. A map that is cut with nothing saying so is
1461	   read as a map that ends there, and for a causal map that is the worst thing it can be read as: the
1462	   reader concludes the argument stops where the window does.
1463	
1464	   So the answer is the one that costs the reader nothing: **the map is never re-laid out, and the
1465	   stage says where it is cut.** A two-pixel rule in `--text-muted` sits at whichever edge has map
1466	   beyond it and at no edge that has not — the same rule, the same weight and the same colour the
1467	   panel beside it already uses for the same fact, drawn as the four sides of one box so a corner
1468	   reads as a corner. The stage measures it about itself, because the two boxes are measured
1469	   differently: a panel is scrolled and a stage is panned.
1470	
1471	   Re-laying out would still move every tile once at the moment the reader starts reading, and it
1472	   would still not put the four tiles on the glass — there is no zoom that fits ten tiles in 1264 ×
1473	   801 and keeps them readable, which is exactly why the zoom floor exists. **Owner:** closed.
1474	
1475	3. **What does an `insert` cost, and where does that show?** **Answered 2026-09-20 by
1476	   [`spec/generation/streaming.md`](../generation/streaming.md), drawn 2026-09-21, and nothing is
1477	   open.** The route answers a `DraftedInsert` — the edit and its own `Receipt` — and the cost is
1478	   drawn beside the drafted claim by the same strip, with the same ten readings, that a generation's
1479	   receipt is drawn by. What made it answerable was learning that an insert is **several** calls
1480	   rather than one: the starting-claim shape drafts the reader's sentence, and then the ordinary walk
1481	   proposes its arrows, one call each. A running total in the browser lost on two counts — it is a
1482	   number added up by something other than the engine, and it vanishes on a page reload. **Owner:**
1483	   closed. See B8.
1484	
1485	4. **Where does a replayed run's pacing come from, and is it the same on every machine?**
1486	   **Answered 2026-09-17 by `spec/generation/replay.md`, and nothing is open.** The delay is fixed on
1487	   the **server** — an argument with a default the builder picks against a measurement, because a
1488	   replay that races teaches a reviewer that the product is faster than it is — so two readers' replays
1489	   are the same length. It is **one setting**, `KATALYST_REPLAY_PACE` in seconds, read once by
1490	   `katalyst.settings` and never a field on the request: a client that could ask for a replay with no
1491	   pause would let anyone with the network tab open skip the thing the recording exists to show. A
1492	   pace of zero means no pause at all, which is the same question answered with a smaller number
1493	   rather than a second switch beside it *(2026-09-21; it was a length and an `instant` flag)*. **The browser
1494	   therefore paces nothing, waits on nothing, and has no pacing code at all** — it reads events as
1495	   they arrive, which is the same thing it does live.
1496	
1497	5. **How long is a refusal strip allowed to get?** Three refusals close an open claim and the caps
1498	   bound the whole run, so the strip is bounded — but nothing says by what, and a run that refused
1499	   twenty proposals would fill the dock and push the Inspector off the screen. Scrolling the strip is
1500	   the obvious answer and it is also the answer that lets a reader miss a refusal. **Owner:** this
1501	   chapter, once a real run has been watched.

   yet* until `beliefs_propagated`, and then they all resolve at once, once.

4. **Do not hide, merge or summarise a refusal.** *Because* watching our own rules turn the model
   down is the evidence that the model is not in charge of the map, and a run that shows only its
   successes is a demo rather than a tool. **Instead:** one row per refusal, every sentence the
   validator wrote, kept on screen for the run and in the transcript afterwards.

5. **Do not draw a refused claim as a faint tile, a ghost or a struck-through box.** *Because* the
   moment it has a box it needs an identifier, and the model would then have caused an identifier to
   exist — which the schema is shaped to make impossible. **Instead:** quote its words in the strip
   and give it nothing else.

6. **Do not draw a bridge to a destination the map did not reach.** *Because* "no path reaches this"
   is the most valuable answer the Verify door has, and a dotted arrow suggesting one might is a
   fabrication in the exact place the honesty bar exists to prevent one (FR-7). **Instead:** the
   engine's sentence, the nearest claim named, and nothing drawn between them.

7. **Do not re-layout the map while it grows to make the picture tidier.** *Because* a map that
   rearranges itself under the reader's eye costs them the tile they were reading, which is the
   failure the whole layout chapter exists to prevent. **Instead:** pin absolutely, let a late arrival
   find a gap, and say out loud what that costs (B3).

8. **Do not estimate the cost, the progress or the remaining claims while a run is going.** *Because*
   a percentage nobody computed is a number nobody computed wearing a progress bar, and the caps that
   would have to be divided by are the server's and are not on the stream. **Instead:** show what has
   arrived, and the receipt when the receipt arrives.

9. **Do not throw on an event name the build does not know, and do not swallow it either.** *Because*
   a browser that crashes on a new event makes the server unable to add one, and a browser that
   drops it silently makes a missing feature look like a working one. **Instead:** ignore it, count
   it, and say so in the transcript.

10. **Do not let the browser build a second version of the world beside the engine's.** *Because* the
    growing map and the propagated world would then be two answers to one question, and the day they
    differ by half a point nobody can say which is right. **Instead:** the drawing is thrown away
    when `beliefs_propagated` arrives, and the engine's world is the world.

11. **Do not fill in "I don't know".** *Because* a `.5` posted on the reader's behalf is the one
    number in the request that nobody elicited, and it would sit on the hypothesis as a `user` belief
    for the rest of the session. **Instead:** send no user belief at all, and let the slot read its
    own absence.

12. **Do not give a box a place because the layout has not answered yet** *(added 2026-09-21)*.
    *Because* the only place available to give is the map's origin, which either belongs to a box
    already standing there or is about to belong to this one at coordinates the layout chose — so the
    box lands where it does not belong and then moves, on the one screen whose whole promise is that
    nothing already drawn moves. **Instead:** draw nothing that has no place, and let the rectangle
    already standing go on saying where the claim is going until the claim itself is drawn.

---

## Open questions

*Raised 2026-09-17.*

1. **Should the stream say when a call goes out?** The eight events say what came back, so the
   browser can draw the frontier but cannot honestly say how many proposals are in flight — three
   calls against one open claim show one rectangle (B2). A ninth event would fix it and would also be
   the first event that carries no decision, only activity, which is a different kind of thing to put
   on a stream. **Owner:** `spec/generation/streaming.md`, if anyone ever wants the count on screen.

2. **Does the map re-lay out once when the run finishes?** **Answered 2026-09-21: no — and the real
   question turned out to be a different one.**

   The measurement, taken on the coordinator's ten-claim run at 1600 × 1000, the size the whole
   interface is designed against: the stage is **1264 × 801**, the map is framed at **0.85** — the
   floor below which a tile would have to become a summary — and at that framing **six of the ten
   tiles are whole on the glass, four are wholly below it and none is cut**. No arrow points
   backwards, on this run or on the chapter's own, so the thing a re-layout would have tidied did not
   happen; what did happen is that **a third of the map was off the screen with nothing saying so**,
   which is far worse and is not a layout problem at all. A map that is cut with nothing saying so is
   read as a map that ends there, and for a causal map that is the worst thing it can be read as: the
   reader concludes the argument stops where the window does.

   So the answer is the one that costs the reader nothing: **the map is never re-laid out, and the
   stage says where it is cut.** A two-pixel rule in `--text-muted` sits at whichever edge has map
   beyond it and at no edge that has not — the same rule, the same weight and the same colour the
   panel beside it already uses for the same fact, drawn as the four sides of one box so a corner
   reads as a corner. The stage measures it about itself, because the two boxes are measured
   differently: a panel is scrolled and a stage is panned.

   Re-laying out would still move every tile once at the moment the reader starts reading, and it
   would still not put the four tiles on the glass — there is no zoom that fits ten tiles in 1264 ×
   801 and keeps them readable, which is exactly why the zoom floor exists. **Owner:** closed.

3. **What does an `insert` cost, and where does that show?** **Answered 2026-09-20 by
   [`spec/generation/streaming.md`](../generation/streaming.md), drawn 2026-09-21, and nothing is
   open.** The route answers a `DraftedInsert` — the edit and its own `Receipt` — and the cost is
   drawn beside the drafted claim by the same strip, with the same ten readings, that a generation's
   receipt is drawn by. What made it answerable was learning that an insert is **several** calls
   rather than one: the starting-claim shape drafts the reader's sentence, and then the ordinary walk
   proposes its arrows, one call each. A running total in the browser lost on two counts — it is a
   number added up by something other than the engine, and it vanishes on a page reload. **Owner:**
   closed. See B8.

4. **Where does a replayed run's pacing come from, and is it the same on every machine?**
   **Answered 2026-09-17 by `spec/generation/replay.md`, and nothing is open.** The delay is fixed on
   the **server** — an argument with a default the builder picks against a measurement, because a
   replay that races teaches a reviewer that the product is faster than it is — so two readers' replays
   are the same length. It is **one setting**, `KATALYST_REPLAY_PACE` in seconds, read once by
   `katalyst.settings` and never a field on the request: a client that could ask for a replay with no
   pause would let anyone with the network tab open skip the thing the recording exists to show. A
   pace of zero means no pause at all, which is the same question answered with a smaller number
   rather than a second switch beside it *(2026-09-21; it was a length and an `instant` flag)*. **The browser
   therefore paces nothing, waits on nothing, and has no pacing code at all** — it reads events as
   they arrive, which is the same thing it does live.

5. **How long is a refusal strip allowed to get?** Three refusals close an open claim and the caps
   bound the whole run, so the strip is bounded — but nothing says by what, and a run that refused
   twenty proposals would fill the dock and push the Inspector off the screen. Scrolling the strip is
   the obvious answer and it is also the answer that lets a reader miss a refusal. **Owner:** this
   chapter, once a real run has been watched.

1	/**
2	 * How big a tile is, and how far the map may be zoomed.
3	 *
4	 * The automatic layout has to know how big every tile is *before* the browser
5	 * has drawn one — it works out where the tiles go from the shape of the map
6	 * alone, and it cannot wait for measurements. So a tile's height is computed
7	 * here, from the claim's own content, by a plain function of plain data. That
8	 * keeps the layout a pure function of the map: the same map lays out the same
9	 * way every time, and the layout can be tested without a browser.
10	 *
11	 * The block heights below were measured once in the browser against the stored
12	 * example and are written down rather than read back at run time. If the tile's
13	 * stylesheet changes a line height or a gap, these change with it — and the
14	 * check for that is visual: a tile whose numbers are wrong has a gap at the
15	 * bottom or loses its last line.
16	 */
17	
18	import type { ClaimView } from "../world";
19	
20	/** How wide a tile is. Settled: 280 pixels, and measurable on any screenshot. */
21	export const TILE_WIDTH = 280;
22	
23	/**
24	 * How tall a tile may be, at the least and at the most.
25	 *
26	 * "Clamped height" is a floor and a ceiling with the content deciding in
27	 * between — not one height for every tile. The floor is what a tile holding
28	 * only a heading, a one-line claim and the three belief chips comes to; the
29	 * ceiling is what the densest tile in the stored example needs, which is the
30	 * hypothesis, with a three-line claim, a reason and two evidence clippings.
31	 * Both are on the eight-pixel grid.
32	 */
33	export const TILE_MIN_HEIGHT = 152;
34	/**
35	 * The ceiling was 272, which was what the densest tile in the stored example
36	 * needed **before a tile could carry badges**. A claim the reader supposed and a
37	 * later edit pushed back down says so on its own face, in one line that names
38	 * the edit responsible — *Supposed · Oct 1 → Retracted · Oct 2 · by "a confirmed
39	 * military strike on Iranian territory"* — and that line is three lines wide on
40	 * a 280-pixel tile. A ceiling that cut it off would hide the one thing the tile
41	 * is there to say.
42	 */
43	export const TILE_MAX_HEIGHT = 320;
44	
45	/* ---- The blocks a tile is made of, in pixels --------------------------- *
46	 * Measured in the browser, at the type sizes and line heights `tile.css`
47	 * sets. Every one of them is a height the browser actually produced. */
48	
49	/** Top and bottom padding together: twelve pixels each. */
50	const PADDING = 24;
51	
52	/** The gap between one block and the next. */
53	const GAP = 8;
54	
55	/** The heading row: what kind of claim this is, and when it settles. */
56	const HEADER = 21;
57	
58	/**
59	 * One line of the claim, at fifteen pixels over a line height of 1.35.
60	 *
61	 * Rounded up wherever it is used, never down: a line that is given a quarter of
62	 * a pixel less than it needs loses the bottom of its descenders.
63	 */
64	const CLAIM_LINE = 20.25;
65	
66	/**
67	 * The three belief chips: owner, number and range, with the rule above them.
68	 *
69	 * Measured at 69 in the browser, which is two pixels more than the 67 written
70	 * here before the chips grew their brightness bars. A row that is two pixels
71	 * short takes them off the bottom of the tile.
72	 */
73	const BELIEF_RAIL = 69;
74	
75	/**
76	 * The line a dead end prints saying why nothing here can be traded. Clamped to
77	 * two lines, and the only reason any tile prints for itself.
78	 */
79	const FINDING = 35;
80	
81	/** One evidence clipping, and the gap between two of them. */
82	const CLIPPING = 21;
83	const CLIPPING_GAP = 4;
84	
85	/**
86	 * One line of a claim's badges, and the hairline and padding the badges
87	 * themselves add to the block once.
88	 *
89	 * Thirteen pixels over a line height of 1.35 is 17.5, and each badge is drawn
90	 * with a hairline round it and a pixel of padding, which lifts a line box to
91	 * about 19. Both measured in the browser against the stored example's strike
92	 * branch, where the tallest badge line in the product — *Supposed · Oct 1 →
93	 * Retracted · Oct 2 · by "…"* — runs to three lines.
94	 */
95	const BADGE_LINE = 19;
96	const BADGE_PADDING = 4;
97	
98	/**
99	 * Roughly how many characters of a badge fit on one line.
100	 *
101	 * The badges flow across the same 256 pixels the claim wraps in, set at thirteen
102	 * pixels in the interface face, whose average character is about six and a half
103	 * pixels wide — so about thirty-eight. An estimate, and safe to be one for the
104	 * same reason the claim's is: the same number decides both how tall the tile is
105	 * and how much room the badges get, so the two cannot disagree.
106	 */
107	const BADGE_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE = 38;
108	
109	/** The separator drawn between one badge and the next, counted into the width. */
110	const BADGE_SEPARATOR = " → ";
111	
112	/**
113	 * Roughly how many characters of the claim fit on one line.
114	 *
115	 * The claim has 256 pixels to wrap in (244 on the two tiles whose outline cuts
116	 * into one side) and is set at fifteen pixels in the interface face, whose
117	 * average character is about eight pixels wide — so about thirty-three.
118	 *
119	 * It is an estimate, and it is safe to be one because the same number decides
120	 * both how tall the tile is and how many lines the claim is allowed to show.
121	 * The two cannot disagree: if the estimate is generous the tile has a little
122	 * room to spare, and if it is mean the claim stops one line earlier than it
123	 * might have. Neither case can push a word out of the box.
124	 */
125	const CLAIM_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE = 33;
126	
127	/** The most lines of the claim a tile ever shows. The rest lives in the panel. */
128	const CLAIM_MAX_LINES = 3;
129	
130	/**
131	 * How many lines of the claim this tile shows.
132	 *
133	 * @param claim The claim, in the words the map serves it in.
134	 */
135	export function claimLines(claim: string): number {
136	  const wanted = Math.ceil(claim.length / CLAIM_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE);
137	  return Math.min(CLAIM_MAX_LINES, Math.max(1, wanted));
138	}
139	
140	/**
141	 * How many lines this claim's badges take.
142	 *
143	 * Zero when it has none, which is every claim on a map nobody has edited.
144	 *
145	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
146	 */
147	export function badgeLines(claim: ClaimView): number {
148	  const badges = claim.badges ?? [];
149	  if (badges.length === 0) {
150	    return 0;
151	  }
152	  const characters =
153	    badges.reduce((sum, badge) => sum + badge.words.length, 0) +
154	    BADGE_SEPARATOR.length * (badges.length - 1);
155	  return Math.max(1, Math.ceil(characters / BADGE_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE));
156	}
157	
158	/** Round up to the eight-pixel grid the whole interface sits on. */
159	function toGrid(height: number): number {
160	  return Math.ceil(height / 8) * 8;
161	}
162	
163	/**
164	 * How tall this claim's tile wants to be, before the grid, the floor and the
165	 * ceiling are put to it.
166	 *
167	 * Kept apart from the bounding below because a height that has been bounded is
168	 * no longer a height you can do arithmetic with: two clamped numbers added
169	 * together can land outside the very bounds each of them was clamped into.
170	 *
171	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
172	 * @param badges How many lines the badges take. Passed in rather than read off
173	 *   the claim so that a caller reserving a line of its own for one badge can
174	 *   say so without building a second claim to say it with.
175	 */
176	function naturalHeight(claim: ClaimView, badges: number): number {
177	  const blocks: number[] = [HEADER, Math.ceil(CLAIM_LINE * claimLines(claim.claim)), BELIEF_RAIL];
178	
179	  // The foot of the tile: the reason a slot has no number, and the evidence
180	  // clippings. It is only there when there is something to put in it — and
181	  // when the badges arrive, having one of those will put it there too.
182	  const foot: number[] = [];
183	  if (claim.kind === "not_tradeable" && claim.beliefs.market.absence !== undefined) {
184	    foot.push(FINDING);
185	  }
186	  const clippings = claim.evidence.length;
187	  if (clippings > 0) {
188	    foot.push(CLIPPING * clippings + CLIPPING_GAP * (clippings - 1));
189	  }
190	  if (badges > 0) {
191	    foot.push(BADGE_LINE * badges + BADGE_PADDING);
192	  }
193	  if (foot.length > 0) {
194	    blocks.push(foot.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) + GAP * (foot.length - 1));
195	  }
196	
197	  return PADDING + blocks.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) + GAP * (blocks.length - 1);
198	}
199	
200	/** Put a wanted height on the eight-pixel grid, inside the floor and the ceiling. */
201	function bounded(natural: number): number {
202	  return Math.min(TILE_MAX_HEIGHT, Math.max(TILE_MIN_HEIGHT, toGrid(natural)));
203	}
204	
205	/**
206	 * How tall this claim's tile is: as tall as its own content, on the grid, and
207	 * inside the floor and the ceiling.
208	 *
209	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
210	 */
211	export function tileHeight(claim: ClaimView): number {
212	  return bounded(naturalHeight(claim, badgeLines(claim)));
213	}
214	
215	/**
216	 * How tall a box this claim's tile needs when how far its number moved gets a
217	 * line of its own.
218	 *
219	 * A tile is as tall as its own content, and the layout has to know that before
220	 * the browser has drawn one — so the height is a plain function of the claim.
221	 * This adds one thing to it: **the movement line is not packed in with whatever
222	 * the edits had to say.** On the busiest tile on the map, *Supposed · Oct 1 →
223	 * Retracted · Oct 2 · by "…"* already runs to three lines, and stringing a
224	 * reading on the end of that run pushes a line out of the box.
225	 *
226	 * The extra line is measured rather than written down — the words and the
227	 * reading are each measured on their own — so if the badge line height ever
228	 * changes, this changes with it.
229	 *
230	 * **The wanted height is worked out once and bounded once.** This was first
231	 * written as three already-bounded heights added and subtracted — with the
232	 * badges, with the reading, less the empty tile — and a bounded height is not a
233	 * number to do arithmetic with. The floor is added twice and taken off once, so
234	 * an ordinary tile is handed more room than its content needs (the busiest tile
235	 * on the stored example: 296 pixels reserved against the 280 it wants), and
236	 * nothing holds the total under the ceiling that each of the three was clamped
237	 * into.
238	 *
239	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
240	 */
241	export function roomFor(claim: ClaimView): number {
242	  const badges = claim.badges ?? [];
243	  const said = badges.filter((badge) => badge.movement !== true);
244	  const moved = badges.filter((badge) => badge.movement === true);
245	  const lines =
246	    said.length === 0 || moved.length === 0
247	      ? badgeLines(claim)
248	      : badgeLines({ ...claim, badges: said }) + badgeLines({ ...claim, badges: moved });
249	  return bounded(naturalHeight(claim, lines));
250	}
251	
252	/* ---- Zoom --------------------------------------------------------------- */
253	
254	/**
255	 * The smallest a word may be drawn on the reader's screen, in pixels.
256	 *
257	 * This is the rule the two zoom numbers below are worked out from, rather than
258	 * a number chosen for how it looked.
259	 */
260	const SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT = 11;
261	
262	/** The smallest and largest of the three type sizes, as `tokens.css` sets them. */
263	const SMALLEST_TEXT = 13;
264	const LARGEST_TEXT = 22;
265	
266	/**
267	 * Below this zoom a tile stops showing everything and shows a summary instead.
268	 *
269	 * **This was 0.6, and it is now eleven over thirteen — about 0.85.** The plan
270	 * settled on 0.6 before the type scale was settled, and the two turned out not
271	 * to fit together: a full tile's smallest words are thirteen pixels, so at 0.6
272	 * zoom they arrive on the glass at under eight, which breaks the rule that
273	 * nothing is ever drawn below eleven. Eleven over thirteen is the exact zoom at
274	 * which thirteen-pixel type lands at eleven pixels, so a full tile is only ever
275	 * shown at or above it, and below it the summary takes over — which sets every
276	 * word in the largest size and so clears the floor all the way down.
277	 */
278	export const SUMMARY_BELOW_ZOOM = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT / SMALLEST_TEXT;
279	
280	/**
281	 * How far out the map may be zoomed.
282	 *
283	 * The summary sets every word it draws in the largest of the three type sizes,
284	 * so the floor is the one zoom at which that size arrives at eleven pixels:
285	 * eleven over twenty-two, which is a half.
286	 */
287	export const SMALLEST_ZOOM = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT / LARGEST_TEXT;
288	
289	/** How far in the map may be zoomed. Past this a tile is merely large. */
290	export const LARGEST_ZOOM = 1.4;
291	
292	/**
293	 * The smallest type size a tile draws at this zoom, in pixels, before the map's
294	 * own scaling is applied.
295	 *
296	 * Multiply it by the zoom and you have what lands on the reader's screen, which
297	 * is what `layout.test.ts` checks never falls below eleven.
298	 *
299	 * @param zoom How far the map is zoomed in, where 1 is life size.
300	 */
301	export function smallestTextAt(zoom: number): number {
302	  return zoom < SUMMARY_BELOW_ZOOM ? LARGEST_TEXT : SMALLEST_TEXT;
303	}
304	
305	/** The smallest a word is ever drawn on the reader's screen, in pixels. */
306	export const TEXT_FLOOR = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT;
307	
308	/* ---- The first frame ----------------------------------------------------- */
309	
310	/** A rectangle in the map's own coordinates. */
311	export interface Box {
312	  readonly x: number;
313	  readonly y: number;
314	  readonly width: number;
315	  readonly height: number;
316	}
317	
318	/** How far the map is moved and zoomed to put something in front of the reader. */
319	export interface Frame {
320	  /** How far in the map is zoomed, where 1 is life size. */
321	  readonly zoom: number;
322	  /** How far the map is slid sideways, in screen pixels. */
323	  readonly x: number;
324	  /** How far the map is slid up or down, in screen pixels. */
325	  readonly y: number;
326	}
327	
328	/** The breathing room left around the map when it is framed, as a share of its size. */
329	const FIRST_FRAME_MARGIN = 0.04;
330	
331	/** The gap left at the edge when the map is too big to fit and has to be panned. */
332	const EDGE_GAP = 16;
333	
334	/**
335	 * How the map is framed the first time it is drawn — and the one promise that
336	 * framing makes: **the first frame never shows summary tiles.**
337	 *
338	 * The obvious rule is "fit the whole map". On a wide screen with the panel beside
339	 * it that lands at about 0.8 zoom on the stored example, which is under the zoom
340	 * at which a full tile's smallest words would be drawn below eleven pixels — so
341	 * every tile would open as a summary, and the reader's first sight of the
342	 * product would be seven boxes with a headline and three numbers in them.
343	 *
344	 * So the rule has a floor, and the floor is the same eleven-pixel rule
345	 * everything else here is derived from: frame the whole map if it fits at a
346	 * readable size, and if it does not, keep the readable size and start at the
347	 * map's beginning, on the left, where the hypothesis is. The reader pans to the
348	 * rest. A tile changes representation rather than shrinking; the same principle,
349	 * applied to the frame rather than to the tile.
350	 *
351	 * @param map Everything the frame has to hold, in the map's own coordinates.
352	 * @param canvas How much room there is for it, in screen pixels.
353	 */
354	export function firstFrame(map: Box, canvas: { width: number; height: number }): Frame {
355	  const fits = Math.min(
356	    canvas.width / (map.width * (1 + FIRST_FRAME_MARGIN)),
357	    canvas.height / (map.height * (1 + FIRST_FRAME_MARGIN)),
358	  );
359	  // Never blown up past life size, however small the map; never shrunk past the
360	  // point where a full tile would have to become a summary.
361	  const zoom = Math.max(SUMMARY_BELOW_ZOOM, Math.min(1, fits));
362	  const place = (room: number, start: number, size: number): number => {
363	    const shown = size * zoom;
364	    return shown <= room ? (room - shown) / 2 - start * zoom : EDGE_GAP - start * zoom;
365	  };
366	  return {
367	    zoom,
368	    x: place(canvas.width, map.x, map.width),
369	    y: place(canvas.height, map.y, map.height),
370	  };
371	}
372	
373	/** How many tiles a single layer may show before the rest are collapsed into one. */
374	export const TILES_PER_LAYER = 7;
375
