1	/**
2	 * Where a tile's ports are, and the one place that says so.
3	 *
4	 * A **port** is the socket a wire attaches to. Every tile has four: a pair on
5	 * the left edge for arrows arriving and a pair on the right for arrows leaving,
6	 * and in each pair the upper socket is for an arrow that fires once and stays
7	 * fired, the lower for one that only holds while its cause holds. What a wire
8	 * means is visible at the socket before you follow it anywhere.
9	 *
10	 * **A port's place is declared, not discovered — and that is the whole point of
11	 * this file.** The drawing library draws a wire between two ports, and left to
12	 * itself it finds out where a port is by measuring the page, through the very
13	 * same browser notification a busy browser drops. A wire whose ends were never
14	 * measured is not drawn at all: the map holds every claim, in its place, and
15	 * says nothing about how they are joined, which is the wrong picture of the
16	 * argument and a silent one. #37 met the same dropped notification as tiles
17	 * that never appeared and answered it by telling the library each tile's box
18	 * outright. A box is not a port, so the wire half of it was left over. This is
19	 * the rest of the same answer: told its box *and* where its ports sit, a tile
20	 * can have its wires drawn on the first frame with nothing measured at all.
21	 *
22	 * So every number a port has is written here, and written **once**. The tile
23	 * puts these numbers straight onto the element it draws; the drawing library is
24	 * handed the same numbers; `wires/plates.ts` places a plate against them. This
25	 * file must never read a port's place back off the screen, and nothing else may
26	 * write one down a second time — two places that have to agree are two places
27	 * that one day will not.
28	 */
29	
30	import type { NodeHandle } from "@xyflow/react";
31	import { Position } from "@xyflow/react";
32	import type { LinkMode } from "../world";
33	import { TILE_WIDTH } from "./geometry";
34	
35	/**
36	 * How wide a port is, in pixels — two steps of the eight-pixel grid the whole
37	 * interface sits on.
38	 *
39	 * It straddles the tile's edge, half of it inside and half outside, which is
40	 * why it is exactly twice the standoff below.
41	 */
42	export const PORT_WIDTH = 16;
43	
44	/** How tall a port is, in pixels: enough for one bar, a gap and a second bar. */
45	export const PORT_HEIGHT = 6;
46	
47	/**
48	 * How far past the tile's edge a wire attaches, in pixels.
49	 *
50	 * A wire that met the tile flush would have its last few pixels drawn under the
51	 * tile's own outline. Eight pixels clear is one step of the grid.
52	 */
53	export const PORT_STANDOFF = 8;
54	
55	/**
56	 * How far down a tile each of the two sockets sits, as a share of its height.
57	 *
58	 * A share rather than a number of pixels, because a tile is as tall as its own
59	 * content: the pair has to stay evenly spaced about the middle on a tile of any
60	 * height. Read by `wires/plates.ts` as well, which has to know where a wire
61	 * will start before a single wire has been drawn.
62	 */
63	export const DOWN_THE_TILE: Readonly<Record<LinkMode, number>> = {
64	  trigger: 0.38,
65	  sustain: 0.62,
66	};
67	
68	/** What a port is called. These four names are what a wire names its ends by. */
69	export type PortId = "in-trigger" | "in-sustain" | "out-trigger" | "out-sustain";
70	
71	/** One socket on the edge of a tile. */
72	export interface Port {
73	  /** Its name, which is what a wire asks for. */
74	  readonly id: PortId;
75	  /** Whether wires leave from it or arrive at it. */
76	  readonly kind: "source" | "target";
77	  /** Which edge of the tile it is on. */
78	  readonly edge: Position;
79	  /** Which kind of push attaches here. Also what the socket is drawn as. */
80	  readonly mode: LinkMode;
81	}
82	
83	/**
84	 * The four ports every tile has, in the order they are drawn.
85	 *
86	 * Arriving before leaving, and within each pair the one that fires once before
87	 * the one that holds — on each edge, the same top-to-bottom order its two
88	 * sockets are drawn in, so each side of the list reads the way that side of the
89	 * tile looks.
90	 */
91	export const PORTS: readonly Port[] = [
92	  { id: "in-trigger", kind: "target", edge: Position.Left, mode: "trigger" },
93	  { id: "in-sustain", kind: "target", edge: Position.Left, mode: "sustain" },
94	  { id: "out-trigger", kind: "source", edge: Position.Right, mode: "trigger" },
95	  { id: "out-sustain", kind: "source", edge: Position.Right, mode: "sustain" },
96	];
97	
98	/** A port's box, in the tile's own coordinates, with the tile's corner at zero. */
99	export interface PortBox {
100	  /** Its left edge. Negative on the left of a tile: the port straddles the edge. */
101	  readonly x: number;
102	  /** Its top edge. */
103	  readonly y: number;
104	  /** How wide it is. */
105	  readonly width: number;
106	  /** How tall it is. */
107	  readonly height: number;
108	}
109	
110	/**
111	 * Where this port sits on a tile of this height.
112	 *
113	 * The one piece of arithmetic in this file, and every other number here and in
114	 * the tile comes out of it. The box straddles the tile's edge so that the wire
115	 * attaches a clear eight pixels outside it, and it is centred on the share of
116	 * the height the socket sits at.
117	 *
118	 * @param height How tall the tile is — the same number the layout reserved for
119	 *   it and the same number the tile is drawn at. A tile that grew a line
120	 *   because an edit touched it moves its ports down with it, and this is where
121	 *   that happens.
122	 * @param port Which of the four.
123	 */
124	export function portBox(height: number, port: Port): PortBox {
125	  return {
126	    x: port.edge === Position.Left ? -PORT_STANDOFF : TILE_WIDTH + PORT_STANDOFF - PORT_WIDTH,
127	    y: height * DOWN_THE_TILE[port.mode] - PORT_HEIGHT / 2,
128	    width: PORT_WIDTH,
129	    height: PORT_HEIGHT,
130	  };
131	}
132	
133	/**
134	 * Every port of a tile this tall, in the shape the drawing library takes them.
135	 *
136	 * Handed over with the tile's box, so that the library knows where both ends of
137	 * every wire are before it has measured anything. It keeps measuring afterwards
138	 * and rebuilds these from what it measures; the numbers are the same numbers,
139	 * because the tile was drawn from them.
140	 *
141	 * @param height How tall the tile is.
142	 */
143	export function portsOf(height: number): NodeHandle[] {
144	  return PORTS.map((port) => ({
145	    id: port.id,
146	    type: port.kind,
147	    position: port.edge,
148	    ...portBox(height, port),
149	  }));
150	}
151	
152	/**
153	 * Which port a wire of this kind leaves from, and which it arrives at.
154	 *
155	 * @param mode Whether the push fires once or has to keep holding.
156	 */
157	export function portsForAWire(mode: LinkMode): {
158	  readonly source: PortId;
159	  readonly target: PortId;
160	} {
161	  return mode === "sustain"
162	    ? { source: "out-sustain", target: "in-sustain" }
163	    : { source: "out-trigger", target: "in-trigger" };
164	}

# Bundle the app's own layout code, then measure the two ways of laying a map out.

set -eu

here=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)

cd "$repo/frontend"
npx rolldown "$here/theAppsOwnLayout.ts" --format esm --file "$out/appLayout.mjs" >/dev/null 2>&1
node "$here/measure.mjs" "$out/appLayout.mjs"

19	const { pinsFor, readPositions, toElkGraph, assignLayers, capLayers, TILE_MIN_HEIGHT, TILE_WIDTH, tileHeight } = app;
20	const elk = new ELK();
21	
22	function eventsOfAKeptRun(path) {
23	  const run = JSON.parse(readFileSync(path, "utf8"));
24	  return run.events.map((payload) => {
25	    if ("generation_id" in payload && "hypothesis" in payload) return { event: "generation_started", ...payload };
26	    if ("proposition" in payload) return { event: "proposal_accepted", ...payload };
27	    if ("claim_in_words" in payload) return { event: "proposal_rejected", ...payload };
28	    if ("path" in payload) return { event: "verdict", ...payload };
29	    if ("dollars" in payload) return { event: "receipt", ...payload };
30	    if ("reason" in payload) return { event: "done", ...payload };
31	    return { event: "unknown", ...payload };
32	  });
33	}
34	
35	function eventsOfARecording(path) {
36	  return readFileSync(path, "utf8")
37	    .split("\n")
38	    .filter((line) => line.trim() !== "")
39	    .map((line) => JSON.parse(line))
40	    .filter((parsed) => parsed.event !== undefined)
41	    .map((parsed) => ({ event: parsed.event, ...parsed.data }));
42	}
43	
44	function growingClaim(proposition) {
45	  return {
46	    id: proposition.id,
47	    claim: proposition.claim,
48	    kind: proposition.kind,
49	    beliefs: {
50	      model: { absence: { code: "while_it_grows" } },
51	      user: { absence: { code: "not_said" } },
52	      market: proposition.beliefs?.market ? { p: proposition.beliefs.market.p } : { absence: { code: "not_quoted" } },
53	    },
54	    evidence: (proposition.evidence ?? []).slice(0, 2),
55	    badges: [],
56	  };
57	}
58	
59	function whatTheLayoutSees(claims, links, skeletons) {
60	  const ids = claims.map((claim) => claim.id);
61	  const { shown, overflows } = capLayers(assignLayers(ids, links));
62	  const drawn = new Set(shown.map((one) => one.id));
63	  const byId = new Map(claims.map((claim) => [claim.id, claim]));
64	  const tiles = shown.map((placed) => ({ id: placed.id, height: tileHeight(byId.get(placed.id)) }));
65	  for (const overflow of overflows) tiles.push({ id: `more-in-column-${overflow.layer}`, height: TILE_MIN_HEIGHT });
66	  const edges = links
67	    .filter((link) => !link.reflexive && drawn.has(link.source) && drawn.has(link.target))
68	    .map((link) => ({ id: link.id, source: link.source, target: link.target }));
69	  for (const box of skeletons) {
70	    tiles.push({ id: box.id, height: TILE_MIN_HEIGHT });
71	    if (box.after !== null && drawn.has(box.after)) {
72	      edges.push({ id: `holding-open:${box.after}->${box.id}`, source: box.after, target: box.id });
73	    }
74	  }
75	  return { tiles, edges, layers: new Map(shown.map((one) => [one.id, one.layer])) };
76	}
77	
78	async function walk(name, events) {
79	  console.log(`\n=== ${name} ===`);
80	  let claims = [];
81	  let links = [];
82	  let skeletons = [];
83	  let placed = new Map();
84	  let positions = new Map();
85	  const arrivedAt = new Map();
86	  const layerWhenPlaced = new Map();
87	  let pass = 0;
88	
89	  for (const event of events) {
90	    if (event.event === "generation_started") {
91	      skeletons = [{ id: "skeleton:hypothesis", after: null }];
92	    } else if (event.event === "proposal_accepted") {
93	      if (event.proposition) {
94	        claims = [...claims, growingClaim(event.proposition)];
95	        arrivedAt.set(event.proposition.id, event.at);
96	      }
97	      const there = new Set(claims.map((claim) => claim.id));
98	      links = [...links, ...(event.links ?? []).filter((link) => there.has(link.source) && there.has(link.target))];
99	      skeletons = (event.frontier ?? []).map((id) => ({ id: `skeleton:${id}`, after: id }));
100	    } else if (event.event === "proposal_rejected") {
101	      skeletons = (event.frontier ?? []).map((id) => ({ id: `skeleton:${id}`, after: id }));
102	    } else if (event.event === "done") {
103	      skeletons = [];
104	    } else {
105	      continue;
106	    }
107	    const { tiles, edges, layers } = whatTheLayoutSees(claims, links, skeletons);
108	    if (tiles.length === 0) continue;
109	    const holding = pinsFor(placed, tiles);
110	    if (tiles.some((tile) => placed.has(tile.id)) && holding.size === 0) {
111	      console.log(`  pass ${pass}: EVERY PIN DROPPED (a box changed height)`);
112	    }
113	    const answer = await elk.layout(toElkGraph(tiles, edges, holding));
114	    positions = readPositions(answer, holding);
115	    const heights = new Map(tiles.map((tile) => [tile.id, tile.height]));
116	    placed = new Map([...positions].map(([id, at]) => [id, { at, height: heights.get(id) ?? 0 }]));
117	    for (const [id, layer] of layers) if (!layerWhenPlaced.has(id)) layerWhenPlaced.set(id, layer);
118	    pass += 1;
119	  }
120	
121	  const finalLayers = new Map(assignLayers(claims.map((c) => c.id), links).map((one) => [one.id, one.layer]));
122	  console.log("  at  column when placed  column at the end  x (pinned)   claim");
123	  for (const claim of claims) {
124	    const at = positions.get(claim.id);
125	    console.log(
126	      `  ${String(arrivedAt.get(claim.id)).padStart(2)}  ` +
127	        `${String(layerWhenPlaced.get(claim.id)).padStart(16)}  ` +
128	        `${String(finalLayers.get(claim.id)).padStart(17)}  ` +
129	        `${String(Math.round(at?.x ?? -1)).padStart(10)}   ${claim.claim.slice(0, 58)}`,
130	    );
131	  }
132	  console.log("  arrows, as the pinned map draws them:");
133	  for (const link of links) {
134	    const from = positions.get(link.source);
135	    const to = positions.get(link.target);
136	    if (!from || !to) continue;
137	    const way = to.x < from.x ? "  <-- BACKWARDS" : to.x === from.x ? "  <-- same column" : "";
138	    console.log(
139	      `    ${String(Math.round(from.x)).padStart(6)} -> ${String(Math.round(to.x)).padStart(6)}` +
140	        ` (columns ${finalLayers.get(link.source)} -> ${finalLayers.get(link.target)})${way}`,
141	    );
142	  }
143	}
144	
145	await walk(
146	  "kept live run 18-24-54Z (Verify door)",
147	  eventsOfAKeptRun(`${REPO}/backend/.runs/hormuz-2026-09-21T18-24-54Z-01M32HVA1F3SX18H513M6GTNPT.json`),
148	);
149	await walk(
150	  "kept live run 18-31-02Z (Verify door)",
151	  eventsOfAKeptRun(`${REPO}/backend/.runs/hormuz-2026-09-21T18-31-02Z-01M32K42Z4036436TG96Q46RN0.json`),
152	);
153	await walk("the committed recording (Explore door)", eventsOfARecording(`${REPO}/backend/recordings/hormuz.jsonl`));
</system-reminder>

# ADR-0007: Build the Workbench canvas on React Flow v12 with ELK layered layout

## Context and Problem Statement

The canvas is the product's first screen (D1, the hero use case). It must render 10–60 rich proposition tiles with typed ports and wires (UX-1, UX-2), grow while the model streams (UX-8), show two worlds at once as a faded-overlay diff (FR-16), and look nothing like a component-library demo (D5(i), the template-UI veto). Which drawing and layout libraries give one developer the most beauty per hour without fixing the look?

## Decision Drivers

* D3, the Workbench aesthetic: the rigor of a visual-programming tool × tiles rich with evidence × a simulation game's sense of world state.
* D5(i): a template-looking UI is a veto condition — we own every pixel.
* UX-4: detail changes with zoom, and text never shrinks below 11 px.
* UX-5: automatic layout by default; a re-layout keeps the focused tile where it sits on screen.
* UX-7: exactly three animations; everything else is opacity in ≤120 ms.
* FR-16 / INV-4 (an intervention changes only what lies downstream of it): the diff must show *only* what moved, in one stable shared layout.
* NFR-7: 60 tiles render and re-layout in under 100 ms.

## Considered Options

=== motion budget ===
15:For an interface chapter the data model is the tokens. A **token** is one of the named values in `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css` — `--dir-up`, `--text-sm`, `--duration-fast` — which every component reads and which no component is allowed to replace with a raw colour, a raw pixel size or a raw duration of its own.
81:### The motion budget
91:Everything else is **an opacity change of at most 120 milliseconds** — `--duration-fast`, which already exists. Nothing scales, bounces, springs, loops or idles. Motion here communicates causality and provenance; it is never decoration, and never a way of making a finance tool feel alive.
93:Two new duration tokens, *proposed here*, since `tokens.css` carries only `--duration-fast`:
96:--duration-wave: 200ms;    /* one wire drawing itself */
97:--duration-stagger: 60ms;  /* the gap from one layer to the next */
100:**Under reduced motion the ordering survives and the tweening goes.** *Tweening* is the in-between frames that make a change look like a movement. When the operating system asks for less movement (`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`), `--duration-fast` and `--duration-wave` go to `0ms` and **`--duration-stagger` stays at 60 ms**. The wave becomes instant per-layer reveals, still in causal order; the number-roll becomes a swap; a ghost transition becomes a hard cut. The ordering *is* the causality, and removing it would remove the one thing the animation was for.
195:### INV-workbench.18 — The motion budget
197:For every animation in the app: it is one of the three budgeted moves, or it is an opacity change of at most 120 milliseconds. And for every one of them under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: every tween duration is `0ms`, and the ordering is unchanged.
199:- **Test:** `frontend/src/styles/__tests__/motionBudget.test.ts` › `test_no_duration_above_120ms_outside_the_three_budgeted_moves` and `test_reduced_motion_zeroes_every_tween_and_keeps_the_stagger`.

### The motion budget

Three animations, and no more.

| # | The move | What it does | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Propagation wave** | Wires draw in causal order, so the eye follows the chain the way the argument runs | about 200 ms each, staggered 60 ms down the map |
| 2 | **Branch creation** | The new lane's colour and name chip arrive, once, with no bounce | about 200 ms *(proposed here)* |
| 3 | **Belief number-roll** | A likelihood that changed rolls from the old figure to the new one | about 200 ms *(proposed here)* |

Everything else is **an opacity change of at most 120 milliseconds** — `--duration-fast`, which already exists. Nothing scales, bounces, springs, loops or idles. Motion here communicates causality and provenance; it is never decoration, and never a way of making a finance tool feel alive.

Two new duration tokens, *proposed here*, since `tokens.css` carries only `--duration-fast`:

```css
--duration-wave: 200ms;    /* one wire drawing itself */
--duration-stagger: 60ms;  /* the gap from one layer to the next */
```

**Under reduced motion the ordering survives and the tweening goes.** *Tweening* is the in-between frames that make a change look like a movement. When the operating system asks for less movement (`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`), `--duration-fast` and `--duration-wave` go to `0ms` and **`--duration-stagger` stays at 60 ms**. The wave becomes instant per-layer reveals, still in causal order; the number-roll becomes a swap; a ghost transition becomes a hard cut. The ordering *is* the causality, and removing it would remove the one thing the animation was for.

# B — a generated map that reads left to right

**Kent's line (3):** *"the boxes are a little chaotic and hard to read… apply a heuristic… avoid arrows that loop back around… legible left to right and top to bottom."*

Measured, not argued. Scripts: `plans/analysis/scripts/ux-round/B/` (`run.sh` builds a bundle of the app's **own** `elkGraph.ts`, `layers.ts` and `geometry.ts` and feeds three real streams through them; nothing is reimplemented).

---

## 1. What is true today

**One sentence: a claim's column is fixed the moment it is first drawn, and a claim can only ever move *right* as later arrows arrive — so the pin holds it left of where it belongs, and the arrow into it doubles back.**

The chain, with files:

* `frontend/src/graph/layers.ts:65` — `assignLayers` puts a claim one column right of the furthest-right claim that points at it. **Depth, not arrival order.** The brief's hypothesis that the column comes from arrival order is measured false.
* `frontend/src/graph/elkGraph.ts:240` — `readPositions`: *"a tile that had a position keeps that position, to the pixel."* The pin holds **x as well as y**. ELK is re-laying the whole map out correctly underneath and we put every placed tile back.
* `frontend/src/graph/elkGraph.ts:64` — `pinsFor` drops pins only when a box changes height. Measured over all three real streams: **0 pin drops in 25, 14 and 12 layout passes.** A tile reserves its belief rail while the map grows (`geometry.ts:177`, `BELIEF_RAIL` is unconditional), so `beliefs_propagated` changes no height and drops no pin. **INV-workbench.64's note that "every tile gains a chip and so every tile can change height" does not describe what happens** — the whole run is one unbroken chain of pins.

**The Verify door makes it acute.** The destination claim arrives at `at: 1` with **no incoming arrows** (`streaming-growth.md` B1; `api/generate.py`). Nothing points at it, so it lands in column 0 beside the hypothesis and is pinned there. On the kept run `18-24-54Z` it ends in column **3** with four arrows into it from claims placed to its right: three point right-to-left, one leaves a tile's right edge and returns into the left edge of a tile in the same column. Both kept live runs used the Brent destination — this *is* the hormuz/brent example Kent typed in, and the form's placeholder invites it (`plans/logs/m4-look/10-form-filled.png`).

**No generated map has a feedback arrow at all.** `reflexive` is false on every link in all three files, and a proposal has no `reflexive` field to set. The feedback rule is not implicated; every backwards arrow is an ordinary one.

**Why nobody saw it.** `streaming-growth.md` open question 2 — *"Does the map re-lay out once when the run finishes? **Answered 2026-09-21: no**"* — was measured on a **ten-claim Explore run**, and its words are *"No arrow points backwards, on this run or on the chapter's own."* True there. The Verify door has no end-to-end test, and every end-to-end test plays the recording, which is an Explore run.

### The table

Three real maps: the committed recording (18 claims, 19 arrows, Explore) and the two kept live runs (Verify). *backwards* = target strictly left of source; *same col.* = an arrow that leaves a right edge and returns into a left edge in the same column; *no fwd room* = the target is not a clear tile-width to the right.

| map | how it is laid out | backwards | same col. | crossings | wire px | tall px |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| recording, 18 claims | **incremental, pinned (today)** | 0 | 1 | 2 | **11 264** | **2 640** |
| | one whole layout | 0 | 0 | 5 | 5 567 | 2 010 |
| live 18-24-54Z, 6 claims | **incremental, pinned (today)** | **3 of 9** | 1 | 8 | 5 729 | 824 |
| | one whole layout | 0 | 0 | 2 | 2 973 | 491 |
| live 18-31-02Z, 4 claims | **incremental, pinned (today)** | **2 of 5** | 1 | 2 | 2 930 | 824 |
| | one whole layout | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 773 | 298 |

Turning `semiInteractive` off changes **nothing** on any of the three — identical output. What a reader would see move, over the whole run:

| policy | tile-moves | on how many arrivals | furthest | backwards left |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| today (pin x and y for ever) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 3 · 2 · 1 same-col |
| **settle once at the end** | 18 / 4 / 4 | **1** | 1 968 px | **0** |
| keep the row, free the column | 44 / 5 / 3 | 14 / 3 / 2 | 800 px | 0 |
| never pin | 159 / 45 / 25 | 18 / 10 / 7 | 1 066 px | 0 |

**Also measured, and someone else's to fix:** `<Controls position="bottom-left" />` (`Canvas.tsx:879`) floats at a 16 px margin, and `firstFrame` starts a map that does not fit at `EDGE_GAP = 16` from the left (`geometry.ts:332,364`) — the same 16 px, so the bottom-left tile sits under the zoom buttons (`plans/logs/evals-look/1280x800-02-inspector-way-in.png`). One line: the first frame must leave room for the controls.

---

## 2. Candidates

**A — The map settles once, when the likelihoods land. RECOMMENDED.**
`beliefs_propagated` already replaces the world wholesale, empties every rectangle and fills every chip at once. At that one event the pins are cleared and the finished map is laid out once, as a whole. On screen: while the run grows nothing moves, exactly as today; when the numbers land, the map arranges itself into its columns in the same frame the chips fill, and from then on nothing moves again.

```
growing            settled
[H]  [Brent]       [H] → [tankers] → [IEA] → [Brent] → [JETS]
  ↘ [tankers] ↗ ↖          (every arrow points right)
      (three arrows doubling back into Brent)
```

In code it is **the path that already exists**: `layoutRunner.ts:174` already clears `placed.current` and re-lays the whole map when `mapKey` changes. The settle is that same clearing, keyed on the phase going to `settled` instead. Roughly: one condition in `useLayout`, one field passed from `GenerationScreen`, ~20 lines. Costs one moment where every tile moves (18 of 18 on the recording, furthest 1 968 px). Risks: the motion budget (answered below) and a reader whose eye is on a tile — `setCenter` on the focused tile already runs on every re-layout after the first (INV-workbench.25), which is what makes it bearable.

**B — Keep the row, take the column from the layering every pass.** A tile keeps its y for ever and its x is always the column its causes put it in, so no arrow can ever point backwards, at any moment. Costs **44 tile-moves across 14 of the recording's arrivals** — movement while the map grows, which is the one thing the growing map promises never happens — and a longer map (7 853 px of wire against the settle's 5 567). It buys a correct picture *during* the run and pays for it with the promise that makes the map feel like it is arriving rather than reshuffling. Not recommended.

**C — Leave the layout alone and narrow the Verify door.** Do not draw the destination claim until an arrow reaches it. Cheapest, and it kills all five backwards arrows on the two live runs — but it leaves the recording's doubled wire and 630 px of dead height untouched, needs a new rule about which claim is a destination, and a rectangle standing where a claim already exists breaks INV-workbench.79 outright. Not recommended.

**Why A.** One rule, one moment, and it is the moment the spec already names as *"the one event that could move a tile a reader is already looking at"* (INV-workbench.64). It removes rather than guards: no heuristic, no per-arrow special case, no second layout policy to keep true. And it is the only candidate that leaves *"nothing already placed moves while the map grows"* standing word for word.

---

## 3. Decisions it touches, and the amendment for each

| Where | Today | The dated amendment |
|---|---|---|
| `streaming-growth.md` **open question 2** | *"Answered 2026-09-21: no — the map is never re-laid out"* | *Reopened and re-answered 2026-09-22, on three real maps rather than one. The 2026-09-21 answer was measured on a ten-claim Explore run, where no arrow points backwards. On a Verify run the destination claim arrives with no causes, is pinned in column 0 and gains four of them: three arrows then point right-to-left. **The map is laid out once more, when `beliefs_propagated` arrives, and never at any other moment.*** |
| `streaming-growth.md` **anti-pattern 7** | *"Do not re-layout the map **while it grows** to make the picture tidier"* | Unchanged in substance; add: *"— and settle it once when the likelihoods land, because the picture a pin leaves behind is not the picture the argument makes."* |
| **INV-workbench.64** | *"every tile that had a position before the event has the identical position after it"*, with `beliefs_propagated` named as an event in it | *…for every event **but `beliefs_propagated`**, which clears every pin and lays the finished map out once. Its note that every tile gains a chip and so can change height is **measured false** (`geometry.ts:177` — the belief rail is reserved while the map grows), which is why the settle has to be asked for rather than inherited.* New test: **`test_no_arrow_points_backwards_once_the_run_has_settled`**. |
| `layout-and-zoom.md` **B3** | *"Pinning holds positions inside a column. It does not hold column assignment"* | Add: *"It holds the x coordinate too — which is how a claim can end up drawn in a column it no longer belongs to, and an arrow into it drawn pointing backwards. That is what the settle exists for."* |
| **INV-workbench.79**, **INV-workbench.22**, **diff-view.md INV-workbench.40** | — | **Untouched, and the plan says so.** `.79` is about boxes waiting for places and rectangles waiting for claims; every rectangle is down before the settle. `.22` is about a claim added strictly downstream. `.40` is about toggling A ⇄ A′ in one coordinate space — *"nothing re-positions when a branch is opened"* is a different promise, and opening a branch already drops every pin (`layoutRunner.ts:174`) under `layout-and-zoom.md` B7. |
| **Motion budget**, `color-motion-type.md` / INV-workbench.18 | three animations, everything else opacity ≤ 120 ms | No fourth animation. The settle is a **cut**: tiles take their new places in one frame, under the `--duration-fast` opacity change that is already the rule for everything else. Under reduced motion it is already a hard cut. |
| **Decision record** | 0007 chose ELK and pinning | **A new record, `proposed`, written first** — next free number is **0023** (0016–0022 are accepted on `adr/05-sound-numbers` and `adr/06-the-trade` and not yet on `main`; confirm before numbering). Amends 0007 with a dated line. |

Covered by something already decided, no question needed: the settle re-frames on the focused tile (INV-workbench.25 / UX-5); it is a cut, not an animation (the budget already says so); the branch promise is untouched.

---

## 4. What waits on Kent

1. **May the map arrange itself once, when the numbers land?** Today, typing the Hormuz sentence with *Brent below $68* as the destination leaves three arrows pointing right-to-left into the Brent tile, which sits beside the hypothesis in column 0. **Recommended: yes** — at the moment every chip fills, the map lays itself out whole; 18 tiles move once on the recording and then nothing moves again, and no arrow points backwards. Alternative: leave it, and the map Kent saw is the map a reviewer sees.
2. **Does it move, or does it cut?** **Recommended: cut** — every tile is in its new place in the same frame the chips fill, with nothing but the 120-millisecond opacity change already in the budget. Alternative: tween the tiles into place over ~200 ms, which is a fourth budgeted animation and needs INV-workbench.18 amended.
3. **Is the map acceptable *during* the run?** The settle fixes the finished picture; for the ten minutes the run takes, the Brent tile still sits in column 0 with arrows doubling back into it. **Recommended: accept it** — the alternative measured at 44 tile-moves across 14 arrivals and costs the promise that a growing map never reshuffles. Alternative: settle on every arrival.

---

## 5. The work, as pull requests

Two deep (R13). Number is the coordinator's to assign; written `NN` here.

**`adr/NN-the-map-settles` — docs, bottom, targets `main`.** Record 0023 `proposed`; the five amendments in §3; the table above quoted into `streaming-growth.md` open question 2 as dated evidence. **~1 session.**

**`feat/NN-the-settle` — on it.** `layoutRunner.ts` takes a `settleOn` key beside `mapKey` and clears the pins once when it changes; `GenerationScreen` passes the phase. Tests:

* **`test_no_arrow_points_backwards_once_the_run_has_settled`** — *the test that would have caught this.* No browser: replays the two kept live streams and the recording through the real `assignLayers` / `toElkGraph` / `readPositions` and asserts every non-feedback arrow's target sits strictly right of its source. It fails on `main` today, three times.
* `test_nothing_moves_until_the_likelihoods_land` — the existing `test_a_tile_keeps_its_place_when_a_later_tile_arrives` (`frontend/src/stream/__tests__/growth.test.ts:136`) split in two at `beliefs_propagated`.
* `frontend/e2e/generate.spec.ts:204` and `frontend/e2e/lateLayout.spec.ts:218` both assert the first tile has not moved **at the end of the run** — both must move their reading to before `beliefs_propagated`, or they fail by design.
* Record 0008 tier 2 (timing-sensitive): the no-browser test above, one cold browser run, the build. **~1.5 sessions.**

Nothing blocks it: it touches no server file, no fixture and no prompt, so it is clear of the shape freeze (R5) and of stack 05's engine lane.

---

1. **May the map arrange itself once, when the numbers land?** Today, typing the Hormuz sentence with *Brent below $68* as the destination leaves three arrows pointing right-to-left into the Brent tile, which sits beside the hypothesis in column 0. **Recommended: yes** — at the moment every chip fills, the map lays itself out whole; 18 tiles move once on the recording and then nothing moves again, and no arrow points backwards. Alternative: leave it, and the map Kent saw is the map a reviewer sees.
2. **Does it move, or does it cut?** **Recommended: cut** — every tile is in its new place in the same frame the chips fill, with nothing but the 120-millisecond opacity change already in the budget. Alternative: tween the tiles into place over ~200 ms, which is a fourth budgeted animation and needs INV-workbench.18 amended.
3. **Is the map acceptable *during* the run?** The settle fixes the finished picture; for the ten minutes the run takes, the Brent tile still sits in column 0 with arrows doubling back into it. **Recommended: accept it** — the alternative measured at 44 tile-moves across 14 arrivals and costs the promise that a growing map never reshuffles. Alternative: settle on every arrival.

---

## 5. The work, as pull requests

Two deep (R13). Number is the coordinator's to assign; written `NN` here.

**`adr/NN-the-map-settles` — docs, bottom, targets `main`.** Record 0023 `proposed`; the five amendments in §3; the table above quoted into `streaming-growth.md` open question 2 as dated evidence. **~1 session.**

**`feat/NN-the-settle` — on it.** `layoutRunner.ts` takes a `settleOn` key beside `mapKey` and clears the pins once when it changes; `GenerationScreen` passes the phase. Tests:

* **`test_no_arrow_points_backwards_once_the_run_has_settled`** — *the test that would have caught this.* No browser: replays the two kept live streams and the recording through the real `assignLayers` / `toElkGraph` / `readPositions` and asserts every non-feedback arrow's target sits strictly right of its source. It fails on `main` today, three times.
* `test_nothing_moves_until_the_likelihoods_land` — the existing `test_a_tile_keeps_its_place_when_a_later_tile_arrives` (`frontend/src/stream/__tests__/growth.test.ts:136`) split in two at `beliefs_propagated`.
* `frontend/e2e/generate.spec.ts:204` and `frontend/e2e/lateLayout.spec.ts:218` both assert the first tile has not moved **at the end of the run** — both must move their reading to before `beliefs_propagated`, or they fail by design.
* Record 0008 tier 2 (timing-sensitive): the no-browser test above, one cold browser run, the build. **~1.5 sessions.**

Nothing blocks it: it touches no server file, no fixture and no prompt, so it is clear of the shape freeze (R5) and of stack 05's engine lane.

---

## 6. What I would not do

* **Not re-layout on every arrival** — 159 tile-moves on the recording.
* **Not pin the row and free the column** — 44 mid-run moves; it buys correctness during the run by spending the promise that makes the map feel like it is arriving.
* **Not add a *Tidy the map* command.** One rule over two: after the settle nothing moves, so there is nothing to tidy.
* **Not touch the feedback-arrow rule.** No generated map has one; a rule about a case that cannot arise is a rule that will be wrong when it does.
* **Not change the ELK options.** Measured: `semiInteractive` off is byte-identical on all three maps. The options are not the problem; the pin is.
* **Not fix the zoom buttons here.** Measured and handed on: the first frame and the controls both use 16 px, so they overlap. It belongs with whoever owns the stage.

---

**Five lines for the coordinator**

1. The mechanism: a claim's column is frozen the moment it is first drawn, and a claim can only move *right* as arrows arrive — so the pin holds it left and the arrow doubles back (`elkGraph.ts:240`, `layers.ts:65`); measured **0 pin drops** across all three real runs.
2. Worst on the Verify door Kent used: the destination arrives at `at: 1` with no causes, is pinned in column 0, ends in column 3 — **3 of 9 arrows point backwards** on one kept live run, 2 of 5 on the other.
3. One whole layout at the end fixes every one: **0 backwards, 0 same-column, wire length halved** (11 264 → 5 567 px on the recording), at the cost of one moment where 18 tiles move.
4. Recommend **the map settles once, at `beliefs_propagated`** — the moment INV-workbench.64 already names; it is a cut, not an animation, so the motion budget is untouched; ~2.5 sessions over two pull requests.
5. Three questions for Kent: may it settle · cut or tween · is the mid-run picture acceptable. And one finding to hand on: `streaming-growth.md` open question 2 was answered on a ten-claim Explore run and is false on a Verify run.

# B — a generated map that reads left to right

**Kent's line (3):** *"the boxes are a little chaotic and hard to read… apply a heuristic… avoid arrows that loop back around… legible left to right and top to bottom."*

Measured, not argued. Scripts: `plans/analysis/scripts/ux-round/B/` — `run.sh` bundles the app's **own** `elkGraph.ts`, `layers.ts` and `geometry.ts` and feeds three real streams through them. Nothing is reimplemented.

---

## 1. What is true today

**A claim's column is frozen the moment it is first drawn, and a claim can only move *right* as later arrows arrive — so the pin holds it left of where it belongs and the arrow into it doubles back.**

* `layers.ts:65` — `assignLayers` puts a claim one column right of the furthest-right claim pointing at it. **Depth, not arrival order.** The brief's arrival-order hypothesis is measured false.
* `elkGraph.ts:240` — `readPositions`: *"a tile that had a position keeps that position, to the pixel."* The pin holds **x as well as y**. ELK re-lays the map out correctly underneath and we put every placed tile back.
* `elkGraph.ts:64` — `pinsFor` drops pins only when a box changes height. Measured: **0 pin drops in 25, 14 and 12 passes.** A tile reserves its belief rail while the map grows (`geometry.ts:177`), so `beliefs_propagated` changes no height and drops no pin. **INV-workbench.64's note that "every tile gains a chip and so every tile can change height" does not describe what happens** — the whole run is one unbroken chain of pins.

**The Verify door makes it acute.** The destination claim arrives at `at: 1` with **no incoming arrows** (`streaming-growth.md` B1). Nothing points at it, so it lands in column 0 beside the hypothesis and is pinned there. On the kept run `18-24-54Z` it ends in column **3** with four arrows into it from claims placed to its right. Both kept live runs used the Brent destination — this *is* the hormuz/brent example Kent typed, and the form's placeholder invites it (`plans/logs/m4-look/10-form-filled.png`).

**Not the feedback rule.** `reflexive` is false on every link in all three files, and a proposal has no `reflexive` field to set. Every backwards arrow is an ordinary one.

**Why nobody saw it.** `streaming-growth.md` open question 2 — *"Does the map re-lay out once when the run finishes? **Answered 2026-09-21: no**"* — was measured on a **ten-claim Explore run**, and says *"No arrow points backwards, on this run or on the chapter's own."* True there. The Verify door has no end-to-end test, and every end-to-end test plays the recording, which is an Explore run.

### The table

*backwards* = target strictly left of source. *same col.* = an arrow leaving a right edge and returning into a left edge in the same column.

| map | laid out | backwards | same col. | crossings | wire px | tall px |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| recording, 18 claims, Explore | **incremental, pinned (today)** | 0 | 1 | 2 | **11 264** | **2 640** |
| | one whole layout | 0 | 0 | 5 | 5 567 | 2 010 |
| live 18-24-54Z, 6 claims, Verify | **incremental, pinned (today)** | **3 of 9** | 1 | 8 | 5 729 | 824 |
| | one whole layout | 0 | 0 | 2 | 2 973 | 491 |
| live 18-31-02Z, 4 claims, Verify | **incremental, pinned (today)** | **2 of 5** | 1 | 2 | 2 930 | 824 |
| | one whole layout | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 773 | 298 |

Turning `semiInteractive` off changes **nothing** on any of the three — identical output. What a reader would see move over a whole run:

| policy | tile-moves | on how many arrivals | furthest | backwards left |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| today | 0 | 0 | 0 | 3 · 2 · 1 same-col |
| **settle once at the end** | 18 / 4 / 4 | **1** | 1 968 px | **0** |
| keep the row, free the column | 44 / 5 / 3 | 14 / 3 / 2 | 800 px | 0 |
| never pin | 159 / 45 / 25 | 18 / 10 / 7 | 1 066 px | 0 |

**Handed on, not mine:** `<Controls position="bottom-left" />` (`Canvas.tsx:879`) floats at a 16 px margin and `firstFrame` starts a map that does not fit at `EDGE_GAP = 16` from the left (`geometry.ts:332`) — the same 16 px, so the bottom-left tile sits under the zoom buttons (`plans/logs/evals-look/1280x800-02-inspector-way-in.png`). The first frame must leave room for the controls.

---

## 2. Candidates

**A — The map settles once, when the run stops. RECOMMENDED.** Whatever takes the run past *growing* — the likelihoods landing, a break, a stream that ends early — the pins are cleared there and the map is laid out once, whole. On screen: while it grows nothing moves, exactly as today; then the map arranges itself into its columns in the same frame the chips fill, and never moves again.

```
growing                          settled
[H]  [Brent]                     [H] → [tankers] → [IEA] → [Brent] → [JETS]
  ↘ [tankers] ↗ ↖  (three arrows          every arrow points right
        doubling back into Brent)
```

**The path and the moment both already exist.** `layoutRunner.ts:174` already clears the pins and re-lays the map when `mapKey` changes. `GenerationScreen.tsx:285` already passes `frameAgainOn={finished ? "the run stopped" : undefined}`, and `Canvas.tsx:463` already re-frames the whole map at that moment — there is an end-to-end assertion for it (`generate.spec.ts:200`: *"The map is framed once more when it stops — the one moment nothing on it is moving"*). The settle is that same flag dropping the pins as well: one condition in `useLayout`, one key beside `mapKey`, ~20 lines. One comment stops being true — `Canvas.tsx:471`, *"Nothing lays a finished map out again."* Costs one moment where every tile moves (18 of 18, furthest 1 968 px); `setCenter` on the focused tile already runs on every re-layout after the first (INV-workbench.25), which is what makes it bearable.

**B — Keep the row, take the column from the layering every pass.** No arrow ever points backwards, at any moment. Costs **44 tile-moves across 14 of the recording's arrivals** — movement while the map grows, which is the one thing the growing map promises never happens — and a longer map (7 853 px of wire against 5 567). Not recommended: it buys a correct picture during the run by spending the promise that makes the map feel like it is arriving.

**C — Leave the layout alone; do not draw the Verify destination until an arrow reaches it.** Cheapest, kills all five backwards arrows on the live runs — but leaves the recording's doubled wire and 630 px of dead height, invents a rule about which claim is a destination, and a rectangle standing where a claim already exists breaks INV-workbench.79 outright. Not recommended.

**Why A.** One rule, one moment, and it is the moment the spec already names as *"the one event that could move a tile a reader is already looking at."* It removes rather than guards: no heuristic, no per-arrow case, no second layout policy. It is the only candidate that leaves *"nothing already placed moves while the map grows"* standing word for word.

---

## 3. Decisions it touches, and the amendment for each

| Where | The dated amendment |
|---|---|
| `streaming-growth.md` **open question 2** (*"Answered 2026-09-21: no"*) | *Reopened 2026-09-22, on three real maps rather than one. The earlier answer was measured on a ten-claim Explore run, where no arrow points backwards. On a Verify run the destination arrives with no causes, is pinned in column 0 and gains four: three arrows then point right-to-left. **The map is laid out once more, at the moment the run stops — the same moment it is already re-framed — and never at any other.*** |
| `streaming-growth.md` **anti-pattern 7** (*"Do not re-layout the map while it grows"*) | Unchanged in substance; add *"— and settle it once when the run stops, because the picture a pin leaves behind is not the picture the argument makes."* |
| **INV-workbench.64** | *…every tile that had a position keeps it, for every event **while the map is still growing**. When the run stops, every pin is cleared and the finished map is laid out once. Its note that every tile gains a chip and so can change height is **measured false** (`geometry.ts:177`), which is why the settle must be asked for rather than inherited.* New test: **`test_no_arrow_points_backwards_once_the_run_has_settled`**. |
| `layout-and-zoom.md` **B3** (*"Pinning… does not hold column assignment"*) | Add *"It holds the x coordinate too — which is how a claim ends up drawn in a column it no longer belongs to, and an arrow into it drawn pointing backwards."* |
| **INV-workbench.79**, **.22**, **diff-view.md .40** | **Untouched, and the plan says so.** `.79` is about boxes waiting for places; every rectangle is down before the settle. `.22` is about a claim added strictly downstream. `.40` is about toggling A ⇄ A′ in one coordinate space — *"nothing re-positions when a branch is opened"* is a different promise, and opening a branch already drops every pin (`layoutRunner.ts:174`) under `layout-and-zoom.md` B7. |
| **Motion budget** / INV-workbench.18 | No fourth animation. The settle is a **cut**: tiles take their new places in one frame, under the `--duration-fast` opacity change already the rule for everything else. Under reduced motion it is already a hard cut. |
| **Decision record** | One new record, `proposed`, written first — next free number is **0023** (0016–0022 are accepted on `adr/05-sound-numbers` and `adr/06-the-trade`, not yet on `main`; confirm before numbering). Amends 0007 with a dated line. |

Covered already, no question needed: the settle re-frames on the focused tile (INV-workbench.25 / UX-5); it is a cut, not an animation; the branch promise is untouched.

---

## 4. What waits on Kent

1. **May the map arrange itself once, when the run stops?** Today, typing the Hormuz sentence with *Brent below $68* as the destination leaves three arrows pointing right-to-left into a Brent tile sitting beside the hypothesis. **Recommended: yes** — at the moment every chip fills, the map lays itself out whole; 18 tiles move once and then nothing moves again, and no arrow points backwards. Alternative: leave it, and the map Kent saw is the map a reviewer sees.
2. **Does it move, or does it cut?** **Recommended: cut** — every tile in its new place in the same frame the chips fill, with nothing but the 120 ms opacity change already budgeted. Alternative: tween over ~200 ms, a fourth animation, needing INV-workbench.18 amended.
3. **Is the map acceptable *during* the run?** The settle fixes the finished picture; for the ten minutes a run takes, Brent still sits in column 0 with arrows doubling back. **Recommended: accept it** — the alternative measured at 44 tile-moves across 14 arrivals and costs the promise that a growing map never reshuffles.

---

## 5. The work, as pull requests

Two deep (R13). Stack number is the coordinator's; written `NN`.

**`adr/NN-the-map-settles` — docs, bottom, targets `main`.** Record 0023 `proposed`; the amendments in §3; the tables quoted into open question 2 as dated evidence. **~1 session.**

**`feat/NN-the-settle` — on it.** `layoutRunner.ts` takes a settle key beside `mapKey` and clears the pins once when it changes; `GenerationScreen.tsx:285` passes the same `finished` flag it already passes as `frameAgainOn`, so the settle and the re-frame are one moment and cannot come apart. Tests:

* **`test_no_arrow_points_backwards_once_the_run_has_settled`** — *the test that would have caught this.* No browser: replays the two kept live streams and the recording through the real `assignLayers` / `toElkGraph` / `readPositions` and asserts every non-feedback arrow's target sits strictly right of its source. It fails on `main` today, three times.
* `test_nothing_moves_until_the_run_stops` — `growth.test.ts:136` split in two at the settle.
* `generate.spec.ts:204` and `lateLayout.spec.ts:218` both read the first tile's place **after** the run has stopped and assert it has not moved. Both must take that reading earlier, or they fail by design.
* Record 0008 tier 2 (timing-sensitive): the no-browser test above, one cold browser run, the build. **~1.5 sessions.**

It touches no server file, no fixture and no prompt, so it is clear of the shape freeze (R5) and of stack 05's engine lane.

---

## 6. What I would not do

* **Re-layout on every arrival** — 159 tile-moves on the recording.
* **Pin the row and free the column** — 44 mid-run moves; buys correctness during the run by spending the promise.
* **Add a *Tidy the map* command** — one rule over two; after the settle nothing moves, so there is nothing to tidy.
* **Touch the feedback-arrow rule** — no generated map has one.
* **Change the ELK options** — measured: `semiInteractive` off is identical on all three maps. The options are not the problem; the pin is.
* **Fix the zoom buttons here** — measured and handed on; it belongs with whoever owns the stage.

---

**Five lines for the coordinator**

1. The mechanism: a claim's column is frozen the moment it is first drawn and can only move *right* as arrows arrive — so the pin holds it left and the arrow doubles back (`elkGraph.ts:240`, `layers.ts:65`); **0 pin drops** across all three real runs.
2. Worst on the Verify door Kent used: the destination arrives at `at: 1` with no causes, is pinned in column 0, ends in column 3 — **3 of 9 arrows point backwards** on one kept live run, 2 of 5 on the other; the feedback rule is not involved.
3. One whole layout at the end fixes every one: **0 backwards, 0 same-column, wire halved** (11 264 → 5 567 px on the recording), at the cost of one moment where 18 tiles move.
4. Recommend **the map settles once when the run stops** — the moment `GenerationScreen.tsx:285` already re-frames at; a cut, not an animation, so the motion budget is untouched; ~2.5 sessions over two pull requests.
5. Three questions: may it settle · cut or tween · is the mid-run picture acceptable. One finding to hand on: `streaming-growth.md` open question 2 was answered on a ten-claim Explore run and is false on a Verify run.
